p: Marginalia is a self-hosted writing tool for long-form fiction co-written with large language models. You write the instructions for each part of the story, the model writes the prose, and Marginalia keeps everything around it in order: the branching story, the world lore, the summaries that keep long books within the model's context, and the prompt settings that shape the style.

It runs in your browser - as a desktop app on your own computer, or as a small server for you and your friends - and works with any OpenAI-compatible API: OpenAI, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM, and others.
The story editor
Books with branching stories – regenerate or swipe a part, branch from any point, move around the story tree, edit the generated text. See Books.
Lorebooks – world and character notes put into the prompt only when they matter: by book tags, text or regex filters, nested lorebooks. SillyTavern world info can be imported. See Lorebooks.
Templates and macros - prompts are Handlebars templates with SillyTavern-compatible macros, so imported lore keeps working. See Templates & macros.
Summaries – older parts are condensed so long books fit into the context window. See Summaries.
Any OpenAI-compatible model - including reasoning models, with per-model limits and switchable generation settings. See Inference providers and Protocols.
Backups - per-book backups with restore and copy, and full database backups on a schedule. See Book backups and Database backups.
Multiple users – each with their own books, lore, and models; administrators manage users, backups, and cleanup. See Administration.
Published books – a read-only reading view you can share. See Publishing & viewer.
Extensions - plugins add features at runtime: chapter markers, lorebook history, AI reviews, side questions to the model. See Extensions.

Marginalia is open source under the MIT License. Pictures used in the screenshots of this manual are credited on the Credits page. Releases are on GitHub; bugs and ideas go to the issue tracker.

This part of the manual is for people who write with Marginalia and for those who run it for others. It explains every screen and setting, from installing Marginalia and connecting a model to branching a story, building a lorebook and backing up the database. You don't need to know anything about programming; a few pages about templates go deeper for those who want to fine-tune what is sent to the model.
If you are new, start with Getting started – it takes you from installation to the first generated part of a book in a few minutes.

You write a story together with a large language model. For each part of the story you say what should happen - the scene, whose point of view, who is present, a few sentences of instructions - and the model writes the prose. Before every part Marginalia builds the prompt for the model from:

Installation

Marginalia has no model of its own. It needs an OpenAI-compatible API to write text: a cloud service (OpenAI, OpenRouter...) or a model running on your own computer (llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM...). Have the API address and an API key ready (a local server that doesn't need one works without a key, see Adding a provider).
Marginalia runs in your browser. You can install it in two ways:
One person on one computer
Port 8080, normally behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS
Server (Docker)
Several users, or access from other devices
Install Marginalia: desktop app or server.
Create the administrator account on the first start.
Follow the quick start: connect a model, create a protocol and write the first part of a book.
The desktop app is a self-contained version of Marginalia for one computer. It brings its own Java runtime and server, listens only on your computer and opens in your default browser.
Download the archive for your system from the releases page. Two variants are published for every system:
Archive
Contents
marginalia-version-os-arch-app
The app: Marginalia.app on macOS, Marginalia.exe on Windows, bin/Marginalia on Linux

A portable folder started with a script, with command line options
Builds are available for Windows x64, macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Linux (x64 and arm64).
Extract the archive and move Marginalia.app to Applications.
Open it. The app is not signed yet, so the first time macOS refuses to open it. Right-click the app and choose Open, or run:
Extract the archive.
Run Marginalia\Marginalia.exe.
SmartScreen may warn about an unknown publisher. Click More info → Run anyway.
Run Marginalia/bin/Marginalia.
Run bin/marginalia (bin\marginalia.bat on Windows).
Starting takes a few seconds. Marginalia then opens in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765 and shows the first start dialog.

p: While it runs, Marginalia shows an M icon in the system tray (in the menu bar on macOS). Its menu has two items:
Open Marginalia - opens Marginalia in the browser again, for example after you closed the tab.
Quit Marginalia - stops the server. Closing the browser tab does not stop Marginalia.
Starting the app a second time while it already runs only opens it in the browser.

To move Marginalia to another computer, quit it and copy the .marginalia folder (with secret.key, which decrypts the saved API keys). Before larger changes, make a database backup.
The portable launcher accepts these options:
With --host 0.0.0.0 (or another address) Marginalia is reachable from your network over plain HTTP. For access from other devices use the server behind HTTPS instead.

c:
marginalia --port 8765        # port to listen on; a free one is picked when 8765 is taken
marginalia --host 127.0.0.1   # address to listen on
marginalia --home /path       # directory that holds the .marginalia folder (default: your home directory)
marginalia --no-browser       # don't open the browser
marginalia --no-tray          # no tray icon; stop with Ctrl+C
marginalia --help

p: Quit Marginalia, replace the app (or the portable folder) with the new version and start it again. Your data stays in .marginalia and is upgraded automatically on the first start; before the structure of the database changes, Marginalia saves a copy of it in db-backups. Extensions are built for one Marginalia version, so update them at the same time (see Managing extensions).
Delete the app or the folder. To remove your data as well, delete the .marginalia folder.
Run Marginalia as a server when several people use it, or when you want to open it from other devices. Every user gets their own books, lorebooks, inference providers and protocols.
Docker with Docker Compose
About 512 MB of memory for Marginalia
For access over the internet: a domain and a reverse proxy with HTTPS (see below)

The first docker compose up builds the image from source, which takes a few minutes. Marginalia then listens on port 8080. Open http://server:8080 and create the administrator account (see First start).

c:
git clone https://github.com/Enerccio/Marginalia.git
cd Marginalia
docker compose up -d

p: Instead of building from source you can use the image published with each release (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). In docker-compose.yml, replace the build: block with image::
latest is the newest release, edge the development version, and 1.1.0 (or 1.1) pins a release. The rest of the file stays the same.

c:
services:
  marginalia:
    image: ghcr.io/enerccio/marginalia:latest

p: Everything is set in docker-compose.yml:
Setting
What it does
ports
8080:8080 publishes Marginalia on port 8080 of the host. Use 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 when only a reverse proxy on the same host should reach it.
volumes

./data holds the database, backups and extensions. Keep it, and include it in your server backups. It is created on the first start if it doesn't exist; on start the container makes it owned by the user Marginalia runs as inside the container (jetty), so the files in it belong to that user's ID on the host.
-Xmx512m
Maximum memory. Raise it (for example -Xmx1g) for many users or very large books.
After changing the file, apply it with docker compose up -d.

c:
services:
  marginalia:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: marginalia-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/var/marginalia/.marginalia
    environment:
      - JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Duser.home=/var/marginalia -Xms256m -Xmx512m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/marginalia/.marginalia/heapdump.hprof

p: Passwords and login cookies are sent with every request. Over plain HTTP anyone on the way can read them. Put Marginalia behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS.
The Save login option on the login screen also needs HTTPS: its cookies are marked secure, so browsers keep them only on HTTPS connections.
Marginalia updates the page over a WebSocket connection, so the proxy must forward WebSocket upgrades. Examples for marginalia.example.com:
Caddy gets the certificate and forwards WebSockets automatically.

Failed logins are throttled per user and per client address (after 30 failures from one address, logins from it are refused for a growing time, up to 15 minutes). Marginalia only believes the X-Forwarded-For header of a proxy you name: without it, all users appear to come from the proxy's address and 30 failures from anyone block everybody for a while. Keep the header in the proxy configuration (as above) and add -DtrustedProxies=address or range of the proxy to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in docker-compose.yml. A proxy on the Docker host reaches the container from the Docker network, normally 172.16.0.0/12; several entries are separated by commas. The throttling is kept in memory, restarting Marginalia clears it.
c: marginalia.example.com { reverse_proxy localhost:8080 }

server { listen 443 ssl; server_name marginalia.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/marginalia.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/marginalia.example.com/privkey.pem; client_max_body_size 100m; # uploads of backups and extensions location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 1h; # long generations keep the connection open } }

p: Inside the container, localhost is the container itself, not the server. To use a model server that runs on the Docker host (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio...), use the address http://host.docker.internal:port/v1 in the inference provider. On Linux, add this to the service in docker-compose.yml:
The model server must also listen on an address the container can reach, not only on 127.0.0.1.

c:
extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"

p: With the prebuilt image use docker compose pull and docker compose up -d instead.
The database is upgraded automatically when the new version starts. Marginalia saves a copy of the database before it changes its structure, but make a database backup of your own first as well.

c:
git pull
docker compose up -d --build

p: rebuild.sh (Linux, macOS) and rebuild.bat (Windows) in the repository root do the update for you; run them from the root, for example from a cron job or a scheduled task. They fetch the remote branch and do nothing when there is nothing new (--force rebuilds and restarts anyway, for example after changing docker-compose.yml). Otherwise they stop the container, git pull, rebuild the bundled plugins and copy their JARs into data/extensions (replacing the installed ones), and start the container again with docker compose up -d --build. If any step fails, the script stops with a message.

The Docker image doesn't contain the extensions, and they have to be built from the same source as the application. You don't need Java or Maven for that: marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml builds all of them in a container, which builds the application first and then every plugin, and copies the JARs into marginalia/plugins/build:

The first build takes several minutes (it downloads the dependencies of the application). Then copy the JARs into data/extensions and restart Marginalia, or load them in Admin → Extensions (see Extensions). rebuild.sh / rebuild.bat do the copying for you, so on a server that uses them the plugins are always updated together with the application.

c:
docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml run --rm plugins

p: The image has a Docker health check: docker ps shows (health: starting) while Marginalia starts (up to two minutes), then (healthy). It is unhealthy when port 8080 stops answering with a page. Docker does not restart an unhealthy container by itself; use the status for your monitoring or an auto-heal tool.

c: docker compose logs -f marginalia

p: When Marginalia starts with an empty database, it asks for the first account instead of showing the login screen. This account is the administrator: it can manage users, database backups, cleanup and extensions.
Creating the administrator account
Fill in:
Field
Username
The login name.
Full Name
The name shown in the application.
Password, Repeat password
Both must match. Marginalia also accepts an empty password - never leave it empty on a server, anyone could then log in as administrator with just the user name.
Administrator is checked and cannot be changed for the first account. Click OK. The page reloads and shows the login screen.
Remember the password. There is no password reset by e-mail. Other administrators can set a new password for a user in Admin → Users.
Log in with the new account. With Save login checked, the browser stays logged in for 30 days. This works only over HTTPS or on 127.0.0.1 with the desktop app (see Server).

From a fresh installation to the first generated part of a story. It assumes Marginalia is installed and you are logged in as the administrator.
Open the Inference Providers tab and click Add Inference Provider.
Enter a Name, for example OpenRouter - Claude.
In General Settings, set Max Context Size to the context size of the model, for example 32000, and Max Response Tokens to the longest part you want, for example 2000.
In Per Type Settings, enter the OpenAI URL (it ends with /v1) and the Api Key (leave it empty for a local server that has no key), click Refresh and pick the Model.
Click OK.
The fields are described in Inference providers, with URLs for common services.
Open the Protocols tab and click Add Protocol.
Enter a Name, for example Default.
Leave Max Context Tokens and Max Reply Tokens empty - the limits of the inference provider are used.
Click OK.
See Protocols.
Open the Settings tab and pick the new provider as Default Model and the new protocol as Default Protocol. Click Save. New books then start with both, so you don't have to select them every time.
Default model and protocol in Settings
Open the Books tab and click Add Book.
Enter the name of the book. The book opens.
On the About tab, check that Model and Protocols are set (they come from your defaults), and add a Description of the story if you want to.
Open the Story tab.
Click + in the bottom right corner. The New Turn Instructions panel opens.
Describe what should happen in Instructions, for example:
A lighthouse keeper on a remote island finds a message in a bottle addressed to her, dated fifty years in the future. Introduce her and the island. About 800 words.
Scene Setting, POV Character and Present Characters are optional; fill them in to give the model more direction.
Click Generate. The text appears while the model writes it. The red Stop button (in place of +) interrupts the generation.
The first generated part
Click + again for the next part. Each part can be edited, regenerated or swiped for an alternative version from its menu (☰); see Story editor and Branches & story tree.

Marginalia has a layout made for phones. You write, edit and regenerate parts, read and tweak lorebooks and manage your models from the phone browser, but the phone layout is not a copy of the desktop one: it is simpler, a few things are missing and not every extension works in it. This page lists the differences.
For reading a book on a phone, there is also the viewer, which is made for it.

l: When the phone layout is used
p: Marginalia looks at the width of the browser window when the page loads. Narrower than 768 pixels gives you the phone layout, anything wider the normal workspace.
Tablets and phones in landscape mode are usually wider than 768 pixels and get the desktop layout.

The layout is not switched while you work. If you turn the phone or tablet on its side, or resize the window, the layout stays as it was until you reload the page. So to get the larger desktop layout on a tablet or a turned phone, turn it and reload; to go back to the phone layout, turn it back and reload again.
A narrow desktop browser window gets the phone layout too, which is handy to try it.
Like the desktop, the phone layout can be added to the home screen like an app (Install app / Add to Home Screen in the browser menu).

The tabs on the left are replaced by a drawer. Tap the menu button in the top bar to open it, tap a tab to switch to it. The tab you are on fills the whole screen and its name is shown in the top bar.
The phone workspace with the drawer open

The drawer has the same tabs as the desktop - Books, Lorebooks, Settings, Protocols, Inference Providers, Agents (only for users who may use agents), Resources and Trash - and the Language selector, Change Password and Logout at the bottom. Extensions may add buttons, but only to the places they know on the phone, see Extensions.
While the Settings tab has unsaved changes, the drawer is locked as on the desktop: save or discard first.

The book list is one column. Above it are the name filter, the tag filter and the sort buttons (Last Modified, Created, Name; tap the active one again to reverse the order), then Add Book and refresh. Each book has two buttons: the pencil opens it, the trash deletes it (into the Trash).
The book list on a phone

The phone shows a reduced lorebook editor. You can pick a lorebook, enable or disable it and its entries, and edit the content of an entry. Everything else is shown as text only: name, order, tags, filtering and insertion mode, negative tags and note. You cannot create, delete, import or export lorebooks, or add entries. Use the desktop for that, see Lorebooks.
The same reduced editor is used in the Lorebook tab of a book.
A lorebook on a phone
The button next to the Enabled check box opens Search and replace for the entries of the lorebook, see Entries.
Search and replace of a lorebook on a phone

Settings are the same as on the desktop, only laid out in a narrow column. The one thing missing is Import Backup as New Book. To bring a backup file back on the phone, create a book, use Import Backup in its Backups tab and restore it there, or import it as a new book on the desktop.
Protocols and Inference Providers list each entry as text with the edit and delete buttons next to it. The editing dialogs are the desktop ones.
Resources is the desktop tab, not adapted to the phone.
Trash shows each deleted object as a card (name, type, when it was deleted). The explanation of the trash is behind the i button. Restoring works as described in Trash.
The inference providers on a phone, with the info button of a shared provider
The trash on a phone

Opening a book shows it full screen. The close button is the ✕ in the top corner, and the tabs - About, Prompts, Lorebook, Story, Branch view, Backups - are one row you scroll sideways. They do the same as on the desktop (see Books), with their fields in one column.
The story tab is one column of parts. The differences from the story editor:

The outline (and the tabs extensions add next to it, such as the Author's Note) is in a drawer. Open it with the button at the top left.
The Summaries button and the settings menu (⚙, with Change Styles For Text, Search and replace and Export story) are in the top bar, not at the bottom.
The + button for a new part is at the bottom.
Search and replace opens the same window as on the desktop, with the fields and buttons below each other:

The first is the part's menu (edit, regenerate, swipe, branch, show prompt, images, summary, delete); the second opens a popup with what the desktop shows in the column on the right of a part: the ids, model, protocol, tokens, words and the turn details.

To reach Marginalia from a phone it has to run as a server: the desktop app listens on your computer only.

An inference provider is a connection to a model: the API address, the API key, the model and its limits. Every book uses one provider. You can have as many as you like, for example a large cloud model for the story and a small local one for experiments, and switch a book between them at any time.
Providers belong to your account. Other users don't see them or their API keys. API keys are stored encrypted (see The data folder).

Adding a provider needs the permission Create own models, which an administrator gives you (administrators always have it, see Permissions). Without it you can only use the providers the administrators share with you; the Add Inference Provider button is not shown.

How long to wait for the API to answer, and for more text once it started writing. The default is 300. Reasoning models may need minutes before the first text; a request that hears nothing for this long fails with a timeout message (the thinking of a model counts as text, so a model that keeps thinking is not cut). How often a request is repeated when the API answers with a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx), or cannot be reached. Marginalia keeps Max Response Tokens of the context free for the response and fills the rest with the prompt: templates, lorebook entries and summaries are counted in, and the oldest parts of the story that don't fit are left out. Marginalia fills the context only up to Max Context Size minus Max Response Tokens. If the finished prompt is still bigger than that (for example because an extension added text, or the token count was off), a warning shows the estimated sizes before the request is sent. The request is sent anyway; the API may reject it or cut the prompt.
The warning about a prompt that may not fit

Reasoning models think before they answer. With Enable Reasoning checked, Marginalia sends the chosen Reasoning Effort (None, Low, Medium or High) to the API as reasoning_effort. More effort usually means better planned text, but slower and more expensive responses. Not every API supports the parameter; if requests fail with reasoning enabled, turn it off.

When the model returns its reasoning (as reasoning_content or reasoning, depending on the server), it is shown above the generated part under View Reasoning. The reasoning is not part of the story and is not sent back to the model.
Reasoning of a generated part
Reasoning counts toward the response: give reasoning models a larger Max Response Tokens, or the text may be cut off after a long reasoning.
Marginalia counts tokens to decide how much of the story fits into the prompt. It asks the provider when it can, and tries these methods in order:
the OpenAI token counting endpoint (/v1/responses/input_tokens),
the /tokenize endpoint of llama.cpp,
the /tokenize endpoint of LiteLLM,
the /v1/messages/count_tokens endpoint of LiteLLM (for Anthropic models),
a local estimate with the OpenAI tokenizer.

The first method that works is used from then on. The local estimate is close for most models but not exact, which is another reason to keep Max Context Size a little below the real limit. Providers of the type Extension count as their extension says; the Google Gemini one uses the local estimate.

On an installation with several users, an administrator can share a provider: check Shared with all users in the provider's dialog (the checkbox is only there for administrators). Every user then finds it in the Model list of their books and in their Inference Providers tab, marked Shared Yes. They can use it, but they can't open it, see its address or API key, change it or delete it; only its owner can. Books, backups and restores that refer to a shared provider keep working for everybody who can see it.
A shared provider in the Inference Providers tab of a regular user
Sharing a provider lets the other users spend the owner's quota with the service. To stop users from adding providers of their own, so that they can only use the shared ones, see Users and providers.

A token limit has a reset (daily, weekly from Monday, or monthly; calendar periods in the time zone of the server) and three limits that can each be left empty for no limit: the tokens sent, the tokens generated, and both together (in total). Whichever is reached first stops the user until the next reset. If all three are set, the sent plus the generated limit must not be below the total (the total could then never be reached), otherwise the dialog refuses to save. For example a total of 100,000 with 100,000 sent and 20,000 generated is fine, a total of 100,000 with 20,000 sent and 10,000 generated is not.
Adding a limit

An administrator can limit what each user may do with a shared provider. In the Inference Providers tab, the administrator who owns a shared provider has a Limits button (a user with a lock) in its row, which opens a table with the limits that were set. Add limit creates a new one: pick the user and a limit type.

Every user sees the shared providers in their tab as read-only rows. The info button (the circle with an i) of a shared provider shows their own limit: what they used in this period, the limits and when they reset. When a limit is reached, the story editor, summaries and extensions show an error instead of sending the request.
Limit type
Meaning
No limit (the same as having none).
Not available

Nothing is reset on a timer: the tokens used start from zero when the user uses the provider (or looks at their limits) for the first time in a new period. The size of a request is known before it is sent, so a request whose prompt would take the user over the sent or in total limit is refused (the prompt is measured with Marginalia's own estimate, which can differ a little from the service's count). The tokens generated are not known in advance: they are counted when the request ends, so the user is stopped only once the limit is reached and the last response can go over it. Users without a limit in the table are not limited.
The limits a user sees, with what was used in this period
The limits of a shared provider
The user can not use the provider; anything that would send a request to it fails.
The user can use up to the given number of tokens per period.

To keep the generated tokens from going over, check Hard limit (only available with a limit of the generated tokens). A request reserves room for the largest response it allows (the Max Response Size of the provider, or the lower one of the protocol), and with a hard limit it is refused when that reserve does not fit into what is left of the generated limit. So a hard limit lower than the response size of the provider refuses every request; the table and the user's info show hard next to such a limit. The hard limit only covers the generated tokens, the in total limit can still be gone over by the last response.
Token limit
Unlimited

The Inference Providers tab shows, per provider, the Tokens sent (the prompt, "prefill") and Tokens generated (the response, reasoning included) you have used with it, added up over all your books, summaries and extensions. A shared provider has a count of its own for each user, so you see only your part.
Administrators also get a Usage per user button on the tab, which opens a table with what every user has used of every provider (tokens sent, tokens generated, requests and the time of the last one).
Usage per user

The numbers are what the service reports. A service that doesn't report them (or a request you stop in the middle) is counted with the local estimate described in Token counting, so those numbers are approximate. A request that fails before any text arrived isn't counted. Unless an administrator has set a limit for you on a shared provider, the counts are only informational.

Marginalia asks the service to report the token counts (stream_options with include_usage). To change that for a provider, put your own stream_options into its Additional Parameters, for example {stream_options: {include_usage: false}}: it replaces what Marginalia sends, and the local estimate is used.

A protocol is a set of generation settings: the sampling parameters (temperature, top P and penalties) and, optionally, its own context and reply limits. The inference provider says which model writes; the protocol says how.

Protocols are separate from providers, so you can keep a few of them, such as a cautious one and a creative one, and switch a book between them without touching the connection. Like providers, protocols belong to your account.
The Protocols tab
Every sampling parameter has an Enable checkbox. A parameter that is not enabled is not set by Marginalia, and the model uses its own default. Enable only what you want to change.
Field
Frequency Penalty
Max Context Tokens
Max Reply Tokens
Name
Nucleus sampling: the model picks only from the most likely words whose probabilities add up to this value (0-1). 0.9-0.95 is a common choice.
Open the Protocols tab and click Add Protocol. Existing protocols are edited with the pen button and deleted with the trash button.
Optional. The longest response. Empty uses the provider's Max Response Tokens.
Optional. Total tokens for prompt and response of books using this protocol. Empty uses the provider's Max Context Size.
Penalizes words by how often they already appeared, which reduces repetition. Usually 0-1.
Penalizes words that already appeared at all, which pushes the model to new topics. Usually 0-1.
Presence Penalty
Randomness of the text. Lower (around 0.7) is more focused and predictable, higher (1.0 and more) is more varied and surprising.

A protocol with Max Context Tokens 128 000 used with a provider of 32 000 gets 32 000: the provider is what the service (or the administrator who shares it) allows.

Marginalia keeps room for the response free and fills the rest of the context with the prompt: templates, lorebook entries, summaries and as much of the story as fits. With a context of 32 000 tokens and responses of up to 2 000 tokens, the prompt gets 30 000 tokens. The response limit is also sent to the API (max_completion_tokens).

Use the protocol limits to keep prompts shorter than the model allows, for example to make long books cheaper and faster with a large-context cloud model, or to keep responses shorter for some books. The protocol limits are also used for summaries of books with this protocol.
Leave both empty unless you need them: the provider's values then apply, and when you change the provider of a book, its limits come along.

A book is one story. You give it instructions part by part, the model writes the text, and the book keeps everything that goes with it: the story tree with all its branches, the prompts that shape the style, the lorebook with the world and characters, summaries and backups.
A book in the story editor
A book is made of parts. Each part is one answer of the model, written from the instructions you gave for it (scene, point of view character, characters present and what should happen).

Parts form a tree. Usually you just continue the story, but you can also write another version of the last part, or go back and continue differently from any earlier part. Each path from the beginning to an end is a branch. The branch you are working on is the active branch; the story editor shows it, and only its parts are sent to the model. See Branches & story tree.
A book without parts opens on About, a book with parts on Story. All changes are saved right away; there is no Save button. Exit closes the book.

Pictures are not part of the text. The model never sees them, they are not in the prompt, they do not count as tokens and they do not change the summaries. They are also not Markdown: a ![](...) link written in the text is not a picture of the part, use Images instead.
Good to know:

Regenerate keeps the pictures of the part, also when the generation fails. Swipe writes a new part (a new version next to the old one), which starts without pictures. Branch Story copies the pictures to the new part.
Pictures belong to your account. In the viewer only you see them; readers of a published book see the text only. A book is published as it is: pictures are not made public with it.
A backup remembers which pictures a part has, but not the picture files. Restoring a backup into another account or another installation gives parts without their pictures.

Removing a picture from a part only takes it off the part. The file stays and is still listed in Resources, where you can download, replace or delete it. Deleting it there removes it from every part that uses it. The file itself stays in the data folder.

The Summaries button in the bottom bar (left of the settings menu ⚙) opens the overview of the summaries of the branch, where they can be edited, deleted and merged into meta summaries. The tooltip of the button shows how many tokens the summaries in use take in the prompt. See Summaries.

The settings menu (⚙) in the bottom bar has Change Styles For Text. It switches the text of the parts between the normal look of the application and a book-like reading style (the one the viewer uses). The setting is saved per book.

In this style paragraphs are justified and long words are hyphenated automatically, using the dictionary of the book's Language (set on the About tab). Hyphenation is done by the browser; for a few rare languages it has no dictionary and the text is simply not hyphenated.

The settings menu (⚙) also has the checkable Highlight Generated Text. While it is on, the text that is still the way the model wrote it is highlighted in every part, so what you added or rewrote stands out. Marginalia keeps the original text of each part and compares it with the current one word by word. A part you never edited is highlighted whole; a part you wrote yourself has nothing highlighted. The switch is not saved: it is off again when the page is opened anew.
Parts that existed before this feature count wholly as generated, because the original text was not kept for them. The highlight is available in the desktop view only, not in the phone view.
Highlighted generated text and the settings menu

Next to the menu below the story there is a command line: type / to see the commands, pick one and press Enter (or the play button) to run it. What a command returns is shown in a small window above the line. See Commands for how to write arguments, what the help shows and how to stop a command that takes a while. The command line is only in the story tab of the desktop layout so far.

A replace in the text a summary describes would make the summary outdated. With Revalidate all summaries on, Marginalia works out again the check value of every summary of the book (those of all branches too, those the replace did not touch, and those that were outdated before), so all of them are valid afterwards. That also turns an outdated summary valid without its text being looked at, so use it when you know the summaries still say the right thing.
A text is found only in the case you typed it (John does not find john). Off: the case does not matter. Locked while Search by regex is on.
After the replace every summary of the book is valid again, see below.
All branches are searched, otherwise only the active one.

The settings menu (⚙) also has Search and replace, which changes a word, a name or a phrase in the whole story at once. The window has a Search for and a Replace with field and these options:
The settings menu with Search and replace
The summaries are searched and changed too.

The table lists every part of the story and every summary that has a match, with its type and id. Open a row to see the matches in it: the text around the match as it is and as it will be after the replacement. A match or a replacement that is too long to show is written as [searched text] or [replace text].
The warning about summaries that would become outdated

When the search is done, the fields and options are locked and the Replace button is enabled. Search again forgets what was found and unlocks the window, so you can change the search. Replace changes the story: the window is frozen completely (even Stop does not work) until it is done, and then it is empty again. Replaced parts are marked as edited, as if you had edited them yourself.

With a regular expression the case is always taken as typed, start it with (?i) to ignore it. Press Search (the button on the right of the fields; on the phone below them). The progress bar shows how far it is and Stop next to it interrupts it. Nothing is changed by a search.

With the option off only the summaries the search covers are brought up to date. Those it does not cover (summaries of branches that are not searched, which share their earlier parts with the active branch; or all of them when summaries are not searched) become outdated. If there are such summaries, Marginalia tells you how many and asks whether to go on. A summary that was outdated already stays so.
The settings menu (⚙) also has Export story, which saves the active branch as a text, Markdown, HTML, Word, PDF or EPUB file. See Exporting a book.
For each new part Marginalia sends:
The master template as the system message: role, lorebook entries, point of view, tense, style and summaries. The jailbreak prompt of the inference provider, if enabled, comes first.

The previous parts of the active branch as the model's own earlier answers - as many as fit into the context limit, newest first. Older parts that don't fit are left out (unless a summary covers them).
The user prompt with the instructions for the new part.
Show Prompt on any part shows exactly what was sent. See Book prompts for the templates.
Marginalia never makes you throw a version away. Every alternative you try is kept as a branch of the story, and you can go back to any of them.
Each part continues the part before it. When a part has more than one continuation, the story splits: each path from the first part to an end is a branch.
The active branch is the one the story editor shows and continues. Only its parts are sent to the model; the other branches don't influence the story.
There are three ways to get a new branch:
What happens
The old version
Swipe (last part)
The model writes another version of the last part.
Stays as a separate branch.
Branch Story (any part)
The story continues from this part on a new branch.
The parts after it stay on the old branch.
Regenerate (last part)
The model writes the last part again, in place.
Replaced - no branch is created.
Swipe and Regenerate are in the menu of the last part only; Branch Story is in the menu of every part.

l: Trying another version of the last part
p: When you don't like the last part, choose Swipe in its menu. The model writes the part again from the same turn details, and the new version becomes the end of the active branch. The previous version is kept as its own branch; you can switch back to it in the Branch view.
To change what should happen before trying again, open Turn Details of the last part and edit the instructions.
Use Regenerate alone when you don't need the old version: it overwrites the part.

To take the story in a different direction from an earlier point, open the menu of that part and choose Branch Story. Marginalia copies the part to a new branch and makes it the end of the active branch, so the story editor now ends with that part. Continue with + as usual.
The parts that came after it are not lost: they stay on the old branch.
Summaries of the copied part are copied with it.
The Branch view tab shows the whole story tree. Each part is a card with its date, scene setting, characters present and instructions; hover over a card to see all its details.
The story tree
The parts of the active branch are highlighted, and its last part is marked.

Click the last part of another branch to make that branch active. The book switches to the Story tab and shows it. Only the ends of branches can be clicked; to continue from a part in the middle, use Branch Story.
Long stretches without any branching (more than 20 parts) are collapsed into a block showing the first ten and the last ten parts. Click the block to show all parts.

The box above the tree searches the text of all branches of the book, not only the active one. Type what you are looking for and press Enter or click Search; the box remembers your last searches, pick one from the list to repeat it. The x in the box clears the search.
A part matches when its text contains every word you typed, in any order: lighthouse key finds the parts that have both words. Put words in double quotes to look for a phrase: lighthouse key.
Use * for any characters: light* finds lighthouse and lightning. Other characters, including %, _ and \, are searched as they are.
Upper and lower case do not matter. For accented letters, a word typed in lower case also finds the same word in UPPER CASE or Capitalized (žluťoučký finds Žluťoučký and ŽLUŤOUČKÝ).
Only the text of the parts is searched, not the instructions, scene setting or the lorebook. Parts that you deleted are not searched.
The branch view with a search

Every part that matches is highlighted in orange and shows the text around the match; the line above the tree says how many parts were found. Long stretches that would be collapsed are opened when they contain a match. The search stays until you clear it or close the book window, and the highlighting is updated when you come back to the tab.
Click Show in story in a highlighted part to read it:
When the part is on the active branch, the book switches to the Story tab and scrolls to it.

When it is on another branch, that branch becomes the active branch first. It ends at the nearest end of a branch below the found part (the newer one when there are two), so the story editor shows the story up to the found part and what followed it. The book then switches to the Story tab and scrolls to the part, which flashes briefly.
Switching the branch is the same as clicking the end of a branch in the tree: nothing is lost, the previous branch stays as it was and you can go back to it from the tree.
Delete in the menu of a part removes just that part. The parts after it move up and continue from the part before it. To remove a whole branch, delete its parts from the end.
The word and token counts on the About tab show both the whole book (all branches) and the active branch.

The Prompts tab of a book holds the texts Marginalia builds the prompt from: two templates, the narrative settings and the summary prompts. They decide the voice of the book far more than the model settings do.
The Prompts tab

Every field is optional. An empty field uses the default from Settings → Templates (see Account & settings), and when that is empty too, the built-in default. The default is shown in grey in the empty field.
So set what all your books share in Settings, and only what is special to a book on its Prompts tab. Changes are saved as you type.

Each field has a hints popover with Insert Default Template, which copies the default into the field as a starting point for your own version. The template fields also list the Available Template Variables and the Available Macros.

All templates can also use the SillyTavern-compatible macros, such as {{user}} (the point of view character), {{description}} (the book's description), {{random::a::b}}, {{getvar::name}} and {{setvar::name::value}}. See Templates & macros for the full syntax and the macro reference.

c: {{#sceneSetting}}Current Location & Time: {{.}}{{/sceneSetting}}

p: The master template becomes the system message, the first message of the prompt. The built-in default has these blocks:
System role - the model is an author continuing the story.
World & lore context - the activated lorebook entries (backgroundLore).
Writing style & mechanics - point of view, tense, style, and general prose rules.
Summary of story so far - the summaries.
If the inference provider has a jailbreak prompt enabled, it is put before the master template.

The user prompt is the last message of the prompt: the request for the part to write. It is filled from the New Turn Instructions (or the Turn Details for Regenerate and Swipe). The built-in default asks for the next section with the point of view character, location, characters present and the plot instructions, followed by rules: no new characters unless requested, follow the instructions, keep the continuity, and output only the story text.
Lorebook entries with the insertion mode Before User Prompt are put right before it; see Entries & activation.

l: How the prompt is put together
p: Earlier parts are sent as the model's own answers, so it continues them in the same voice. When the story is longer than the context limit, the oldest parts are left out first; summaries keep them in the story in condensed form.
Show Prompt in the menu of any part shows the exact prompt that part was written from.

c:
system     jailbreak (if enabled) + master template
user       [ Generate story. ]
assistant  part #1
user       [ Generate more story. ]
assistant  part #2
...        (as many earlier parts as fit)
user       lore "Before User Prompt" + user prompt

p: Put rules that apply to every part (no new characters, length, formatting) into the user prompt: being the last message, it has the strongest effect.
Put lasting facts about the world and characters into the lorebook, not into Style.
Ask for a length in the instructions ("about 800 words") rather than relying on the response limit, which cuts the text off.
After changing a template, generate a part and check it with Show Prompt.

A model can only read a limited amount of text at once (its context). When a book grows beyond that, Marginalia leaves out the oldest parts, and the model forgets what happened in them. Summaries keep that history in the prompt in condensed form.
A summary belongs to one part and covers that part and all parts before it, back to the previous part with a summary:
Here S1 (on part #4) covers parts #1-#4 and S2 (on part #8) covers parts #5-#8.
When the next part is generated:
all summaries of the active branch go into the master template, oldest first, in the {{summaries}} block (Summary of story so far in the default template);
the parts covered by summaries are not sent any more;
the parts after the newest summary (#9 and #10 above) are sent in full, as many as fit.
Summaries are made only when you ask for them; Marginalia doesn't summarize on its own.
Pick the part that ends a stretch of the story you want to condense, for example the last part of a chapter.
In its menu (☰) choose Generate summary.
The summary dialog shows the summary as the model writes it (and its reasoning, for reasoning models). Stop interrupts it and discards the summary.
When it's done, close the dialog with Exit.
A summary being generated

The part menu now has View summary, which opens the summary again, and Delete summary, which removes it. To change a summary, edit it in the Summaries overview, or delete it and generate it again, possibly with a different summary prompt.

The summary is written by the book's model, with the book's protocol, and must fit into the context limit together with the text of the parts it covers. To summarize a long stretch with a small model, summarize in smaller steps.

Editing a summary changes what the model gets, nothing else: the summary stays valid. Only the text can be edited, not the reasoning.
The trash icon of a summary does the same as Delete summary in the part menu. For a meta summary it asks what to do, see Unwinding a meta summary.
Summaries stay in the prompt for good, so a long book fills the context with them. A meta summary condenses several summaries into one: it is a summary of summaries.
Here M merges S1, S2 and S3. It belongs to the part of the newest merged summary (#9 above, which had S3) and replaces that summary on the part. From then on:
only M goes into the {{summaries}} block, instead of S1, S2 and S3;

Open the Summaries overview.
Tick the Select box of the summaries to merge. At least two. You tick the summaries in use only (the ones on the top level of the grid).
Click Create meta summary.

Marginalia merges everything from the newest to the oldest ticked summary, including the summaries in between that were not ticked. The meta summary dialog works like the summary dialog: it shows the text as the model writes it, and Stop cancels it and changes nothing. When it ends, close the dialog with Exit and the overview shows the result.
Ticked summaries and the meta summary being generated
A meta summary can merge meta summaries too: tick them like any other summary. The merged ones are shown under the new one, with their own merged summaries under them.
The summaries to merge and the request for the model must fit into the context limit, so with a small model merge a few summaries at a time.
Deleting a meta summary (the trash icon in the overview, or Delete summary in the part menu) asks:
Button
Unwind

Removes the meta summary and puts back the summary it replaced on the part. Summaries that were merged into a meta summary made of meta summaries come back one level at a time, the way they were made.
Delete
Removes the meta summary and leaves the part without a summary. The summaries it merged are in use again (but the one it replaced is gone).
Cancel
Does nothing.
After unwinding, the summaries that were merged are in use again and the overview shows them on the top level.
Deleting a meta summary
The request for a meta summary is the Default Meta Summary Prompt of the book (on the Prompts tab, or the default from Settings → Templates). It gets two variables:
Variable
{{summaryBlocks}}
The summaries to merge, oldest first, separated by an empty line.
{{backgroundLore}}
The lorebook entries that were active when the part of the meta summary was written.

The built-in prompt asks for the events to be chained into shorter entries - roughly half the size - without losing names, items, agreements or unresolved plot threads, and without adding anything new.
A summary is only valid for the exact text it was made from. When you edit or delete a part covered by a summary, the summary no longer matches.

Marginalia checks this when it generates the next part. Outdated summaries are removed and you are asked Invalidated summaries for messages with IDs: [...]. Continue generation without those summaries? Answer Yes to generate without them, or No to stop and generate new summaries first. Either way the outdated summaries are gone; the parts they covered are sent in full again (as far as they fit) until you summarize them again.
A search and replace in the story keeps the summaries it covers valid and warns about the ones that become outdated.

A meta summary is outdated when a part it covers is edited or deleted, but also when a summary it merged is deleted. (That is why the merged summaries can't be edited: the change would make the meta summary outdated.) Removing an outdated meta summary is the same as unwinding it: the summary it replaced comes back, and is checked as well. If it is outdated too, it is removed in the same way.
When you branch from a part with a summary, the new branch gets a copy of the summary. A copied meta summary keeps what it replaced, so it can be unwound in the new branch.
The request for a summary is the Default Summary Prompt of the book (on the Prompts tab, or the default from Settings → Templates). It gets two variables:
Variable
{{text}}
The text of the parts to summarize, oldest first.
{{backgroundLore}}
The lorebook entries that were active when the summarized part was written.

The built-in prompt asks for a detailed, chronological ledger of events - every beat, action and change of state - rather than a short retelling, because the summary is meant for the model, not for a reader. Replace it if you prefer shorter summaries or a different format.
Summarize at natural breaks: the end of a chapter or a scene.

When the summaries start to take too much of the context (the tooltip of the Summaries button shows how much), merge the oldest ones into a meta summary. Repeat it later with the meta summary and the summaries after it.

Summaries stay in the prompt for good. With many of them, the prompt can fill the context by itself, and generating stops with Contextual limit not sufficient. Then shorten them (a more concise summary prompt), merge them into meta summaries or raise the context limit.
Keep facts that must never be forgotten (names, relationships, rules of the world) in the lorebook rather than relying on summaries.
Check what the model got with Show Prompt on the next part.

The title page and the table of contents of an exported PDF

When the text contains chapters, the file gets a table of contents after the title page. A chapter is a part of the story that contains a Markdown heading (a line starting with #, e.g. # Chapter 3: The Harbour) - the same rule the Chapter Marker plugin uses in the story sidebar. The first heading of a part is its title, parts without a heading belong to the chapter before them. A story without any heading has no table of contents.
