The PDF and Word files have the page number in the footer of every page except the title page. The number is the position of the page in the file, so the title page is page 1 and the first page after it is page 2. The other formats have no pages of their own.

With Include title page, the file starts with the book title and the author on a page of their own. The page is made from a built-in template (DEFAULT_EXPORT_HEADER_TEMPLATE), which isn't editable in the application yet.
The export is a snapshot of the branch when you choose Export. Parts generated or edited afterwards are not in the file.
The exported file is kept only until you close the download dialog. Export again if you need it later.
Summaries, lorebooks, instructions and the model's reasoning are not exported, only the text and the images of the parts. To save all of it, make a backup.

A book backup is a snapshot of one book: its settings and prompts, all parts in all branches, summaries, tags and the lorebook. Use backups to go back to an earlier state of the story, to make a copy of a book, or to move a book to another Marginalia installation or user.
Book backups are separate from the database backups that administrators make of the whole installation.
The Backups tab of a book

On the Backups tab of the book, click Take Backup. The backup appears at the top of the list with its Date the number of Messages (parts) it contains and the number of Images (the pictures of the parts) its parts use.
Backups can also be taken automatically, see below.

A backup remembers which pictures the parts have (and their captions), but not the picture files. This keeps backups, and the automatic ones, small. The pictures stay in your Resources. To take the pictures with a backup you pack them when you export it.
Click Restore next to the backup and choose:
Option
What is restored
Full Restore
Everything: name, description, publishing, prompts and other book settings, tags, model, protocol, lorebook, and all parts.
Messages Only Restore
Only the parts (all branches) and summaries. The book's current settings, prompts and lorebook stay as they are.
Restoring replaces all parts of the book with those from the backup. Parts written after the backup are gone. Take a backup of the current state first if you might want it back.
The book window closes and opens again with the restored book.

The pictures of the restored parts are the ones the backup lists, as long as you still have them in Resources. A picture you deleted since is gone from the part. Restoring does not bring back deleted picture files, unless the backup comes from an export with pictures that you imported.

Model and protocol are looked up among your inference providers and protocols: first the exact one from the backup, then one with the same name. If neither exists, the book keeps its current model or protocol.

Lorebooks in the backup are compared with yours. When a lorebook with the same name but a different identity exists, Marginalia asks for each one whether to Link to existing or Create new from the backup. Lorebooks that you don't have at all can be imported (Import) or left out (Don't import).
Choosing what to do with lorebooks

Clone Backup creates a new book from the backup, under a name you enter. The original book is not changed. Use it to try something radical with a copy of the book, or to start a new book from the same opening.
If the backup uses pictures, Marginalia asks With images or Without images:

With images gives the new book its own copies of the pictures (the same files, new entries in Resources), so deleting or replacing a picture in one book does not touch the other. Pictures you have deleted since the backup was taken are left out.
Without images clones the text only.
Clone with or without images
Export downloads the backup as a JSON file (book name_backup.json). Keep it as an extra copy, or take it to another installation.
If the backup uses pictures, Marginalia asks whether to pack them:
Exporting a backup that has pictures
Without images downloads the JSON right away, as above. The pictures are only listed in it.

With images packs the backup and all its pictures into a ZIP file (book name_backup.zip). A progress bar shows how many pictures are done; the file is built on disk one picture at a time, so even a book with many large pictures does not use much memory. When it is ready, click Download. The file is kept only until you close that dialog.
If a picture can't be packed because you deleted it or its file is missing, the dialog tells how many were left out.

The ZIP contains backup.json (the same JSON), resources.json (the list of the pictures) and the pictures. You don't have to unpack it: both ways of bringing a backup back accept the .zip as well as the .json.
There are two ways to bring a backup file back:
Import Backup on the Backups tab adds the file to the backup list of this book. Nothing changes until you Restore it.
Import Backup as New Book in the Settings tab creates a new book from the file.
Both accept a .json or a .zip file. The file is uploaded to the server and read from there, so a big backup is no problem.

When the file is a ZIP with pictures, the pictures are added to your Resources first, and the backup then uses them. A picture you already have (the same file) is not stored again: the existing one is used, so importing your own export does not add anything. A JSON file without pictures is imported as it is.

Importing as a new book gives the new book its own entries in Resources, also when you already have the same pictures: the entries point to the same files, so no disk space is used twice. If the file has no pictures (a plain JSON), the new book gets copies of those pictures that the file lists and that you still have; those you don't have are left out. Anything in the file that is not a usable picture (not a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, or too big) is ignored.

l: Importing a backup as a new book
p: Open the Settings tab and click Import Backup as New Book.
Enter the New Book Name - the upload is enabled once the name is filled in.
Upload the backup file.
Decide about the lorebooks, if asked.
The new book appears in the Books tab.
The trash button removes a backup for good. Automatic backups are not rotated: they stay until you delete them.
Marginalia can take a backup on its own while you write. Set the default for all books in Settings → General Settings → Backup Strategy:
Strategy
No Backups
No automatic backups.
After N Messages
A backup after every N generated parts.
After N Minutes
A backup after a generated part when at least N minutes have passed since the last automatic backup.
To use a different strategy for one book, check Per manuscript override on its Backups tab and choose the strategy and the number there. Unchecking it returns the book to the default from Settings.
Automatic backups are taken only after a part is generated, so a book you only read doesn't get new backups.
Each backup is a JSON file in the Marginalia data folder:

With the Docker version this is ./data/data/login/... on the host. The files are not in the database, so a database backup doesn't contain them. Include the whole .marginalia folder in your own backups.
The picture files are not in the backups either, they are in the data/your login/images folder next to backups. They are also not in a database backup, see there.

c: ~/.marginalia/data/<your login>/backups/manuscripts/<book id>/

p: The viewer is a reading view of your books: just the text of the story, without the editor around it. It works well on phones and tablets. Publishing a book lets other users of the same Marginalia installation read it in the viewer.
The viewer is at /view on your Marginalia address, for example:
desktop app: http://127.0.0.1:8765/view
server: https://marginalia.example.com/view
It uses the same login as Marginalia.
The viewer's book list

The list shows your books, with their tags and when you last opened them. Filter it by Name (books whose name starts with the text) and Tags (books with all the selected tags). Sort it by Last Opened or Name; clicking the active sort button again reverses the order.
Click a book to read it.

The reading view shows the active branch of the book from the first to the last part, in the book reading style (justified, with hyphenation for the book's language). Other branches, the turn instructions and the metadata are not shown. The arrow button in the top left corner returns to the list.
Reading a book
What you read is the book as it is now: new parts appear the next time the page is opened.
Pictures of the parts are shown under the text, but only to you, the owner. Readers of a published book see the text without the pictures.
By default only you can open your books in the viewer. To let other users read a book:
Open the book and check Published on its About tab.

Copy the reader link that appears under the checkbox on the About tab. The link is the address of your installation (including its context path, if Marginalia is not served from the root), followed by /view/ and the book's ID: address of Marginalia/view/book ID. In Docker, where Marginalia runs as the root application, it looks like https://marginalia.example.com/view/0b6f3c1e-...; if it is deployed under a context path such as /marginalia, the link is https://example.com/marginalia/view/0b6f3c1e-.... (You can also copy the same address from the browser's address bar when the book is open in the viewer.)
Send the address to the other users.

Other users need an account on the same Marginalia installation; they log in and see the book. Published books don't appear in their viewer list, only the address opens them. They can only read the book, not change it.
Publishing shares the book as it is: only the text of the parts is shared, the pictures of the parts stay private.
Uncheck Published to stop sharing: the address then shows Book not found to everyone but you. Deleted books can't be opened at all.
(picture)
A small preview of images.
Column
Created
Name
Size
The name of the file as it was uploaded.

The part or other object the file was added to, e.g. ChatMessage #123. nothing means that the file is not used by anything. (gone) behind the name means that the object was deleted or no longer exists, the file is probably not needed any more.
The Resources tab

The Resources tab lists the files you have uploaded to Marginalia. For now these are the pictures of the parts of your books. The tab is the place to find a picture again, to download it, to swap it for a better one without touching the books that use it, and to throw away what you no longer need.
The size of the file.
The table loads as you scroll, so it stays fast with thousands of files. Click a column header to sort by it; the newest files are first by default.
The type of the file, e.g. image/png.

This is only a note kept for you. Marginalia does not enforce it: a picture still works after the part it was added to is gone, and the same picture can be used by more parts (for example after you branch the story, the branch has the same pictures as the part it was made from).
Type
Used by
When the file was uploaded.
The download button (arrow down) in the row saves the file to your computer.

The upload button in the row opens a dialog where you choose a new file. The new content is saved as a new file and the entry now points to it, so everything that uses the entry shows the new content; you don't have to change the parts. Use it to swap a picture for a better version or to fix a wrong upload.
A picture can be replaced only by a picture (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, up to 10 MB, as when adding images).
The name of the entry becomes the name of the new file.
The previous file is not deleted from the data folder, see below.
Replacing the content of a resource

The trash button in the row deletes one file. To delete several, tick them in the first column and choose Delete selected above the table. The tick box in the header selects all files. Marginalia asks before it deletes.
The file disappears from the table and from the parts that use it: a part simply shows no picture any more. Text, summaries and exports of the part are not changed.
The entry is only marked as deleted. The cleanup in the administration removes it from the database for good.
The file stays in the data folder (data/your login/images) for now, also after cleanup. Deleting a resource does not free disk space yet.

Until the cleanup removes the entry, you can bring it back from the Trash: the file is still in the data folder, so the picture works again. After the cleanup only a backup of the whole database made before contains the entry; the file itself is still in the folder.

An agent is a model that works on one of your books on its own, for a long time, calling the commands you allow it as its tools: it can read the story, check it against the lorebook and report to you. The Agents tab is where you create them, set what each may do, start and stop their runs, talk to them in the console and clone them.

Start runs the agent: it works in the background, one round at a time, calling the commands you allowed and its own file tools, until it finishes, asks you something, reaches a limit or you pause or stop it (see A run). It works on a hidden copy of the book, so your book is never touched while it works (the book itself is locked); when it is done you review its result and take over what you want.

The tab is there only if an administrator gave you the Agents permission (administrators always have it, but the limits are the same as for everybody: the defaults unless they fill in the settings of their own permission, so an administrator who needs more agents, runs or room in the workspace sets it there; a changed limit reaches a run that is working when it is paused and resumed). On a phone each agent is a card with the same buttons, see On a phone.
Agent ID
An agent has at most one run that is not over, and a book has at most one agent.
Asks whether to keep the result (the run can be resumed later) or discard it.
Button
Clone
Column
Console
Copies the agent, see Cloning.
Delete
Edit
Goes on with a paused or stopped run (shown instead of Start).
Moves the agent, with its runs, to the trash.
Name

Opens a menu. Start immediately: the agent works on its task (its instructions) on its own and you hear of it when it asks or finishes. Start in console: opens the console and tells the agent not to work yet but to ask you at once what you want it to do; the run is then a conversation that goes on until you press Finish.
Opens the agent.
Opens the console of the agent.
Pause
Pause now
Pauses a run that works or waits for you.
Resume
Shown while the agent works: pauses it without waiting for the round to end, see Pause and Stop.
Start
Starting is refused, with the reason, when the agent is disabled, has no model, or you have all the runs you may work at once.
Status
Stop
The buttons at the end of a row depend on the run:
The identifier of the agent.
The name you gave it.

What its run is doing: Running, Waiting for you, Waiting for approval, Pausing, Paused, Stopping, Stopped, result kept, Done, waits for the review, Applied. An agent without a run says Not running, or Disabled when it is switched off.
@file:/path
@result

A command that is going on is told to stop, and a command that is written to be stopped (the ones that write with a model, search and replace) ends at once and leaves what it had done so far. One that can't be stopped may still finish; either way the agent is told that it is not known whether the call was done and checks the state with a read command when it goes on. The commands of the sub-agents are cancelled the same way when the run is paused, stopped or sent a message at once.

A command that sends pictures to a model of its own, such as generate-lore-entry, takes an images parameter: a list of paths of image files of the workspace (at most 8). It is the model of the command, not the agent's, that has to see them, so the agent can pass images even when its own model does not see images.
A question for you. The run waits (Waiting for you).

A run is the job of the agent. It works in rounds: the model is asked once, it answers with text and/or calls to its tools, the results go back, and so on. Every round is saved, so a run can be paused and go on later, even after the server was restarted. The agent has the commands you allowed and these of its own:
ask_user
checkpoint, checkpoint_list, checkpoint_restore, checkpoint_delete
Compacts its own context: when the round ends it writes the summary of its earlier work, as with /compact. It is told to save its notes to a file first. See Context filling up.

Done: the agent called finish (in a run you started immediately). A run you started in the console is a conversation: the report of the agent comes to you like a question, the run waits for your next message, and only Finish in the console (or Stop) ends it. The result of a Done run waits for your review.
Failed: the runner itself broke; the reason says what.
Files
finish
get_run_status
get_sync_report
How a run ends a stretch of work:
How many rounds and tokens it has used, how much context, and the longest answer it can write. The agent is also told these limits of its model in its prompt, so it writes a long text in parts.
Images for commands
Its checkpoints: saves a restore point of the working copy and its workspace (with a label), lists them, goes back to one (when the round ends) and deletes one it does not need.
Its report: the run is Done. The report is shown as the reason of the status.
Its to-do list.

Like @file:, for the result of a command: a text argument that is exactly @result is replaced by the whole result of the last command the agent called, @result:3 by the result with that number (list_command_results shows the numbers). A generated text goes from one command to the next, or into write_file and append_file, without the agent writing it out.

list_files, read_file, write_file, append_file, replace_in_file, regex_replace_in_file, grep_files, move_file, copy_file, merge_files, unzip_file, delete_file in its own workspace (notes it keeps between runs). Next to the workspace it sees the read-only file /AGENTS.md, your instructions as the run started with them, which it can read again whenever it likes and never change. list_files and grep_files take a name pattern (glob, for example *.md or chapters/*.md), copy_file copies a folder with everything in it (a quick way to keep a version of the notes), merge_files joins several files into one without the text passing through the model (the last name of a path may be a pattern such as /chapters/*.md), unzip_file unpacks a zip file of the workspace into a new folder. list_command_results and save_command_result keep the long result of a command without the agent writing it out again: the last ten results are kept whole (the agent sees a long one cut), and one is saved to a file by its number, the newest when none is given; it then passes the file on as @file:/path.

Looks at an image file of its workspace (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP): the picture is shown to the model in the next message. Only an agent whose model is marked as seeing images (The model sees images in the agent) has it. A large image is scaled down before it is sent, a GIF shows its first frame, and only the newest four images stay in front of the model (an older one becomes a note, and the agent can look again). The images come from you (Upload file, or attached to a message); the agent can't make one.

Not a tool but a way to call one: a text argument of a command that is exactly @file:/notes/chapter.md is replaced by the contents of that file of the agent's workspace, so the agent can write a long text to a file once, check it, and pass it to a command (the result shows the short reference in the call, the command gets the text). write_file and append_file take it as their content too, which copies a file or adds it to another: a long file can be written in parts, each part within the longest answer of the model, and put together this way.
Only after a resume that took over changes of yours: lists again what you changed in the book while the run was paused and what of it came into the agent's copy, see Resuming a run.

Pause takes effect between two rounds: the model request and the calls that are going on finish first. That can take long (a slow model, a long generation), so there is Pause now: it cancels the request to the model, whose answer is thrown away, and the call that is going on, answers the calls of the round that were not made as such, and the run is Paused in a moment. What the thrown away request would have cost is lost; resume as usual. Stop does the same: it does not wait for the request or the call that is going on, they are cancelled and the run ends at once (kept or discarded as you chose).

Paused, with the reason: the limit of rounds, the token budget or the context limit is reached, the model could not be asked (an error of the provider, your limit on the AI), or the server was restarted. Resume goes on from the last complete round; a call that was in the air when the server stopped is reported to the model as "outcome unknown".
request_compaction
Tool
update_plan
view_image
Waiting for you: the agent answered without a tool call, or asked you something. Answer it in the console.
While the agent waits for a free place at its model (see One model, several agents) it is Running; a Pause or Stop ends that wait at once.
Console opens a window for the latest run of the agent, with eight tabs: Run, Runs, Workspace, Checkpoints, Context, Book copy, Sub-agents and Diagnostics.

Run shows the transcript: what you told the agent, what it said (both as Markdown, so lists, headings and emphasis show as such), and every command or file tool it called, folded to one line with the arguments (click it to see them and the result, shown as plain text). When the model sends its reasoning (what it thought before it answered), a folded Reasoning block shows it before the answer, and the download has it. Whether you get any depends on the model and the server: it has to report it, and your AI has to have reasoning switched on. Every message has the time it was written at the right of its first line (the time of day, with the date when it was another day; hover for the whole time), so you can tell how long the agent worked and when it stopped. The state of the run, the context (how many tokens the last request used of the limit of the model, so you see how close the run is to a pause), the rounds and tokens it used (and the token budget, when there is one) stay above it and the box for your message under it, while the transcript scrolls. What the agent waits for is in the transcript where it was written, as a bubble of its own that stays there when the run goes on:
a Question of the agent, when the run is Waiting for you; write the answer in the box and press Send (or Ctrl+Enter), and the agent goes on;
a Report of the agent, when it called finish.

In a conversation you can also write while the agent works. The message is queued: it appears as a dashed bubble at the end of the transcript and the agent reads it as soon as the round it is in is over: the request to the model that is on its way and the calls it made finish first, and the next request already contains your message (several queued messages go together as one). When it should not wait even for that, press the small Send now (lightning) button on the bubble: the agent drops the round it is in (the request to the model is canceled, a command that waited for your approval is refused, calls that were not made are marked as skipped) and reads your message next. The trash button next to it takes the message back as long as the agent has not read it yet (the same for a queued command). Commands that already ran stay done. Queued messages are lost when the server restarts, and a run that is not a conversation (started immediately) does not take messages while it works.

Under the transcript is the command line of the application (the one of the story tab: type /, the list and the help of the command appear above it) with what you can run on the agent: /compact, /clear-workspace and the commands the agent may call that only read or add data (a command that changes or removes data is not offered, it would ask you to confirm in a window of the book, which a run does not have). You run the command, not the agent: it is told, in a message of yours, that you ran it and what it answered (and that what it read earlier may be out of date if the command changed the working copy), so it never believes it made a call it did not. It works as a message: where the run waits (Waiting for you) or is Paused the command runs at once and the run stays as it is; where a conversation works it is queued, a dashed bubble marked Command, and runs at the end of the agent's turn, where the agent would have waited (the agent does not go on because of it). The small Run now button on the bubble drops the round the agent is in, runs the command and lets the agent go on from there. A command that takes long holds the box: wait for it before you write to the agent.

/compact [what to stress] frees the context. The agent is asked to read everything so far and write a summary (what you asked, what is done, what it found, its notes and its plan, what it was about to do); that summary replaces everything before it in what the model reads. In the transcript you still see all of it, and the summary as a folded block, Summary of the earlier work; the export keeps it too. The text after the command, if any, is what the summary should stress. The request is the agent's own and its tokens count against the run. The question the agent is asked is its Compaction prompt: the one of the agent, else your default in Settings, else the one of the administrator, else the built-in one. If the context is already so full that the request does not fit, the oldest messages are left out of it (the summary says how many). Do it before the context is full, the usage line shows how close it is. Right after the compaction the context shown is an estimate of what the next request will hold (the summary, the system prompt and the definitions of the tools); the first answer of the model after it replaces it with the real number.

Context filling up. Once the context of the model passes 75% of its cap the agent gets a notice after every round (a message of the run, you see it in the transcript): how full it is, and that it should save what it must not lose to a file of its workspace, update its plan and call request_compaction. Above 90% the notice says that the run stops when the context is full. If the agent does not compact before the context passes the Compact at share of its definition (90% unless you say otherwise), the run does it by itself: the same compaction, the summary begins "compacted automatically" and the agent is not warned on top of it. A compaction that fails changes nothing, the agent is told, and the run tries again only some rounds later. The compaction the agent asks for is the same as yours (its Compaction prompt, see Creating and editing an agent, its tokens count against the run); if it fails, nothing is changed and the agent is told. The notices need a context cap: the lowest of the cap of the agent and the limits of its model.

A call the model server could not read. When a model writes a long text inside a call, its answer can end in the middle of the text (the limit of one answer, the reply tokens of the protocol or the max completion tokens of the AI, is reached, a server default applies when neither is set, or the model simply stops; the context, however full, is a different limit), and the server refuses the incomplete call ("Failed to parse tool call arguments as JSON"). Asking again with the same conversation would make the same mistake, so the run does not just pause: the agent is told in the transcript that its last answer could not be used and that nothing was done, and to write long text to a file of its workspace in several smaller steps; then it is asked again, up to three times in a row. If it keeps failing the run pauses, and what it was told stays in the transcript, so a Resume asks a different question than the one that failed. The same goes for a sub-agent.

A call that was cut off but reached the application (the call result says "not valid JSON ... cut off in the middle") stays in the transcript as the model wrote it, so you can read it, but it is sent back to the model with empty arguments: a server that reads the earlier calls again would otherwise refuse every following request, and the run could not go on without a rewind.

Runaway calls. A model can fall into a loop and write the same call hundreds of times in one answer; the results would fill the context before the next request. The run makes at most 32 calls of an answer, and a repeat of a call that only reads (the same tool with the same arguments, in the same answer) is made once. The calls that are left out are not in the transcript, and the agent gets a notice that says so.

/clear-workspace [what to keep] deletes the files and all the folders of the workspace of the run (after you confirm, as with the button of the workspace). Name what to keep after it, separated by spaces: files, folders (with everything in them) or patterns such as *.md or chapters/*.md, a path with spaces in double quotes (/clear-workspace /notes.md /my drafts *.png). The folders above a kept file stay. If something named is not there nothing is deleted. /AGENTS.md and the checkpoints are not part of the workspace and are never touched. The agent is told what was deleted and what was kept. In the transcript a command you ran is a bubble with the command and what it answered.

When the model of the agent sees images (see Creating and editing an agent), Attach image is next to Send: pick a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP file, or paste a picture from the clipboard into the message box (Ctrl+V), and it waits above the box (the cross takes it back) until you send. Up to eight images go with a message; the text may be empty. The images are saved in the uploads folder of the workspace (a name that is taken gets a number: map-2.png), within the limits and rules of the workspace, and the model is shown them with your message. Delete them in the Workspace tab when you no longer need them.
The buttons at the bottom are Pause, Resume and Stop, which do what they do in the table, and Finish, which ends a run that waits for you (its work is over, Done).

The window looks at the run every two seconds while it is open; Refresh does it at once. The Run tab shows the latest run that was not discarded, so a run that finished or failed can still be read there until the agent starts a new run; older runs are in Runs.

Runs is the history of the agent: every run it had, the latest first, with its date, status, rounds, tokens and result. Use the eye to open a run in the Run tab and read its steps and its report again (the run you open stays there until you open another one), the arrow to download its transcript as a Markdown file (what was said and when, every command with its arguments and result, the report, the conversations of the sub-agents), and the bin to delete it. A deleted run goes to the trash. A run that is going on can't be deleted, stop it first. Runs you stopped and discarded are in the list too, so you can read what they did or delete them; the Run tab shows them only when you open them.

Workspace shows the files of the agent: its notes and reports, which it keeps between runs. Click a folder to go in (Up goes back), click a text file to read it, use the arrows to download a file or the bin to delete it, and Clear deletes everything (stale notes mislead a fresh run). New folder creates a folder in the open one and Upload file puts a file from your computer there, so you can hand the agent a brief, a style guide or a draft. The same rules hold as for the agent's own files: names can't have \ : | ? *, a trailing dot or space, or be too long or too deep, the limits of file size and number of files apply, and an uploaded file must be text (UTF-8), because the agent can only read text, an image (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, recognised by what the file contains, not by its name; up to 5 MB, and it counts against the total and the number of files like any file) or a zip file (up to 10 MB, kept as it is; the agent unpacks it, see below). A file is never replaced by an upload: delete the old one first. Files can't be changed while the agent works, pause it first. The workspace has a limit of size, file size and number of files, which your administrator can set in your permission; the line under the table says how much is used. The name AGENTS.md at the top is taken by your instructions, which the agent sees there (the file can't be written or deleted).

Upload a zip file in the Workspace tab (Upload file) when the agent should work on many files at once, for example the chapters of a draft, and ask it to unpack it: the agent has the tool unzip_file, which unpacks /uploads/draft.zip into the new folder /uploads/draft (or into a folder it is given; the folder must not exist yet). Unpacking is all or nothing and an archive is never trusted:

Only text files (UTF-8), images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) and zip files are kept. The other entries are left out and named in the answer to the agent. A zip file inside is stored, never unpacked on its own.
The files must fit what the workspace has room for (size, file size, number of files), or nothing is unpacked.

An archive with an entry that leads above the folder (../x) or starts with / is refused whole, and so is one with the same name twice (also differing in case), a name that is both a file and a folder, more than 5 000 entries, or an encrypted or damaged one.
A zip bomb is refused: an archive that unpacks to more than the workspace can hold, or to more than 100 times its own size.

An agent can hand a job to a sub-agent: a helper with a conversation of its own that does one task and answers with a text. It has the same commands and files as the agent and works in the same working copy and workspace (what it changes stays), but it does not know the conversation of the agent, so the agent has to say everything in the task. The point is that what the sub-agent reads and tries stays out of the context of the agent: checking a chapter, auditing the names, drafting a part.
Set Most sub-agents in the agent to how many may work at once. Zero (the default) is none: the agent is not even told they exist.
With one, the agent starts a sub-agent and waits (it is parked) until the sub-agent is done; the call returns its answer.

With more, starting a sub-agent returns at once and the agent can go on, start others, look at them (agent_status), wait for an answer (await_agent) or stop one (cancel_agent). The call that reaches the limit waits until one of them is over and returns what ended.
Rules that hold either way:
A sub-agent can not start sub-agents, finish the run, ask you, or make checkpoints; it ends by answering with a text.
Everything counts in the one budget of the run: rounds, tokens, the limits of the model. A sub-agent that hits a limit fails and says so; the agent then hits the same limit.
How many requests are on their way to the model at once is the Requests to the model at once your administrator gave you (one when not set): with one, the agent and its sub-agent take turns.
Calls that change the book or the workspace are done one at a time, whoever makes them, so two sub-agents never write at the same instant. Still, do not tell two of them to change the same part.

Pausing the run pauses the sub-agents too. They stop at their next stable point (between two requests or two calls, at once when you pause at once) and what they said and did is kept with the run, so a Resume goes on where everything was: the sub-agents go on with their conversation, and a call of the agent that waited for one (await_agent, or spawn_agent with a limit of one) waits again, as if nothing had happened. A sub-agent that was over before the pause is still there for the agent to ask about. Stopping a run and keeping it does the same; discarding it, a restore of a checkpoint (the book the sub-agents worked in is replaced) and the agent finishing or asking you something end them for good. An agent that ends its turn while sub-agents still work is told once; if it does it again they are stopped.

Their conversations are not in the Run tab. The Sub-agents tab of the console shows them: pick one above to read what the agent told it, what it said, the commands it called with their results and how it ended (the answer it gave, or why it failed or was cancelled), in the same blocks as the transcript. It follows the run while it works, and it shows the sub-agents of an older run too (pick that run in the Runs tab first). A spawn_agent call in the Run tab has a Sub-agent button that opens its conversation. A conversation the agent went back over (a rewind) is greyed and marked forgotten by the agent. The download of the run (in the Runs tab) has a section for each sub-agent, with its task, its state and every message and call.

A local server often has one slot (one GPU): ask it for two answers at once and both crawl or time out. Set Concurrent requests of agents in the settings of the model (1 for one slot) and the requests of your agents to it take turns, in the order they came: the others wait, their runs stay Running, and a Pause or Stop ends the wait. It counts the model requests of all the agents of all users who use that model, the commands that write with it included. It does not hold up your own writing in the story window, and that does not count against the agents either.

An agent that needs you, finishes or fails tells the open screens of the application (the badge on the tab, a notice). When no screen of yours is open it can also send a short message to an address you give in Settings ("Message to a URL when an agent needs you"): your ntfy topic (the ntfy app on the phone shows it at once), a Gotify message URL or a Discord webhook; pick the Format the service wants. Send a test message tries it with what is in the fields. The message names the agent and says what it wants ("waits for you", "finished", "asks for the approval of the command ...", "failed", "was paused: reason") in your language. Also when the application is open sends it in any case.

The server calls the address, so an administrator can turn this off for everybody (Admin, Agents). Treat the address as a password when it holds a secret: anyone who knows it can read what is sent, the server never writes it to its log, redirects are not followed, and only http and https are called.
When the agent needs you, you are told wherever you are in the app:
a number on the Agents tab counts the agents that wait for you, and the Console button of such an agent is highlighted;
a notice pops up with an Open button that opens the console of that agent.

The agent needs you when it asks you something or waits for your next message, asks you to approve a command, finished, failed, or was paused by itself (a limit is reached, the model could not be asked, the server was restarted). A pause you asked for does not count.

Agents work while you are away, so this does not depend on the app being open: the number is there when you log in again, and every browser window you have open gets the notice. Opening the console of the agent clears it (the other windows update).

When the agent is set to Ask first and wants a command that changes or removes data, the run stops in Waiting for approval and a window pops up over the console with the command and its arguments. Approve lets it run, Deny tells the agent that you refused and it goes on. Pausing or stopping the run refuses the command too. The command still works on the copy of the book. If the console is closed, the window is there as soon as you open it.

Every run works on a copy of your book and of its lorebooks that the app makes when the run starts: the messages, summaries, tags and settings as they are at that moment, and the lorebook with its sub-lorebooks. The copy is hidden: it is not in the lists of books and lorebooks. Whatever the agent does, it does to the copy; your book stays as it was.

When the agent has Write the book with the model of the agent on (the default), the copy also gets the model of the agent (the AI and the protocol of its main model profile) in place of the AI and the protocol of your book, every time the run starts or is resumed. So the commands that write with a model (/next, /swipe, /regenerate, the summaries) and the model commands of extensions (the Lore Generator, the Arc Outline) use the agent's model even when your book is set to another one, or to none; a profile named in the call still wins. With the setting off they use the model of the book. This is not a change of your book: the review does not list it and applying the result leaves the AI and the protocol of your book as they are.

A paused run keeps its copy and works on it again when you resume it. A run that is Done, or that you stopped and kept, keeps it until you take over its result or discard it. When the run is Failed, you discard its result, or its changes are applied, the copy is deleted for good, and the next run makes a new one from the book as it is then.
A paused or kept run does not hold the lock on your book, so you can edit the book meanwhile. When you Resume the run, its working copy catches up with what you did:

What you changed and the agent did not (a part, a lorebook entry, a setting, a tag...) comes into the copy. A part you added comes in too and the agent can build on it; what you deleted is deleted from the copy.

What you and the agent both changed to different texts stays as the agent has it: nothing the agent did is lost. It is a conflict that you resolve when you review the result, with both texts in front of you.
What you changed and the agent deleted stays deleted, and what you deleted and the agent changed stays in the copy; the review shows both.

Nothing needs a click: the sync is part of resuming, and it takes a moment (a few seconds when you changed hundreds of items). The state of the copy before it is saved as an automatic checkpoint. The agent is told what happened, by the names it knows the items by, in a message when it goes on ("While the run was paused the user changed the book..."), and can ask again with get_sync_report. To tell it something more, write to the run as usual.

When a run is Done (or you stopped it with Stop and keep the result) the agent row and the console have a Review changes button. It opens a window with everything the agent changed, compared with your book as it is now, one line each:
Book: its name, description, language, point of view, tense, style and templates, its tags, and the data an extension keeps in the book (an arc outline, the character tracker).
Part: a part whose text, instructions, scene setting, point-of-view character, present characters or summary the agent changed, a part it wrote, a part it deleted.
Lorebook and Entry: a lorebook or an entry the agent made, changed (also moved, renamed, or with other tags, or other subbooks) or deleted.

Tick the lines you want, then Apply the picked changes. The buttons above the list tick all of them, none, only new parts (the new branch the agent wrote, nothing else) or everything without conflicts. A line that needs another (a new part needs the part it follows if that is new too) brings it along when you tick it, and loses its followers when you untick it. Click a line to see it on the right: the text of your book now and the text that will be written, which you can edit before you apply. If you write nothing, the agent's text is applied.

Your book may have changed since the run started (you can edit it as soon as the run is not working). What only you changed is not in the list and stays. What both of you changed to the same thing is no change. What both changed to different texts is a conflict: it starts unticked, and when you tick it the text you see on the right replaces the text of the book. Use the book's puts the book's text into the box (the line then changes nothing for that field), Use the agent's puts the agent's back; or write the result yourself. A line that can't be taken over (the part it follows, or the lorebook it is in, was deleted from your book) says so and can't be ticked.

Under the texts, Differences shows what changes word by word: what is only in the book now struck through in red, what is only in the text to apply in green (it follows what you write in the box). For a conflict it also shows what the agent changed and what you changed since the run started, each from the book as it was then, so you can see who did what. A line the agent changed in more than one thing (a part whose text and scene setting changed, an entry with a new content and note) has a Take this change box beside each of them: untick one to apply the line without it, the book keeps its own value of that field. The place of a part in the story goes with the part and has no box, and what the agent made or deleted is taken or left as a whole. Show in the copy (on a line the agent made or changed) opens the copy of the book at that part or entry, to read it in its place.
A lorebook that other books use is marked Shared: the change goes to the lorebook itself, so the other books get it too. It starts unticked.

Applying is done to the book in place: the parts keep their addresses, other books keep their links to a lorebook, and what the agent deleted goes to the trash. A backup of the book as it was is taken first (it is among the backups of the book, with its lorebooks), and the changes are made all together or not at all. Show the branch the agent ended on also switches the book to the branch the agent was on, when it is among what you applied. The summaries of parts that were edited are outdated as after an edit by hand; the agent's own summaries are taken over as they are.

When the changes are applied the run is Applied and its copy and checkpoints are deleted. Discard the result throws the copy away and leaves the book as it is. Until you do one of the two the agent has an unfinished run and can't start another.

The Book copy tab shows the book the agent works on, to read: the story, one branch at a time (pick the branch above; each part with its number, the swipe it is among the others after the same part, its words, scene setting, point of view and, folded, its instructions and summary), and the lorebooks with their entries (pick one to see its content, note, tags and settings). It is not a window of your book: nothing in it can be changed, no backup is made of the copy and no extension sees a book open. It is read when you open the tab and when you press Refresh, also while the agent works, so it shows what the agent has written so far. It is there while the run has its copy (not after the result was applied or discarded).

The Diagnostics tab counts what the run did from its transcript, to find out what an agent needs from its tools and its prompt. It works for any run, an old one too (pick it in Runs first), and is made when you open the tab and when you press Refresh.

Overview: rounds and calls, how many calls failed, the time of the model, of the calls and of pauses (a gap of 30 minutes or more between two steps is a pause, not work), the context at its peak and at the end, the tokens, compactions, your messages and the notices the runner gave the agent (an unreadable call, too many calls, a full context).

Tools: for each tool the calls, the errors, the results that were cut, how often it was the only call of a round, the characters the agent wrote, how many calls passed a text as @file: or @result, how many wrote a long text (300 characters or more) out and how many of those copied it from a result the agent had just been given, the tokens of its results (about, from the characters), the share of all results, the longest result and the time.

What the model wrote: the characters of the arguments, of the text beside the calls and of the reasoning, in all and for each block of 25 rounds with the time of the model, to see where its output goes and whether it stopped using @file at some point. Longest arguments shows the start of the biggest calls, with the path of a file tool.

Rounds lost to a pattern: the same tool called round after round (three or more), marked when a search came right before it; and the calls made again with the same arguments. These show where a tool that takes many items, or more calls in one answer, would save rounds.

Errors with the arguments of the first call that got each message (to see what the model sent when a call failed), the biggest results, the slowest rounds, the compactions and the sub-agents with the tools each one called.

Download gives the report as Markdown, Download JSON as JSON, Copy puts the Markdown on the clipboard. The times are the gaps between the stored rows, so they are approximate: the time of an answer includes waiting for a free place at the model.

The Context tab shows what the model reads with its next request, taken apart, so you can see where the tokens go and debug an agent that behaves oddly. It is made when you open the tab and when you press Refresh (not while the run works: it counts the tokens of every part).

Three charts: the kinds of parts against the limit of the context (the prompt of the agent, your instructions, the notes of the runner, the tool definitions, the summary of a compaction, your messages, the answers of the agent, the results of its calls, and what is free), every part in the order it is sent (a bar for each, in the colour of its kind: a tool whose description is huge or a result that fills the context stands out), and the context at each answer of the model: a stacked bar of what it was made of (the same kinds, estimated), the size the model reported as a line and the limit as a dashed line. Where the line is above the bars, the model counted more than the estimate (images, the format of the provider); a bar that drops is a compaction or a rewind.

A table of the parts with the kind, name, tokens and share of the context. Pick a row to read exactly the text the model is sent for that part: a section of the system message, the description and parameters of one tool, a message, the arguments of a call or the result of one.

Download gives the whole context as one Markdown file (the system message with its sections, every tool with its description and schema, the conversation message by message, each text in a code fence), Copy puts the same text on the clipboard.

The sizes of the parts are estimates; the number the model reported is the real one (the request and its answer). In the chart of the answers the prompt, the instructions and the tools are as they are now (an older answer may have had others if you changed them), the conversation is as it was then: a summary replaced what was before it, and what a rewind went back over is gone from the answers after it (a compaction that was itself rewound is not brought back, the bars after it are a little too small). The system message and the tools are the ones the next request would use, so a change of the prompt, the instructions or the allowed commands shows at once. The messages are the transcript as stored, without what a resume adds (a "go on", the answers to calls an interruption left open). Reasoning is not part of the context (the model is not sent it back) and images show as their file names. What a compaction replaced is not in the context either; the Run tab and the Runs download still have it.

A checkpoint is a restore point of the working copy of the run (the parts, summaries, lorebooks and the data of the extensions, with the handles the agent was given) and of the workspace of the agent, so that a job that went wrong can be undone: the agent goes back with checkpoint_restore, or you do it in the Checkpoints tab of the console. Who makes them:
Start of the run, made when the run begins. It is never rolled out.

Automatic, made by the run before a round in which the agent calls something that may change the book or the workspace (a command that is not a plain read, or a file tool that writes), and only when something changed since the last checkpoint. The last five are kept; the oldest goes when a new one is made.
Made on purpose, by the agent with checkpoint (it is told to make one before a risky step) or by you with Save a checkpoint. They stay until deleted.

All the checkpoints of a run share a quota that the administrator sets in the permission (100 MB when empty). Part of it is kept for the automatic ones, so that the agent can't use it all up; a checkpoint made on purpose that does not fit is refused, nothing is deleted behind the back of whoever asked. The agent then gets the list and deletes what it does not need (not the checkpoint of the start, and not the newest one); you can delete any in the tab. Each is an archive (a ZIP of the book as JSON, the pairs and the workspace files) you can download.

Restore makes the working copy again from the checkpoint: it is a new copy, the old one is deleted, the workspace is the saved one (files written after it are gone) and the handles of the agent for the items that were there still work. The state before is saved as an automatic checkpoint first, if there is room, so a restore can be taken back. A restore takes about as long as the start of a run (half a minute for a book of two thousand parts). You can restore while the agent does not work; the agent restores itself between two rounds and is told what came back. The checkpoints go when the run lets go of its copy.

Rewind is a restore that also takes the conversation back. A restore alone leaves the agent remembering work that is no longer in the book, so a run you want to send in another direction needs a rewind: the working copy and the workspace go back to the checkpoint, the messages after the place where the checkpoint was made are greyed in the transcript (you can still read them, and the export has them) and the agent no longer reads them, and a notice tells the agent what happened, so it does the work again if it is still needed. The run has to be paused or stopped (pause an agent that waits for you first); you Resume it afterwards and it goes on from the notice. A checkpoint can only be rewound to while its place in the conversation is still part of it: after a rewind to an earlier checkpoint the later ones (of the conversation that was undone) can only be restored. A checkpoint made before the rewind existed does not know its place and can only be restored. What a compaction did after the checkpoint is undone with the rewind; the agent reads the messages the compaction had replaced again.

Going back to a message. You do not have to pick a checkpoint: every message you wrote to the agent has a Rewind button under it in the transcript of the Run tab. It takes the conversation back to before that message: the agent forgets the message and everything after it, and the working copy and the workspace go back to the newest checkpoint that was made before it (the runner makes one before every round that changes something, so this is usually right at the message). The state of a run is only known at its checkpoints, so when the closest one is older than the message, the messages between that checkpoint and yours are forgotten too; the confirmation tells which checkpoint it is and how many messages go. The forgotten messages stay in the transcript, greyed. The button works while the agent waits for you (it is paused for it), is paused, or was stopped and kept; while the agent works it is disabled. You Resume the run afterwards, and it goes on from the notice.
A disabled agent can't be started; its runs that exist are not touched.

New agent opens the same window as Edit:

On (the default): the commands that have a model write something - the next turn, swipes, summaries, and the commands of extensions such as the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline - use the model above, whatever model your book has. Off: they use the model of your book (an extension command falls back to your default model from Settings when the book has none). That is how you mix models: a strong one that thinks and a cheaper or more fluent one that writes. A command can still name another model profile of the agent.
Optional limits of one run. The limit your administrator gave you applies in any case.
Required.
See below.
System prompt
The book the agent works on, required. Only books that have no agent are offered, and the book of an agent can't be changed later.
The model and the protocol the agent talks with. Both, or neither; an agent without them can't be started.
The model sees images
Tick it when the model takes images (the API of the model does not say, so you do). The agent then has view_image and you can attach images to your messages; without it it never gets a picture.
What happens when the agent wants a command that changes or removes data: Run them, Ask first (a window asks you to approve it) or Refuse them.
What the agent is asked when you /compact it: to write the summary that replaces its earlier work. Empty follows the default, like the system prompt, with the same info icon.

What the agent is told to be. Leave it empty and the agent follows the default - yours from Settings, else your administrator's, else the built-in one - which is shown in grey. The info icon has Insert Default Template, which fills the default in so you can edit a copy of it; clear the field again to follow the default.

When the context of the model passes this share of its limit and the agent did not compact its work itself, the run does it: the agent writes the summary of its earlier work, which replaces it. Empty is 90, zero never (the run then stops when the context is full), otherwise 50 to 99.
Write the book with the model of the agent

Your instructions to the agent, added to its prompt in every run. The agent can read them, never change them. Empty follows your default from Settings, if you have one (it is shown in grey), else there are none. Under it a line says what the prompt, the instructions and the ticked commands weigh in every request, in tokens (an estimate, with the tools for files and for the run and the notes of the runner on top).

The agent is offered only the commands you tick. The table lists every command with its effect (Destructive changes or removes data, Non-destructive only reads or adds). The Selection box ticks many at once: All, None or All non-destructive (the default for a new agent), or a role; ticking a command yourself makes the selection Custom. Commands that an extension brings stay allowed when the extension is not loaded, you just don't see them. The Tokens column is what the definition of the command (its name, description and parameters) adds to every request of the agent, and the line under the instructions adds up the ticked ones: the whole set is about 20 000 tokens, so a smaller selection (a role) leaves more room in the context for the work.
The roles are sets of commands for a job. All of them can read the book and the lorebooks (every command that only reads, those of extensions too), and none can remove data:
Role
Besides reading
Auditor
Nothing: continuity checks, name and term audits, reports.
Lore keeper
Creates and updates lorebook entries and lorebooks, their tags and sub-lorebooks.
Editor
Edits and appends to parts, sets their fields, keeps the summaries (also has the model write them again) and the book information and tags.
Drafter
Adds parts and branches, edits and appends, lets the model write the next turn (/next, /swipe), keeps the summaries, creates and updates lorebook entries of what it invents.
Every command ticked adds its definition to every request, so a role is also the cheapest way to a small prompt for a weak model.

The phone layout has an Agents tab in the drawer, for users who may use agents, with the count of the agents that need you beside its name. Each agent is a card with its name, its state and the buttons of the table (they wrap onto more lines). The windows - the console, the review, the agent's settings - fill the screen, their buttons wrap, and the review shows the table above the detail of the item. Everything works as on the desktop, only smaller; for long work with the transcript or the review a larger screen is more comfortable.

Clone asks for a name and a book that has no agent, and copies the definition of the agent and its files (not its runs) to a new agent of that book. You can have as many agents, clones included, as your administrator allows (five unless they set another number); at the limit New agent and Clone are off and say why.

While a run of an agent works or waits for you, its book is locked: you can read it, but nothing changes it, so the agent never works on text that moves under it. The book list does not open a locked book, it tells you which agent holds it, and generating, editing, search and replace, summaries and deleting the book are refused. Pause or Stop the run to edit the book again; a paused, stopped or finished run does not lock it.

The lorebooks of the book are locked with it: the lorebook the book uses and its sub-lorebooks. On the Lorebooks tab such a lorebook is shown the way it is on a phone, as plain text and without any editing, with a note that says which agent holds it; Refresh shows it for editing again after you paused or stopped the run. Other lorebooks are not affected.
(tick box)
Above the table, Type shows only one kind of object, Refresh loads the table again.
Column
Deleted

Deleted objects stay in the trash until an administrator runs the cleanup, which removes them from the database for good. Whatever the cleanup has removed can no longer be restored (only a database backup made before still has it).

Deleting in Marginalia does not destroy anything right away: a deleted book, lorebook, story part or inference provider is only marked as deleted and hidden from your lists. The Trash tab lists these deleted objects and brings them back.

Opens the saved data of the object, see below.
Selects the object for restoring. The box in the header selects all objects.
The kind of object: book, lorebook, lorebook entry, message (a story part), summary, model (inference provider), protocol, tag, resource...
The name of the object. Story parts and tag links have no name and show their id; use Extended Content to read a story part.
The table loads as you scroll. The most recently deleted objects are first.
The Trash tab

Tick the objects you want back and click Restore Selected. Marginalia asks before it restores them. The objects are back in their lists, exactly as they were deleted, and the other tabs are refreshed.

l: Objects that belong to other objects
p: Deleting an object deletes what belongs to it, and restoring it brings that back: a book takes its story parts, their summaries and its tags with it, a lorebook its entries, a story part its summary and the parts below it, an inference provider its usage numbers. You don't need to tick them: restore the book, and its story comes with it. They show up in the table as separate rows (a book with a long story fills the table with its parts); restoring one of them alone only works when the object it belongs to is not deleted. Something you had deleted on its own earlier (an entry, a story part) comes back with its lorebook or book too, as Marginalia can't tell it from what was deleted together with it.
Some objects can't live without another object:
an entry needs its lorebook,
a story part and a summary need their book,
a book needs its model (inference provider), its protocol and its lorebook, as long as it uses them,
a tag link needs its tag.
An object whose lorebook, book... is deleted can only be restored together with it: tick both. If you tick only the entry, Marginalia restores nothing and tells you what is missing:
Nothing was restored. These objects need a deleted object that is not selected. Select it too, or leave them deleted. Lorebook Entry "Dragon" needs the deleted Lorebook "Bestiary" (lorebook)
Restore refused because the lorebook of the entry is deleted too
Tick the object it names and restore again. Objects that are not deleted any more (restored in the meantime, or an object you didn't delete) are not a problem.

A story part that was deleted from the middle of a story had its following parts moved to its parent. Restoring it brings the part back under its parent as a new branch, without the parts that followed it: they stay where they were moved to. Restore a whole book instead of single parts when you want the story as it was.

Waiting for the cleanup is not always what you want: a story part or a lorebook entry you know you never need again can be removed right away. Tick it and click Delete Permanently; Marginalia asks first, and this can't be undone.
Deleting a story part for good

Only story parts and lorebook entries can be deleted permanently (with their summaries and tags). The button is disabled while anything else is ticked: books, lorebooks and the rest wait for the administrator's cleanup, so you can't remove a whole book by accident.

Story parts that are below a removed part are not removed with it, whether they are deleted or not: they move to its parent, as when you delete a part in the editor. If the part was the position a book was open at, the book opens at the parent instead.
Marginalia deletes nothing when something can't be removed (for example an extension still needs the object) and tells you which one.

Marginalia keeps much of an object's data (the text of a story part, the settings of a lorebook entry, notes that extensions saved) as JSON next to it. Extended Content in a row shows it, so you can check what an object contains before you restore it, for example to find the right story part. Objects without such data (resources) have no link; an object that has none shows This object has no extended content.

Administrators see the deleted objects of all users and can restore any of them. The User filter above the table shows the objects of one user; the User column tells whose they are. Restored objects go back to their owner.
The same table is in Admin → Cleanup (Trash), so you can see what the next cleanup removes. Objects of a deleted user can't be restored: they depend on the user.
The phone layout can only select lorebooks, enable and disable them and their entries, and edit the content of an entry. Everything else on these pages needs the desktop layout.

A lorebook holds what the model must know about your world: characters, places, history, rules, terminology. Each piece of knowledge is an entry. Before every generated part, Marginalia decides which entries are relevant and puts them into the prompt - so the model knows who Captain Varro is when he walks into the scene, without every entry taking up space in every prompt.
The lorebook editor
A book uses one lorebook (on its Lorebook tab).

A lorebook can include other lorebooks as sub lorebooks. Their entries take part too, so you can keep shared material (a world used by several books, a cast of characters) in its own lorebook and include it where needed.
Each entry has the text that goes into the prompt, and conditions that decide when it is used.

c:
Book ──uses──▶ Lorebook "Saga" ──sub lorebooks──▶ "Characters", "Places", "Magic"
                   │                                   │
                 entries                             entries

p: For each generated part, an entry is activated when all of these are true:
the entry and its lorebook are enabled;
its tags fit the book's tags (if it has any);
its filter matches the instructions for the part (if it has one).
Activated entries are inserted in their order - into the lore block of the system prompt, or right before the request for the part. See Entries & activation.
Entries without tags and without a filter are always active: use them for what the model must always know.
Lorebook entries can use templates and macros - SillyTavern world info keeps working.
SillyTavern world info can be imported.
Book backups contain the book's lorebook with its sub lorebooks.
The Lore Generator extension writes the content of an entry with the model, from the lore you already have.
The Lorebook VCS extension keeps a revision history of entries.
Creating lorebooks - the lorebook editor, sub lorebooks, using a lorebook in a book

The two tags buttons of the toolbar open one window that puts a tag on many items, or takes it off them: Tag lorebooks lists your lorebooks, Tag entries the entries of the selected lorebook. Pick the Tag (or type a new one and press Enter); the list shows every item with its tags, and the items that have the picked tag come first with the tag highlighted. A row's + and - buttons apply or remove the tag for that item; tick several items (the box in the header ticks all) and use Apply the tag to the checked or Remove the tag from the checked at the bottom to do it for all of them. The tags it puts on entries are the ordinary ones, see Tags; negative tags are set on the entry itself.

l: Using a lorebook in a book
p: Open the book and its Lorebook tab, and pick the lorebook in the Lorebook field. The editor below shows the lorebook, so you can add and change entries while you write. Clear the field to write without a lorebook.
A book uses one lorebook. To use several, create a lorebook that includes them as sub lorebooks, and use that one.
The same lorebook can be used by any number of books. Changes to it affect all of them from the next generated part on; parts that were already written keep the lore they were written with.
Sub Lorebooks includes the entries of other lorebooks in this one. A typical setup:
Sub lorebooks can have sub lorebooks of their own; all levels are included.
A lorebook can be a sub lorebook of several lorebooks. When it is reached more than once, its entries are still used only once.
A lorebook can't include itself, directly or through other lorebooks: such a choice is refused with Cannot select sub lorebook: cycle detected.
A disabled sub lorebook is left out together with everything it includes.
The entries of all included lorebooks are put together and sorted by their order, regardless of which lorebook they come from.

Delete Lorebook removes the lorebook from your lists. Books that used it no longer get its entries, and lorebooks that included it as a sub lorebook skip it. The data stays in the database until an administrator runs Cleanup, and until then you can restore the lorebook from the Trash; copies in book backups and exported files are not affected.

Search and replace (right of Add Entry) changes a word, a name or a phrase in the name, the text and the comment of all the entries of the lorebook at once. It works like the search and replace of the story, without the options for summaries and branches: Search lists the entries with matches (the table shows their names) and the matches in them as they are and as they will be, Replace changes the entries. It has the options Search by regex (see Regular expressions) and Case sensitive (on by default; locked while the regex is on, which can use (?i) to ignore the case). Entries that are disabled are searched too. On the phone the button (an icon next to the Enabled check box) opens the same window in the phone layout.

Before each generated part, Marginalia goes through the entries of the book's lorebook and its sub lorebooks. An entry is activated when:
the entry is enabled, and so is its lorebook;
none of its negative tags is a tag of the book;
it has no tags, or at least one of them is a tag of the book;
it has no filter, or the filter matches the instructions for the part.
All conditions must hold. An entry without tags and filter is always active.
Tags connect entries with book tags (set on the book's About tab). Use them to share one lorebook between books that need different parts of it:
Entry tags
Negative tags
Active in a book tagged...
always
winter
winter, book-2
winter or book-2
book-1
anything but book-1
winter, unless it is also book-1
Tags must match exactly. A negative tag always wins over a tag.
Tags can also be given to a whole lorebook (the Tags field of the lorebook; lorebooks imported from files can carry them). They then count as tags of each of its entries.

A filter activates the entry only when the request for the part mentions it. It is matched against the user prompt of the part as it is sent - the Scene Setting, POV Character, Present Characters and Instructions you entered, inside the wording of the user prompt template.
Mode
Matches when
Text
The text appears anywhere in the request, ignoring upper and lower case. varro matches Captain Varro.
Regex
The regular expression matches anywhere in the request, ignoring case, across lines.
For example, the regex \b(varro|captain)\b matches the whole word Varro or Captain, and varro.*(harbor|docks) matches only when Varro and the harbor or the docks are both mentioned, in that order.

Filters check the instructions for the new part only, not the text of earlier parts. An entry about Varro is activated when Varro is mentioned in the scene, characters or instructions of the part you are writing - put him into Present Characters when he is in the scene.
The request also contains the text of the user prompt template itself. A filter for a word the template uses (the default one mentions characters, plot, tone...) is always active.
An invalid regular expression never matches; the entry stays inactive.
Combine tags and a filter when an entry should only be used in some books, and there only when it's relevant.

Activated entries are put into the prompt sorted by Order, lowest first. Entries with the same order keep the order in which they were created. Entries from all included lorebooks are sorted together.

The import always creates new lorebooks - the lorebook and its sub lorebooks, with the same structure - even when you already have lorebooks with the same names. The imported lorebook is selected in the editor. Tags are matched by name with your existing tags, or created.
Files from older Marginalia versions (a single lorebook without sub lorebooks) can be imported too.
Lorebooks also travel inside book backups. Restoring or cloning a backup can link to lorebooks you already have instead of creating copies; see Restoring a backup.

You don't need to read these expressions; edit them only if you know regular expressions.

c: (?s)^(?=.*(?:\Qdragon\E|\Qwyrm\E))(?=.*(?:\Qfire\E))

p: SillyTavern settings without a Marginalia counterpart are listed in the entry's Note, for example Imported from SillyTavern, not supported: probability 50%, inclusion group "weather". These are:
probability, inclusion groups, sticky, cooldown and delay - the entry is simply active whenever it matches;
insertion at depth - the entry goes before the user prompt instead.

The biggest difference is what the keys are matched against. SillyTavern scans the recent chat; Marginalia matches the request for the part being written - its scene, characters and instructions - not the earlier story. An entry that SillyTavern activated because a name came up in the last messages is activated in Marginalia when you mention the name in the turn instructions. Recursive activation (entries activating other entries) is not supported either.
After importing, look through the entries and decide which should be always active, which keep their filters, and which are better handled with tags.

Commands are small actions you run by typing them, instead of clicking through menus: look something up in the story or the lorebooks, search and replace, take a backup. Extensions add commands of their own, for example to generate a lore entry or to make up names. The same commands are what an agent works with, so a command does one clear thing and says what it does: you can read it while you type.
The command line is the field next to the menu below the story, in the story editor.

Click into the command line and type /. The list shows all the commands, each with its name and a short description. Typing more narrows the list: the filter looks at the name of the command, its title and its description.

Pick the command with the mouse, or with the arrow keys and Enter. A command that needs nothing runs at once; for one that takes arguments, /name is written into the field and you continue with the arguments. The list of commands, opened by typing a slash

Type the arguments and press Enter, or click the play button next to the field, to run it. The field is emptied as soon as the command starts; a text that is not a command stays, so you can correct it.
Text that does not start with / is not a command, and nothing is run. Clicking away from the field or pressing Esc never runs anything, so you cannot start a command by accident.
While you type, a small window opens above the field. It covers part of the story but moves nothing, and it closes when you leave the field or run the command. It shows:
what the command does,
the forms the command has (see Forms) that fit what you have typed so far, with the argument you are typing now highlighted and its description,
what the command returns,
a hint when you have typed more arguments than the command takes, or when no command has that name.
The help of /search-replace-lore-entries while its second argument is typed
While you are still typing the name, the list of commands is the help.
