One command can take different arguments: /hello-world with nothing, and /hello-world something with one argument are two forms of the same command. Marginalia picks the form by the number of arguments you typed and by what they look like. If no form fits, a notification says that the command does not take these arguments, and the help shows the forms it does have.

When a command returns something, it is shown in a window above the command line. Close it with the cross, with Esc, or just carry on: it disappears when you type something new or run another command. A command that returns nothing shows no window.
The result of /take-backup above the command line
If a command fails, or there is no such command, you get a notification with the reason.

Most commands answer at once. A command that needs time shows a window with an animated bar and a Stop button, and the story is locked until the command is done. Under the bar the command can say what it is doing now and, in smaller letters, the detail of the step. Stop cancels the command; it should return immediately. You can try it with /hello-world-async.
The window of a command that is running
Every command says what it does to the data that already exists, and the command bar shows it as a small label next to the command, in the list and in the help:
Destructive (red) - the command changes or removes data that exists, like the search and replace commands that rewrite the book. Point at the label to see the explanation.
Non-destructive (green) - the command only reads data or adds new data, like /take-backup, which adds a backup and changes nothing else.

The label is information for you; it does not stop the command when you run it. An agent goes by it: it is not given a destructive command, or has to ask you first, or runs it, as set for that agent. A command that asks for confirmation by itself is described below.

A command that changes a lot can ask before it does. The search and replace commands have no preview, so after the search they show how many matches they found in how many items and what would be replaced by what, and only Yes changes the book; No leaves everything as it was. The question stays until you answer it.

Search and replace in the story of the open book, like the Search and replace window of the story tab. The options are true/false, in this order, and each one you leave out has the default of that window (regex no, case sensitive yes, summaries yes, all branches no, revalidate yes); to set one, give those before it too. maxHits refuses a replace that finds more matches than that, and with dryRun true nothing is changed: the answer counts the matches and shows a few, which is how an agent looks before it replaces. There is no preview: after the search you are asked whether to replace the number of matches found, and only Yes changes the book. The replace cannot be stopped.

What it does

Which entries a generation would use for a text, or for a turn like the one that made a part, and why (no filter, filter found, or not used because it is switched off, a tag of the book decides, or the filter is not in the text), with the lore text and its tokens. The text may be the handle of a part.

The commands above that read the book (/get-book-info to /get-template-variables) change nothing; they answer in JSON text, so an agent can use them as well. Every row of an answer has a handle: the identifier of the part (or lorebook, or entry), which does not change when parts are added, moved or deleted. A part is given by its handle, or by its position on a branch, the first part of the story being 1; a branch by the handle of any part of it, or by its number from /list-branches (the numbers follow the creation of the ends of the branches, so they change when a branch is added or deleted). Positions and numbers are easier to type, handles are what an agent should use, and the commands that change the story take handles only. Without a branch the commands work on the active branch. Lists are paged with offset and limit, long texts are cut into slices (offset, length) and the answer says the total length. As with the other commands the options are positional: to set one, give those before it too.

The commands that read the lorebooks (/list-lorebooks to /preview-lore-activation) work the same way and reach only the lorebooks of the open book: the root lorebook and its subbooks. A lorebook is its handle or its number from /list-lorebooks (the root is 1), an entry its handle or its number in the lorebook, in the order of the lorebook (the first entry is 1); the numbers change when entries or subbooks are added or removed. Without a lorebook the root lorebook is used.

The commands that have the model write (/next, /swipe, /regenerate, the two summaries) take time and show the Stop window.

These commands change the open book (or the working copy of an agent, which is where an agent's changes go). A part, lorebook or entry is always given by its handle, never by a position or a number: those move when something is added or deleted, and a position that was right when it was read may be another part by the time it is written. The options are positional as before. A command that removes text or data is DESTRUCTIVE and asks you to confirm (an agent is covered by its destructive mode instead); adding and changing are not. An edit of the story can make summaries outdated (a summary carries the hash of the story it describes): the answer lists them and says what to do, /revalidate-summaries if they are still right, /regenerate-summary if not.
What it does

A regular expression (regex) is a short pattern that describes text instead of spelling it out: "the word Harry, but not Harrys", "any two words in quotes", "three or more spaces in a row". Marginalia uses them in two places:
Search and replace of the story and of a lorebook, and the matching commands, when Search by regex is on. The pattern finds the text, the replacement can reuse pieces of it.
The Regex filter of a lorebook entry, which decides when the entry goes into the prompt.
The dialect is the one of Java. This page shows what you will use most; the complete reference is linked at the end.

You do not need regexes for plain words. With Search by regex off the text is searched exactly as typed, so a . or a ( in it is just a dot or a bracket. Turn the regex on only when a single fixed text is not enough.
[^] is anything but a quote
[^abc]
[abc] [a-z]
\. is a dot, \? a question mark, \( a bracket
\.{3} is three dots in a row

\bcat\b finds cat but not concatenate

\d\d finds 42
^Chapter finds Chapter at the start of a line

a letter or a digit
A match of no length at all (a pattern like a* that can match nothing) is ignored by Search and replace.
any one character (not a line break)

Brackets make a group, and a vertical bar inside a group is "or": (Mr|Mrs) Dursley finds Mr Dursley and Mrs Dursley, and \b(Voldemort|You-Know-Who)\b finds either name. A ?, * or + after a group applies to all of it: (very )+good finds very good and very very good.

By default a regex ignores nothing: harry does not find Harry. Put (?i) at the start to ignore the case: (?i)harry finds Harry, HARRY and harry. (The Search and replace windows lock Case sensitive while the regex is on, so this is how you switch it off there; the lorebook Regex filter always ignores the case.)

l: Taking the match into the replacement
p: Everything a regex puts in round brackets is a group, numbered from the left by its opening bracket: the replacement $1 is the text of the first group, $2 of the second, $0 all of the match. In (\w+), (\w+) the first group is the word before the comma, the second the word after it, so $2 $1 swaps them: Potter, Harry becomes Harry Potter.
You can name a group, (?last\w+), (?first\w+), and use the name in the replacement: ${first} ${last}.
A $ or a \ that should stay as itself in the replacement has to be escaped: to put $5 into the text, write \$5. Without the regex the replacement is always taken exactly as typed.
If the pattern is wrong (a bracket that is never closed) or the replacement names a group the pattern does not have, a notification says so and nothing happens; a search never changes anything.
A lookahead (?=...) and a lookbehind (?=...) look at the text around the match without taking it, so only the part outside them is replaced:
Search
Finds
Harry(?= Potter)
Harry only when Potter follows (and leaves Potter alone)
(?=Professor )McGonagall
McGonagall only after Professor
Harry(?! Potter)
Harry not followed by Potter
* and + take as much as they can: in He said yes and no the pattern .* matches the whole yes and no. Add a ? (.*?), or say what is not allowed ([^]*), to stop at the first closing quote.
The search treats every line on its own: . does not cross a line break, and ^ and $ match at the start and the end of every line of a part, not only of the whole text. To match a line break write \n.

The filter of a lorebook entry set to Regex is matched against the request for the part, anywhere in it. It ignores the case, and . does match line breaks there, so varro.*harbor finds Varro and the harbor even on different lines. Typical filters:
\bvarro\b - Varro as a whole word.
\b(varro|captain)\b - Varro or the captain.
varro.*(harbor|docks) - Varro and then, later, the harbor or the docks.
dragons? - dragon or dragons.
(?!no )magic - magic, unless it stands right after no.
An invalid regex never activates the entry, and the reason is written to the log. See entries and activation for the rest of how an entry is chosen.

/search-replace-parts and /search-replace-lore-entries take the regex as the third argument (true), after the search and the replacement. The command line splits on spaces, so a pattern or a replacement with a space is put in double quotes. A backslash in front of a letter is passed on as it is (\b, \d), but \\ becomes a single backslash and \ a quote, so a literal backslash in the pattern is \\\\.

The commands show no list of matches: they ask you whether to replace the number of matches found. When you are not sure about a pattern, try it first in the Search and replace window, which shows every match as it is and as it will be.

c:
/search-replace-parts "\bHarry\b" Henry true
/search-replace-parts "(\w+), (\w+)" "$2 $1" true
/search-replace-parts "(?i)\bharry\b" Henry true

p: Try a pattern with Search first and open a few of the rows: the window shows each match with its surroundings, as it is and as it will be. Replace only when the result is what you wanted.
Start simple and add to the pattern step by step; a pattern that finds too much usually needs \b around a word, or ? to stop a *.
A backup before a big replace is cheap (/take-backup), and a replace cannot be stopped once it has started.
Changed summaries: when the replace touches the text that a summary was made from, the window warns that the summary would become outdated; see Search and replace.

This page covers the basics. Java's full syntax, with every construct, flag and character class, is in the documentation of java.util.regex.Pattern, and the replacement syntax ($1, ${name}, \$) in Matcher.appendReplacement.

Extensions are installed by an administrator for the whole Marginalia installation, in Admin → Extensions: they are JAR files, uploaded with Load Extension (.jar). See Managing extensions for the details.
Once installed, an extension is available to every user. An extension loaded while Marginalia runs shows up in windows opened afterwards: close and reopen a book (or reload the page) to see it.

Extensions hook into the user interface of one Marginalia version. An extension built for a different version may stop working or break parts of the application. Use the extensions that come with your version of Marginalia.
The thirteen extensions above are part of the Marginalia source code (marginalia/plugins) and are built separately; see the plugins README.

The phone layout has its own classes, so an extension has to support it. Arc Outline, Author's Note, Chapter Marker, Character Tracker, Instruction Exporter and Reviewer do; Side Query, Lore Generator and Lorebook VCS add nothing on a phone (see Using Marginalia on a phone). Name generator, Name provider, Gemma 4 tools fix and Google Gemini have no screens of their own (Google Gemini only adds a provider to the model dialog, which a phone has as well), and Chinese localization is in the language selector of the phone menu. Extensions are installed from the Admin page, which a phone doesn't have.

Extensions with settings add a section to Settings → Extension Settings (the third tab of the Settings page). These settings belong to your account, like the rest of Settings, and are saved with its Save button.

Extensions keep their data together with the data it belongs to - reviews with the story part, conversations with the book, revisions with the lorebook - so it is included in database backups. Whether it is also part of book backups and exports is described on each extension's page.
Uninstalling an extension doesn't delete its data: installing it again brings it back.

A note to the model that is sent with every generation of the book: the tone you want right now, what the current chapter is about, a reminder the model keeps forgetting. Unlike the instructions of a turn, the note stays until you change it.
The left sidebar of the story editor gets an Author's Note tab next to Outline. Changes are saved to the book as you type and used by the next generation.
Field
Insert into prompt
Turns the note on or off without deleting it.
Insertion depth

Where the note goes, counted in messages from the end of the prompt: 0 - after the instructions of the turn (the very last message), 1 - right before them, 2 - before the last story part, and so on. A large depth puts the note right after the system prompt.
Role
Whether the note is sent as a System, User or Assistant message.
Author's Note
The text sent to the model. An empty note is not sent. Below it, an estimate of its size in tokens.
Author's Note (private)
Notes for yourself - plans, reminders. Never sent to the model.
The closer the note is to the end of the prompt, the stronger its effect. Depth 1 with role System is a good start. The note is not processed as a template: macros are sent as they are written.

A generation sends the system prompt first, then the story as a chat - each part as an answer of the model to Generate story - and the instructions of the turn last. With depth 1 the note is inserted right before the instructions:
system prompt (template, lore, summaries)
story parts…
the Author's Note
the instructions of the turn

The note's tokens are taken from the room for the story: a longer note means fewer story parts in the prompt. A note that doesn't leave room even for the rest of the prompt stops the generation with Contextual limit not sufficient.
The note is stored with the book, so it is part of book backups and copies.

Pick it and the page reloads in Chinese; the choice is saved in your account, so it is used on every device you log in on. Every user picks their own language.

l: The outline as a source for other extensions
p: The outline is offered to other extensions as a source of data about the book: in Side Query check Arc outline in the plug popover to send the arcs, their states, descriptions and chapters with your questions. There are two versions: Arc outline is the terse one (descriptions only), Arc outline (with notes) adds the note of every arc and chapter under its description, which is where the details of generated arcs and chapters are. Your private notes are sent only when you check the second one.
Generate

On the right you see the reasoning of the model as it is written and, as soon as the answer begins, the arc it proposes - a name, a terse description and a longer note - shown like an arc of the outline (the note under its description) and growing as the answer streams in. The description is what the outline shows, so the model is asked to keep it to a couple of sentences and to put the details into the note, which ends up in the Note of the saved arc. When the model is done, its answer is checked; if it is not a valid arc (for example the note is missing), the dialog says so and the arc can't be saved.

l: Importing an arc from the story
p: Import from story in the menu of the wand asks the model to read a part of your story and write it down as one arc with its chapters, so you can bring a book you have already written into the outline. The model always reads the active branch of the book, as it is when you open the dialog. The dialog is like the one for arcs, with these choices on the left:
From message, To message
The range of the story to send. The messages of the branch that have text are numbered from 1; at first the whole branch is chosen. Under each field you see the beginning of the message it points to.
Number of chapters (optional)
Choose a number to get exactly that many chapters (an answer with another number is rejected), leave it empty to let the model divide the story where it naturally divides.
State of the imported arc and its chapters
Finished at first, because the story is written; choose Current or Planned if you need it.
Token counter

How many messages the range has and their approximate tokens, and the approximate tokens of the whole prompt (instructions, lore, outline and story) next to what the model takes. It turns into a warning when the prompt does not fit, then choose fewer messages. It follows the range, the number of chapters, the prompt and the model.
Prompt
The instructions for the model, with the variables , , (the messages of the range) and. It starts as the Story import prompt of Settings → Extension Settings → Arc Outline.

There are no name tools here, the names are in the story. On the right you see the reasoning, then the arc and its chapters as the model writes them. Save as arc adds the arc with its chapters at the end of the outline; every one of them keeps the reasoning and the answer of the model and has its own robot button. A long story is best imported in several steps, one arc for each range.
The wand button on an arc asks the model to divide that arc into chapters. The dialog is like the one for arcs, with these choices on the left:
What the model knows of the story

Whole story so far: the arcs up to this one, with all their chapters. Arc summaries only: the same arcs without chapters. Arc summaries and finished chapters: the same arcs with only the chapters you marked Finished. Arcs after this one are never sent.
What you want from the chapters in general
Pace, tone, what must happen. Can be empty.
Number of chapters

Write it in words ("about eight") or choose an exact number. A number adds a text area for each chapter where you can say what it should contain; all of them are optional. Using one of the two clears the other. With an exact number, an answer with a different number of chapters is rejected.
Prompt
The instructions for the model, with the variables , , , and ``. It starts as the Chapter generation prompt of Settings → Extension Settings → Arc Outline.

On the right you see the reasoning, then the arc with the chapters it already has, and the new chapters as the model writes them. Save as chapters adds them at the end of the arc, each with a terse description and the details in its note (like arcs). Every new chapter keeps the reasoning and the answer of the model, and has its own robot button.
Generating the chapters of an arc
An arc or chapter written by the model keeps its reasoning and the answer it came from. The robot button on it opens them in a small popover, out of the way.

The outline and its generators are also commands, for the command line and for agents. They work on the book that is open (an agent: on its working copy), and an open Arcs tab shows the change at once. Arcs and chapters are given by number, as the outline shows them: the first arc is 1, the first chapter of an arc is 1 (the numbers change when something before them is added, removed or moved). A command that changes an arc or a chapter takes only the fields you give it; an empty text clears a description or a note.

The three generating commands use the same prompts as the dialogs (your Extension Settings → Arc Outline, or the defaults), the model and protocol of the book (your default model when the book has none) and no name tools: a caller that wants names gets them with the commands of the Name generator or the Name provider and writes them into the specification. Like the dialogs they save only when asked: with save false (the default) they return the arc or the chapters as JSON and store nothing, with save true they add them to the outline (an arc at the end, chapters at the end of the arc) and the answer has their numbers. A story that is too long for the model is refused by /import-arc-from-story: choose fewer messages. The generating commands take a while, and stop when the run is stopped.

When you open an existing character, the dialog also lists its relationships: the ones the character points to (→), the ones that point to it (←) and the unidirectional ones (↔), each with a name and a tagline. The trash button deletes a relationship.

To add one, search for the other character, choose the Direction (this character → other, other → this character or both ways), enter a Name (e.g. employs, friends) and optionally a Tagline, and press Add relationship (the button is above these fields). Relationships are saved at once. A new character can get relationships after it has been saved.

If your characters are already in the lorebook, the wand menu creates them for you. Import lore entries as characters opens a dialog with the entries of the book's lorebook and of all its sub lorebooks, sorted by their order. Each shows its name and a checkbox, and an i icon that shows the content of the entry in a popover, for a quick look before you decide; the checkbox in the header of the list checks or clears all of them. Import creates a character with the name of every checked entry (the tagline, note, icon and color stay empty for you to fill in), Close leaves without importing.
Entries are not compared with the characters you already have: importing the same entry twice creates two characters.

Relationship map shows all relationships of the book as a graph. Every character that has a relationship is a circle with its icon (or a box without one) on its color, with its name and tagline; every relationship is an arrow between two characters with its name and tagline. An arrow points at the target; a unidirectional relationship has an arrow at both ends. Characters without relationships are not in the map.

The characters are arranged in rings around one character - at first the one with the most relationships: the characters it is related to are on the first ring, theirs on the second and so on. Double-click a character to arrange the map around it. You can also drag the characters, move the map and zoom with the mouse wheel.

Chapters in the outline
When the text of a part contains a Markdown heading - a line starting with # - the part's entry in the outline shows the heading instead of the usual #n (DB ID: m) label, highlighted:
shows in the outline as 5. Chapter 3: The Harbour - the number is the part's position in the branch, followed by the heading. Parts without a heading keep their normal label.
The heading can be on any line of the part; when there are several, the first one is used.
Any heading level works (#, ##, ###...).
The outline updates as soon as you save an edit: add a heading to start a chapter, remove it to merge the part back.

c:
# Chapter 3: The Harbour

Rain had been falling on Ostra since dawn...

p: There is nothing to configure. Either write the heading into the part yourself, or ask the model for it in the instructions, e.g. Start a new chapter titled "The Harbour" with a Markdown heading.
The default user prompt tells the model not to write titles or chapter headings. When you want the model to write them, say so explicitly in the instructions, or change that rule in the user prompt.
The headings are part of the story text, so they are also sent to the model and shown in the viewer and in backups.
The same rule finds the chapters in the table of contents of exported books.
Copies the instructions of the story, with the scene setting, POV character and present characters, to the clipboard.

The extension adds Export instructions to the settings menu (⚙) of the story editor. It goes over the parts of the active branch, from the first part to the current end of the story, collects the fields each part was generated from and copies them as one text. Every filled field is written as its name followed by a colon and its contents on the next line; the parts are separated by a blank line, in the order of the story:
Export instructions in the settings menu

Empty fields are left out, and so are parts with nothing filled in. Paste the text anywhere - to keep the plot outline of the book, to reuse the instructions in another book or to hand them to someone else.

c:
Scene Setting:
A harbour town at dawn
POV Character:
Mara
Present Characters:
Mara, the harbourmaster
Instructions:
Mara arrives and is questioned.

Scene Setting:
...

p: There is nothing to configure. Open a book and choose Export instructions in the settings menu; a notice confirms that the text is on the clipboard. When the branch has none of these fields filled in, nothing is copied and you are told so.
Only the active branch is exported - to export another one, switch to it first.
Browsers only allow a page to write to the clipboard when it is opened over https:// or on localhost. Over plain http:// on another address the item has no effect.
Makes function calling work with Gemma 4 models whose API expects another role for the results of the calls.

When the model calls a function, Marginalia sends the result back to it in a message with the role tool. Some servers that run Gemma 4 expect the role tool_responses instead, and answer an error or ignore the result otherwise.

The extension changes the role for such models: when the Model of an inference provider contains gemma4 or gemma-4 (in any letter case), the results of function calls to it are sent as tool_responses. Requests to other models are not touched. It is a port of the SillyTavern extension SillyTavern-Gemma4-Tools-Fix.
There is nothing to configure. Load the extension in Admin → Extensions; it applies to the next request.
Adds Google's Gemini models as an inference provider, over Google's own API instead of an OpenAI-compatible one.

Google also offers an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which works with the normal OpenAI Compatible provider. This extension talks to the Gemini API directly (the Google Gen AI SDK), which gives the things the compatible endpoint doesn't: the summaries of the model's thinking shown as reasoning, the thinking level of Gemini 3 and the thinking budget of the earlier models, the safety filters, and the exact token counts Google reports.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions, as described in Managing extensions. The JAR is large (about 14 MB): it contains Google's SDK and the libraries only the SDK needs. Nothing else in Marginalia uses them.

Once it is loaded, the Type list of the inference provider dialog has a new entry, Extension, and the Provider list at the top of the Per Type Settings tab offers Google Gemini (it is chosen for you while it is the only one). Without a loaded extension that provides AIs, Extension is not offered.
Api Key
Field
Fill in the General Settings (context size, response size, reasoning) and the settings of the provider on the Per Type Settings tab, then click Test Connection.
Get an API key in Google AI Studio.
How long to wait for Google to answer, and for more text once it started writing. The default is 300.
How often a request is repeated when Google answers with a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx), or cannot be reached. The default is 2, 0 turns retrying off.
Model
On the Inference Providers tab click Add Inference Provider, enter a Name, choose the type Extension and the provider Google Gemini.
Optional. Empty uses Google's API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com), set it to send the requests through a proxy.
Retries

Sends BLOCK_NONE for the adjustable safety categories (harassment, hate speech, sexually explicit, dangerous content). Fiction often runs into the filters. Google still blocks some content whatever is sent.
Test Connection lists the models and asks the chosen one for a few tokens, with the values in the dialog (before you save them).
The general settings of a provider of the type Extension
The Inference Providers list with a Google Gemini provider
The key of Google AI Studio. It is stored encrypted and not shown again; when you edit the provider, click Reset to enter another one.
The model to use, e.g. gemini-2.5-flash or gemini-3-pro-preview. Refresh lists the models your key can use for writing text; you can type a name that is not in the list.
The Per Type Settings of the Google Gemini provider
The provider is then on the list like any other, with the name of the provider in the Type column:
Timeout (seconds)
Turn off the safety filters
URL
The reasoning settings are those of the general settings of the provider, like for any provider:
With Enabled Reasoning off the model thinks as it does by default and its thinking is not shown.

With it on, the model sends the summaries of its thinking and they are shown as the reasoning of the story part. The Reasoning Effort sets how much it thinks: for Gemini 3 models it is the thinking level (low, medium, high), for the earlier models a budget of 1 024, 8 192 or 24 576 thinking tokens. None is the same as off.

Thinking tokens count as generated tokens, and they are taken from the response size you set: if the model uses it all for thinking, the story part comes back empty and the error says the response size was used up. Raise Max Response Tokens or lower the effort.

Everything a story needs works as with an OpenAI-compatible provider: streaming, stopping a generation, summaries, extensions that call the model, functions the model can call (the Name generator offers some), and images and files attached to a message. The tokens a user uses are counted in the Tokens sent and Tokens generated columns from the numbers Google reports, and the limits of a shared provider apply.
The token counts shown in the story (the size of a part, the prompt) are an estimate made by Marginalia, not Google's own count, so they differ a little from what Google bills.

l: When the extension is not loaded
p: The providers you created stay in the list when the extension is unloaded, with the type Extension: google-genai, and work again when the extension is loaded. While it is not loaded, a book that uses such a provider can't generate: the error tells you to load the extension or to choose another provider. The provider can still be opened and its general settings changed; the Gemini settings are only shown when the extension is loaded, and they are not touched.
Vertex AI (Google Cloud with a project and credentials). Only API keys of the Gemini API are supported.
Image generation and the other output types of Gemini: only text is written.

Revision history for lorebook entries: keep earlier versions of your lore and switch between them - for example the state of the world before and after a war, or a character at different points of the story.
Lorebook VCS is not available in the phone layout.
A revision is a snapshot of the whole entry: name, content, note, enabled, order, filter and filtering mode, insertion mode, tags and negative tags.
The revision bar of an entry
‹ / ›, or the list
A typical use:
Change revision 2 to the character after the events of chapter 10.
Control
Deletes the current revision and switches to the previous one. The last remaining revision can't be deleted.
n / total, Modified
Open the entry of a character and click + - revision 2 is a copy of revision 1.

Revisions work like slots. The entry always shows one of them - the current revision - and what you change in the entry belongs to that revision. Generation always uses the entry as it is, so the current revision is the one the model sees.
Saves the entry as it is now as a new revision and makes it current.
Switch to the previous / next / chosen revision. Your edits stay in the revision you leave; the other one is loaded into the entry.
The first time an entry's details are opened, its current state becomes revision 1.
Which revision is current, and when it was last changed.
With the extension installed, the details (⌄) of every lorebook entry start with a revision bar:
Write. When you go back to edit chapter 5, switch to revision 1 with ‹; switch back with › later.
The lorebook editor gets a Lorebook Revisions row with two buttons. They work on the lorebook selected in the editor:
Button
export
Downloads the history of all entries of the lorebook as lorebook_vcs_history.json.
import
Import Marginalia VCS JSON - a history exported by this extension; Import SillyTavern VCS Extension JSON - history from SillyTavern's lorebook version history extension.
An import replaces the history of the lorebook; when the lorebook already has a history, or the file was exported from a different lorebook, the import asks for confirmation first.

A Marginalia history is matched to the entries by the entries themselves first. Entries it doesn't find - for example when the history comes from another copy of the lorebook - are matched by the name and order of their current revision, or by the name alone when only one entry has it. Histories that match no entry are skipped; the confirmation says how many.

SillyTavern history is matched to the entries by their position in the lorebook, so import it into a lorebook imported from the same world info, before you add or delete entries. The trigger keys of its revisions become the entry's filter, the same way the world info import converts them.
The history is stored in the database with the lorebook, so database backups include it. It is not part of lorebook exports or of the lorebooks in book backups.

Importing a lorebook creates new entries. To move the history to an imported copy, export it from the original and import it into the copy - the entries are then matched by name and order (see Lorebook revisions).

Lets the model write the content of a lorebook entry for you. It reads the lore you already have, so the new entry fits the world, and compacts the result into the short, dense form lore entries work best in.
Lore Generator is not available in the phone layout.

With the extension installed, every row of the lorebook editor gets a wand button (Generate lore entry). It opens the generator for that entry. If the entry already has content, the dialog says so at the top: copying the result to the entry replaces the content.

The generator starts with your Default Model and Default Protocol from Settings, see Account & settings. The Model and Protocols lists under the header of the dialog let you use another model or protocol for this generation (the choice is not saved); the protocol is optional. Without a model it only shows a warning.
The lore generator
The two choices at the top of the dialog decide which lore goes into the request:
Choice
Current Lorebook (default) / All Lore
Only the entries of the lorebook the entry is in, ignoring its sub lorebooks; or the entries of that lorebook together with all its sub lorebooks.
Only up to position (n) (default) / All entries

n is the order of the entry. Only the entries that come before it are shown (a lower order, or the same order and created earlier), so the model builds on what already exists and doesn't get lore that was written after the entry. All entries shows everything.

The entry you are generating is never included, with or without content. Whether other entries or lorebooks are enabled, their tags and filters and their insertion mode are ignored: what you pick here is what is sent, in the order the entries are inserted into a prompt. The templates of the entries are processed as usual.

The generation prompt is what you ask the model to write. The prompts are listed in the box next to the choices, in the same top row; the text of the selected one is in the text area on the left, and you can change it for a single generation without saving. The two halves of the dialog are separated by a splitter you can drag.
Button
Save
Saves the text under the selected name.
Save as
Asks for a name and saves the text as a new prompt (or replaces one of that name, after asking).
Delete
Deletes the selected prompt. When the last one is deleted, the built-in DEFAULT prompt comes back.

The built-in prompt has placeholders in brackets (the subject, the details to include, the length, the structure): fill them in before you run it. Prompts belong to your account, and the one you used last is selected again the next time the dialog opens.
The right side has two tabs.

Generation - Run Generation sends the lore followed by the generation prompt. The answer appears as it is written, with the model's reasoning (when it gives any) in a Thinking Process section above it. Stop (in place of Run Generation) ends it early; what was written so far is kept.

Compaction - available once there is a generation. Run Compaction sends the same lore followed by the compaction prompt, with the generated text in it, and the model condenses it into a compact entry. The compaction prompt is set in Settings → Extension Settings → Lore Generator; when it is empty, the built-in one is used (it strips the prose and keeps the facts). Running the generation again discards the compaction.
The compaction of a generated entry
While the model is working, all controls are frozen except Stop; you can't close the dialog either.

When you Copy to Lore Entry, the options of that generation are stored with the entry: the prompt text, which saved prompt it came from, the lore and entries choices and the checked name categories. Opening the generator for that entry again restores them, taking priority over the prompt you used last and your saved name categories. An entry that was never generated into opens with the usual defaults. The options belong to the entry, so they travel with backups and exports of the lorebook.

When the Name generator or the Name provider extension is loaded, the top row has a Name tools button. It opens a table of the name categories of both with a checkbox each. The categories of the Name generator (names made up to sound like a category) start with Generator: , the ones of the Name provider (real names, each with its original spelling) with Provider: . The list is long, so it loads as you scroll and has a filter field above it: type a part of a name to show only the matching categories. The checked categories always stay in the table, whatever the filter says. The checkbox in the header checks or unchecks all the categories shown at that moment, and a line below the table counts how many are checked. The checked categories are saved with your account, so they stay checked the next time. While at least one is checked, the model can list them and ask for names of them during the generation (not the compaction), instead of inventing names. The model gets the tools of the extensions that have a checked category: check only Generator: categories and it gets the generator's, only Provider: ones and it gets the provider's, both and it gets both, none and it gets no tools.
Name tools with a filtered table of categories

A short hint for each kind of tools the model gets is added to the end of the generation prompt. The built-in hint of the Name generator asks the model to call the tools instead of inventing names, to pick from what it gets, and allows it to modify or remix the names when none fits as it is (combine parts of two, change an ending, adjust the spelling). The built-in hint of the Name provider asks it to pick a name from the real names it gets and to keep it as it was returned (the romanized one, with the original next to it when that suits the setting), without making up another spelling; a forename and a surname of the same country may be combined. You can replace them with your own in Settings → Extension Settings → Lore Generator (Name generator hint and Name provider hint, empty means the built-in one; a generator hint you saved before keeps working as it is, and so do the categories you checked before, they count as Generator: ones). The button shows how many categories are checked. Without both extensions there is no button; they can be unloaded and installed again while Marginalia runs, the button comes back.

Under the prompt you can add files for the model to look at: reference images, a map, a character sheet. Drop them on the upload area, choose them, or paste them into the prompt with Ctrl+V (a screenshot or a copied file becomes an attachment; pasted text is inserted as usual). Up to 20 MB each. They are listed with their name, type and size, and the trash button removes one. They are sent with the generation, not the compaction, and you can add and delete them only while no generation runs.

Whether the model can use them depends on the model and the inference provider: images are sent as images, audio only as WAV or MP3, other files as files. When the provider refuses an attachment, you get a message and nothing is generated.

Copy to Lore Entry is available when the compaction has a result. The compacted text becomes the content of the entry, and the generated text before the compaction goes into its note. Both are replaced. If the compaction is one code block (the built-in prompt asks for that, to make the text easy to copy), the code block around it is removed. The lorebook is refreshed, and the dialog stays open; Exit closes it.

The generator also works without the dialog, as three commands for the command line and for agents. They do the same two steps as the dialog and, like the dialog, they store nothing: they return the text, and putting it into an entry (what Copy to Lore Entry does) is up to the caller, so all three only read. The lorebook and the entry are given by number, as in /list-lorebooks and /list-lore-entries; the model is your default model and protocol.
Command
What it does
/list-lore-templates [template]
Lists your saved generation prompts (name, length, start of the text) and the one used last. With a name it returns the whole text of that prompt.
/generate-lore-entry [prompt [template [lorebook [entry [order [scope [limit [images]]]]]]]]

Generates a text with the lore of the lorebook and returns it. The text sent is a template followed by the prompt of the caller (see below). With images the model also looks at pictures, as with the attachments of the dialog.
/compact-lore-entry text [lorebook [entry [order [scope [limit]]]]]
Compacts the text with the same lore and returns the result, without the code block around it.

The entry the text is for decides which lore the model sees. Give its handle or its number as entry (and the lorebook it is in, by handle or number, when you give the number) and the lore is the same as in the dialog: with limit UP_TO_POSITION (the default) the entries before it, the entry itself never. An entry that does not exist yet has no number: give the order it will get instead (the order of /list-lore-entries, lower comes first) and the model sees the entries before that order; without either, the text is written for a new entry after all the others. scope is CURRENT_LOREBOOK (the default) or ALL_LORE, limit is UP_TO_POSITION or ALL_ENTRIES, as in the dialog.

A generation is only as good as its prompt, so the command always starts from one of your saved generation prompts (see Prompts): the one named in template, or the one used last when none is named. The prompt of the caller follows it under the heading Task for this entry and is where the subject, the facts, the length and the sections go, which is what the template asks for. template none sends the prompt alone, for a caller that has written the whole prompt itself, for example after getting the text of a template from /list-lore-templates and editing it. A command that is called with a template and no prompt sends just the template.

The images of /generate-lore-entry are the images the dialog would attach to the generation. An agent passes a list of paths of image files of its workspace (/refs/map.png; at most 8, PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, scaled down when large), which you put there with Upload file in the Workspace tab. The command bar has no way to name an image, so images is for agents. It is your default model that looks at the pictures: if it does not take images the command fails and says so. Only the generation takes images, as in the dialog; /compact-lore-entry works on the text alone.

The model gets no name tools here. A caller that wants names asks for them first, with /generate-names of the Name generator or /pick-real-names of the Name provider, and writes the ones it likes into the prompt. An agent can also take the text of a template from /list-lore-templates, change it and pass the result as the prompt.

The prompts and the compaction prompt are stored with your settings, so database backups include them. Nothing is stored with the lorebook; the generated text exists in the dialog only until you copy it.

Gives the model real names to pick from instead of inventing them: the most common forenames and surnames of many countries. Where the Name generator makes up new names that only sound like a category, this extension hands out names that exist, each with the original spelling next to the romanized one: Satō and 佐藤.

The extension has no screen of its own and nothing to configure. Other extensions offer its functions to the model: the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline, where you choose which lists the model may use. Its lists have the prefix Provider: there, the ones of the Name generator Generator: , and you can check lists of both, of one of them or of none.
The Name tools of the Lore Generator with one list of each extension checked
Function
What it does
list_real_name_lists
Lists the lists of names.
pick_real_names
Picks up to 100 different names of one list at random. Every name is a pair, the romanized name and the original one.

A list with fewer names than asked for returns all of them. The model is told (see the Name provider hint of the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline) to pick a name from what it gets and to write it as it was returned, with the original next to it when that suits the setting; it may combine a forename with a surname of the same country.
The same names are available as commands, for the command line and for agents, which can use them in their own prompts (for example for /generate-lore-entry of the Lore Generator):
Command
What it does
/list-real-name-lists
Lists the lists as a JSON array.
/pick-real-names list count
Picks up to 100 names of the list at random and returns them as a JSON array of pairs, the romanized name and the original one.
Both only read.

There are about 180 lists, named Country - Surnames and Country - Forenames: surnames of 75 countries and forenames of 106 (Japan - Surnames, Czechia - Forenames, Kosovo - Surnames). Forenames of both genders are in one list. A list has from 5 to about 150 names, the most common ones of the country. The names are not made new: a name you get is a name that people have.

The data is the popular names by country dataset (CC0), which takes them from Wikipedia's lists of the most common surnames and the most popular given names. The names written in non-Latin scripts (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Cyrillic...) have a romanization, either one from the source or one made by machine translation, so check the spelling when it matters.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions. It applies to the next generation, also when it is installed after the extensions that use it or unloaded and installed again. Without it and without the Name generator there is no Name tools button.

Gives the model a way to ask for names instead of inventing them. The names come from lists of real names - given names and surnames of many countries, places, deities, monsters, drugs, companies, foods, and more - and are made new by a Markov chain, so they sound like the category without being copies of it.

The extension has no screen of its own and nothing to configure. Other extensions offer its functions to the model; at the moment that are the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline, where you choose which categories the model may use; their categories have the prefix Generator: there, next to the Provider: ones of the Name provider, which hands out real names instead of made up ones.
Choosing the categories of names in the Lore Generator
Function
What it does
list_name_categories
Lists the categories of names.
generate_names
Makes up to 100 new names of one category. Optionally with a shortest and longest length.

Without a length, the names are as long as the names of that category usually are (a category of long company names gives long names, one of short forenames short ones). The model can ask for other lengths between 2 and 30 letters. A small category may return fewer names than asked for, because the chain runs out of different ones. The model is free to pick one of the names, change it or combine two of them; see the Name generator hint of the Lore Generator.
The same names are available as commands, for the command line and for agents, which can use them in their own prompts (for example for /generate-lore-entry of the Lore Generator):
Command
What it does
/list-name-categories
Lists the categories as a JSON array.
/generate-names category count [min_length [max_length]]
Makes up to 100 names of the category and returns them as a JSON array. Different names each time.
Both only read.
There are about 1270 categories. Their names say what they are:
Given names and surnames of the world, from Kate Monk's Onomastikon: Europe Western - France - Surnames, Ancient World - Egypt - Male, India - Hindu Gods - Goddesses. Several hundred of them.

Surnames of 75 countries, the romanized surnames of the popular names by country dataset (CC0): Armenia - Surnames, Japan - Surnames, Kosovo - Surnames. They are small lists (6 to about 150 names), so the chains stay short and the new names are close to the real ones; for the real ones themselves use the Name provider.

Lists from other collections: gods, angels, demons, ancient cities and states, emperors, planets (fantasygen), Corpora (animals, tarot, Tolkien names, Game of Thrones houses, drugs, hospitals, fabrics, gemstones, programming languages...) and markov-namegen-lib (Pokemon, dragons, cocktails, banks, Roman place names...).

Each category has a chain of the length that suited it best (short lists get short chains, which repeat the originals less) and the lengths its names usually have. The lists themselves are not part of Marginalia: only the probabilities are, so the original names can't be read out of the extension. Some of the sources have licences of their own, see the plugin README.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions. It applies to the next generation; extensions that use it find it when it is loaded, also if it is installed after them or unloaded and installed again - there is no need to restart the Lore Generator. Without it, the Lore Generator has no Name tools button.

Lets the model review what you've written: reader reactions, an editor's critique, a continuity check - whatever you prompt it for. Reviews are kept with the part, next to the story, and never become part of the book.
A review of a story part

Opens the review dialog. When the part has no review yet, one is generated right away.

In the review dialog:
‹ / › page through the reviews of the part; › on the last review generates a new one;

click the text of a review to edit it; it is saved when you click outside the field;
Thinking Process shows the reasoning of reasoning models;

By default the review uses the same prompt the part was written from (Use standard prompt info): the system prompt with the lore and summaries, the earlier parts, then the part itself, and finally the review prompt. The model reviews the part with the full context of the story.
The pre-prompt of the profile, if set, comes first as a system message.
Option

A different review prompt for this review. Starts with the prompt of the profile.

On: the prompt the part was written from, as above. Off: only the story parts, with the options below.

(off only) Adds the lore that was active when the part was written.

(off only) How many tokens of story to send: the parts up to and including the reviewed one, newest first, as many as fit. Starts with the room for the prompt of the model.
With Use standard prompt info off, the dialog shows the size of the request (Total tokens). Generate opens the review dialog with these options; further reviews generated in that dialog use them too.

A system message sent first, e.g. You are a demanding fiction editor.
As a line editor, point out clichés, repetitions and weak verbs in the last part, with suggestions.
Click Save at the top of the Settings page to keep the changes.
Create a profile for each kind of review and select the one you want before reviewing. A cheaper model for reviews saves cost: set it as the profile's Reviewer Model.
Describe how a first-time reader would feel at the end of this part, and what they expect next.
Field
List continuity errors in the last part compared to the earlier story. Quote the passages.

Reviewer settings are in Settings → Extension Settings → Reviewer Settings. They are organized in profiles:
The default post-prompt simulates a discussion on a story forum: a made-up thread with thirty replies from different readers, positive and negative. Other ideas:

The Reviewer settings
Reviews are stored with the story part, so they are part of book backups and copies. Branch Story doesn't copy them. Profiles are stored in your user settings.
A chat with the model next to your story: ask about the plot, check continuity, brainstorm names or the next chapter - without adding anything to the book.
Side Query is not available in the phone layout.
Side Query next to the story
The left sidebar of the story editor gets a Side Query tab next to Outline. Drag the divider to give it more room.

The tab holds conversations, each in its own tab: + opens a new one (Tab 2, Tab 3...), the pen renames a tab, × closes it (the last tab can't be closed). With Enable AI Tab Naming in the profile, the model names a tab after its first answer, unless you renamed the tab yourself. Conversations belong to the book and are kept until you close their tab.
Type a question into the box at the bottom and click SEND. The answer appears as it is written; STOP (in place of SEND) interrupts it.
Button
SEND
Sends the question.
UNDO
Removes the last message. If it was your question, it goes back into the box to be edited.
REGENERATE
Removes the last answer and asks again.

Every message has buttons to move it up or down, edit it, copy it to the clipboard, and exclude it from the context (or include it again). Excluded messages stay in the conversation but are not sent to the model - useful to drop a wrong answer without deleting it.
The options above the conversation choose what is sent with your questions:
Option
Lorebook
The lore of the book (see below).
Chat Logs from … to
The story parts of the active branch in that range, numbered from 1 as in the outline: 1 to 6 are the parts #1 to #6.
Plug button
Opens a list of the data other extensions offer, with a checkbox for each (see below).
Tokens
The approximate size of the request.

Lorebook collects the lore like a generation does: the book's lorebook and its sub lorebooks (disabled lorebooks are skipped), the enabled entries whose tags match the book's tags, with macros processed. Keyword filters are not applied - there is no story prompt to match, so every applicable entry is sent. Variables set by the entries are not stored.
The plug button opens a popover with the additional sources that other extensions offer, for example the Arc Outline offers your outline. Every source has a checkbox; the list has up to two parts:
About the book: a checked source is added to the request after the lorebook, under its name.
About story parts: a checked source is asked for every story part in the Chat Logs range and what it returns is added after the text of that part. It has an effect only while Chat Logs is on.

The choice is kept with the tab. If an extension is not installed (or stopped) its sources are not in the list and not sent, and they come back when the extension does. With none offered the popover says so.
The request is built like this:

one system message: the profile's Initial System Query, the lorebook entries (Lorebook Context), the checked sources about the book and the story parts (Chat History Context, labelled with their outline numbers Message #1, #2..., each followed by the checked sources about story parts);
the messages of the conversation that are included, as a chat. The profile's Instructions Before User Input are put at the start of your last question, before its text.
The model and protocol come from the profile (see below), by default those of the book. A cheap, fast model is usually enough for questions about the story.
Questions you ask often can be saved:
Save prompt (disk icon) saves the text in the box under the name selected in the list, or asks for a name;
Save prompt as... saves it under a new name;
pick a name in the list to put the saved text into the box;
the trash button deletes the selected saved query.
Saved queries belong to your account and are available in every book.
Some useful ones:
List every named character that appeared so far, with one line about each.
Which threads of the plot are still open?
Suggest five names for a harbor town in this world.
Side Query settings are in Settings → Extension Settings → SideQuery Settings, organized in profiles like the Reviewer ones. The selected profile is the one used:

Conversations are stored with the book, so they are part of book backups and copies. Profiles and saved queries are stored in your user settings.

Everything you create in Marginalia belongs to your account: books, lorebooks, tags, inference providers, protocols and settings. Other users don't see them (except books you publish), and you don't see theirs.

Change Password opens a dialog with your Username, Full Name, Current Password, Password and Repeat password:
enter your current password for every change (leave it empty if your account has no password);
to change the password, enter the new one in both password fields;
leave both password fields empty to change only the name and keep the password;

Click OK to save. With a wrong current password nothing is saved.

Changing the password ends all saved logins (Save login), on every device including this one: they have to log in again with the new password. If a device was lost or your password leaked, changing the password logs that device out. Sessions that are open right now (a browser tab still showing the workspace) stay logged in until they log out or their session expires.

The Language selector above the buttons switches the user interface to another language. The choice is saved in your account: the page reloads with the new language, and so does every other page you have open (on another device too), and it is used again the next time you log in. The login screen itself is always in the default language.

The list contains only the languages that are installed. English and Japanese come with Marginalia; an administrator can add more by loading an extension, for example Chinese localization. Texts a language doesn't translate are shown in English. Dates are written the way that language does. Your books and their texts are not translated, only the interface.

An account can have an empty password; you then log in with the user name only. If an administrator cleared your forgotten password, log in this way and set a new password with Change Password right away. That is handy for the desktop app on your own computer, but never do it on a server others can reach.

Administrators manage the Marginalia installation: user accounts, database backups, cleanup of deleted data and extensions. The first account, created on the first start, is an administrator; it can make other users administrators too.
Administrators are also normal users with their own books - they don't see other users' books, lorebooks or settings.

Administrators have an Admin button at the bottom of the workspace. It is only in the normal layout: the phone layout (a window narrower than 768 pixels) has no Admin page, so open Marginalia in a wider window (and reload the page) for administration. It opens the admin page with six tabs:
Tab
Users
Creating, editing and deleting accounts, and giving users permissions. See Users.
Database Backups
Backups of the whole database, on demand or on a schedule, and restoring them. See Database backups.
Cleanup
Permanently removing deleted data. See Cleanup.
Help assistant
The chat that answers questions from the manual: the model, the prompts and who pays for it. See Help assistant.
Agents

The system prompt and the compaction prompt that agents follow when neither they nor their user have one of their own. Empty is the built-in prompt; the info icon has Insert Default Template, which fills it in so you can edit a copy. What users may do with agents is their permission. Also Agents may send messages to the webhooks of users: the server calls the address a user typed in their settings when an agent needs them and they have the application closed (When you are not there); turn it off where that is not acceptable.
Extensions
Installing and removing extensions. See Managing extensions.
Everything Marginalia stores is in the .marginalia folder in the home directory of the user that runs it (./data on the host with the Docker setup):
Path
marginalia.sqlite (with -wal, -shm)
The database: users, books, lorebooks, settings, everything.
secret.key
Key that encrypts the API keys in the database. Created on the first start; without it, saved API keys can't be read.
db-backups/
Database backups.
data/login/backups/manuscripts/book id/
Book backups of each user.
extensions/
Installed extension JARs.
desktop/logs/
Logs of the desktop app.

To back up a whole installation, stop Marginalia and copy this folder (including secret.key). While it runs, use database backups for the database; book backups and extensions are plain files and can be copied at any time.
The Users tab of the admin page lists all accounts with their Username, Full Name and whether they are an Administrator.
The Users tab
Click Add User.
Fill in Username, Full Name, Password and Repeat password.
Check Administrator if the user should manage the installation.
Click OK.
Give the user name and password to the person; they can change the password later themselves (see Account & settings).

Marginalia accepts an account with an empty password - anyone can then log in with just the user name. Only do that on the desktop app on your own computer. Creating a user without a password asks for confirmation first.
The user name must be unique.
The pen button opens the same dialog for an existing user:
change the user name, full name and the administrator flag;
leave both password fields empty to keep the user's password as it is;
to set a new password, enter it in both password fields;
to clear the password, tick Clear password (the password fields are disabled) and confirm. The account then has no password.
You don't need the user's current password for any of this. A new or cleared password ends all the user's saved logins.
Marginalia has no password reset by e-mail. Either:
set a new password here and tell it to the user, who can change it later with Change Password; or

tick Clear password, tell the user to log in with their user name and an empty password, and to set a new password right away with Change Password (leave Current Password empty). The administrator never learns the new password this way.
Until the user sets a new password, anyone who knows the user name can log in to a cleared account. On a server, clear the password only when the user can log in right away.
The last administrator can't lose the administrator flag: The last administrator cannot be deleted or demoted.

Adding an inference provider needs the permission Create own models; administrators always have it. A user without it can only use the providers the administrators share. The providers a user already has keep working and can still be edited. See Permissions.

The key button in the row of a user opens their permissions: what the user may do beyond the ordinary, such as adding their own models or asking the help assistant. A new user has none, give them what they need after adding them.
The trash button deletes the account after confirming. You can't delete your own account or the last administrator.
The user can no longer log in, saved logins on their devices stop working, and the user name becomes free for a new account.

Their books, lorebooks, inference providers (with their API keys), protocols, tags and settings disappear with the account - nobody can see them any more - and the next Cleanup removes them from the database together with the account.

The user's files (uploaded images and resources) are kept: their folder in the data directory is renamed to login-deleted (login-deleted-2... if that name is taken), so a new account with the same user name starts with an empty folder. Delete the renamed folder by hand once you don't need it.

A permission lets one user do something that is not for everybody. Administrators give permissions to users one by one; a user who has none can do everything else in Marginalia as usual (write books, build lorebooks, use the models that administrators share).
Permission
What it allows

A database backup is a complete copy of the Marginalia database: all users with all their books, lorebooks, settings and extension data. Use it to protect the installation against mistakes and failures, and to move it to another computer. To back up a single book, users have book backups.
The Database Backups tab

Click Create Backup on the Database Backups tab. The copy is made while Marginalia runs, consistent even when people are writing. It appears in the list with its Name, Created date, Type (Manual or Scheduled) and Size. The toolbar shows the current size of the database.
Each backup has:
Button
Download
Downloads the backup file (.sqlite) - keep a copy outside the server.
Restore on restart
Restores the backup, see below.
trash
Deletes the backup.

Upload Backup adds a backup file (.sqlite or .db) to the list, for example one downloaded from another installation. The file is checked first and refused with The database can't be restored: ... and the reason when it is not a SQLite database, is damaged, is not a Marginalia database (another application's database), or comes from a newer Marginalia version than the one running.

A database backup contains everything, including the password hashes of all users and their API keys. The API keys are encrypted with the secret.key file in the data folder, which is not part of the backup - but anyone with both the backup and secret.key can read them. Keep downloaded backups as safe as the server itself.

The files are stored in the db-backups folder of the data folder. Copies Marginalia makes itself - pre-restore-... before a restore and pre-migration-... before an upgrade - are in the list too, shown as Manual, so they are never deleted by the rotation of scheduled backups. Book backups and extension JARs are separate files and are not part of a database backup.

Uploaded files (the pictures of the parts) are not part of a database backup either. The database only knows them as entries of the Resources tab; the files are in the data/login/images folder of the data folder. That is fine: after a restore the entries are the ones from the time of the backup and the pictures they use are still in the folder. Files of pictures that were added after the backup are just left over (nothing refers to them) and take disk space. To keep the pictures safe, include the whole data folder in your own backups, or pack them into a book backup.

When you restore a backup on another installation, copy secret.key from the original installation as well (with Marginalia stopped), otherwise the saved API keys can't be decrypted and every user has to enter them again.

Click Save Schedule to apply it. The status line shows when the last scheduled backup was made and when the next one is due.
When Marginalia wasn't running at a scheduled time - typical for the desktop app, which runs only while you write - it makes the missed backup about 30 seconds after the next start.

To turn scheduled backups off, uncheck Create backups automatically and click Save Schedule. The expression is kept, so you can turn the backups on again later. It is still checked - an invalid expression is never saved - but while the backups are off, the field may also be empty.
A database can't be replaced while Marginalia uses it, so a restore happens on the next start:
Click Restore on restart next to the backup and confirm. The tab shows Database restore is scheduled. Restart the application to apply it. - Cancel Restore undoes it.
Restart Marginalia: quit and start the desktop app, or docker compose restart on the server.

On the start, the current database is moved to db-backups/pre-restore-time-marginalia.sqlite - it appears in the list, so a restore can be undone by restoring that file - and the backup takes its place. A backup from an older Marginalia version is upgraded automatically.

The backup is checked again before it is swapped in (the same checks as for Upload Backup, also Restore on restart refuses a backup that fails them). If it fails the check, or upgrading it fails, Marginalia keeps (or puts back) the current database and starts normally; the refused file is moved to db-backups/rejected-restore-time-marginalia.sqlite and the log says why.
Everything after the backup is lost: books, parts and settings created since. Users who are logged in have to log in again if their account changed.

When a new version of Marginalia is going to change the structure of an existing database, it first saves a copy as db-backups/pre-migration-time-Vversion-marginalia.sqlite, where the version is the one the database was at. The copy is in the list of backups, so an upgrade can be undone by installing the old version of Marginalia and restoring that copy. The last three copies are kept. A new installation has nothing to copy, and if the copy can't be made (for example the disk is full), the log says so and the upgrade goes on.
A migration that fails halfway is rolled back by itself and Marginalia does not start; the copy is for an upgrade that went through but did something you don't want.
Create a backup and Download it.
Install Marginalia on the new computer, create a temporary administrator on the first start.
Upload Backup, Restore on restart, restart.
Log in with the accounts from the backup.
Copy the data folder (book backups and the pictures of the parts) and extensions folder from the old data folder as well. Or simply stop Marginalia and copy the whole .marginalia folder.

Stop unloads the extension immediately without removing it: it disappears from the screens it added to, but its JAR and data stay, and it is listed with the state Stopped. The button then reads Start, which loads it again (it is checked first, like at the start of the application; if the check fails, it stays stopped and the report is shown). A stopped extension stays stopped after Marginalia restarts. Uploading a new version of a stopped extension starts it.

The stop is remembered by an empty file named like the JAR with .STOPPED added (sidequery.jar.STOPPED) in the extensions folder. On a server without access to the UI, create it to keep an extension from starting, or delete it to let the extension start on the next start.

Log opens the log of the extension: what the extension itself wrote with the logger Marginalia gives to extensions (Logging). It shows the last part of the file, Refresh reads it again and Clear deletes it. The file is extensions/name.jar.log (for example sidequery.jar.log); when it grows over 2 MB it is moved to .log.old and a new one is started. It is deleted when the extension is unloaded. Extensions that don't log anything have an empty log. What the extension logs also goes to the application log (named extension.name, at the level of the line), so it is in the log of the server too; problems of Marginalia itself are only there.
The log of an extension

Unload asks for confirmation, then stops the extension immediately and deletes its JAR (and its log) from the extensions folder. Its data stays (see Where extension data is kept); loading it again brings the data back.

To install a newer version of an extension, Load Extension (.jar) with the new file - the file name doesn't matter. The installed version is unloaded, its JAR deleted and the new version started in its place. If the new version fails to load, the upload shows the error and the old version keeps running.
If an uploaded extension can't be loaded, the upload shows Failed to load extension: ... and its JAR is not kept.

Marginalia checks an extension against the version it is running in before it starts it. An extension that does not fit - typically one built for another version of Marginalia - is not loaded. An upload shows the report of the check and is not kept; an extension in the extensions folder stays in the list, not started, with Invalid in the Verification column, and the report is in the log. The check is repeated after Marginalia is updated, so an extension that worked before can be refused afterwards: get the version of the extension that was built for the new version of Marginalia and load it. While an extension is invalid, a red bar at the top of the workspace tells everybody: an administrator sees which extensions on hover, other users are asked to tell the administrator (an extension you stopped yourself is not counted). Next to each extension's JAR you'll find a small .valid or .invalid file with the report; it is removed with the extension and can be left alone.
The red bar over the workspace when an extension is invalid
The verification report of an extension that does not fit, and a stopped extension (Start button)

An extension in the extensions folder that fails to start (for example one built for another version) doesn't stop the others from loading. It is listed with the state Installed or Resolved instead of Active and can be removed with Unload. A file that isn't an extension at all is skipped and not listed - delete it from the extensions folder. The log (docker compose logs, or desktop/logs/marginalia.log for the desktop app) has the details of the error.

The help assistant is a chat that answers questions about Marginalia from its manual. An administrator chooses which model it uses and gives the permission Help assistant to the users who can ask it, in their permissions (administrators always can); they need no model of their own. Users that existed when the permissions were introduced got it if the assistant was on at the time; new users have none.

Once a user can use it, they see a round robot button in the bottom right corner of the window. It opens the chat; the panel says which model answers and warns when the user's limit applies (see Who pays). The model looks the answers up in the manual (it can search it and read its pages), names the pages it used as links to the published manual (they open in a new tab), and explains: it changes nothing and does not see the user's books. It can also look at what went wrong when something fails (see When something goes wrong) and take the user somewhere, if you allow it (see Showing the way). The conversation is kept until the user logs out (closing the panel or reloading the page keeps it), the broom button clears it.
The help assistant answering a question

The button appears when a user opens Marginalia, and the model and the limit warning are read each time the panel is opened; if you take the permission away or remove the model, users who already have the page open lose the button when they reload it (or when they open the panel).

The Help assistant tab
