PermissionService (domain.security.service) answers what an administrator allowed a user to do, see Permission. checkPermissions(user, type) is false when the user has no Permission of the type or it is not granted; getPermission(user, type) returns the object (null when there is none, a deleted one does not count); getPermissions(user) lists them. The permission is found by its holder, not by its owner (the owner is only the administrator who gave it), and the user is loaded again through UserService first - the session's user bean is a scoped proxy with an id, login and name only (an unknown or deleted user has nothing). Administrators are not special here, callers that let them do everything check AdminGuard.isAdmin() too (AIService.canCreate, HelpAssistantService). Changing permissions is for administrators: save, saveWithoutEvent, delete and setGranted(user, type, granted) (changes the existing permission or creates one owned by the current administrator) call AdminGuard.requireAdmin(). The migration that created the first ones (PermissionsMigration) does not go through the service, it runs without a user.
The dialog behind the key button of the user list is ui.dialogs.permissions.PermissionsDialog (see UI); the services it uses are PermissionService and SessionManager.reloadUser.

Failed logins are limited twice. Per user (User.failedLogins, lockedUntil, in the database) and per client address (UserServiceImpl.addressFailures, in memory). Both use the same back-off, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to 15 minutes, after 10 (user) or 30 (address) consecutive failures; the address limit is higher because several users can share an address. A failure counts against the address whatever the user name was, so a password spray over many accounts is stopped even though no single account fails often.
The address comes from UIUtils.clientAddress(Configuration) (LoginCheckRoute.clientAddress() in the login routes), which asks ClientAddressResolver:
The address of the connection is used by default. X-Forwarded-For is ignored, because any client can send it.

When trustedProxies (configuration.properties, or -DtrustedProxies=...) lists the connecting peer - addresses or CIDR ranges - the header is read from the right and the first address that is not a trusted proxy is the client. Entries left of it were sent by the client and are never used. The private network is not trusted by itself.
Host names are never resolved and a bad trustedProxies entry stops the start.
Without a proxy nothing needs to be configured. Behind one, list the proxy, otherwise all users share its address and 30 failures from anyone block everybody for a while.

analyze() builds the plan of what can be purged (from the Hibernate metamodel and @CleanupReferences), purge() executes it. Extensions with their own references register a CleanupContributor (collectReferences to block purges, beforePurge to clean up). See Cleanup references.
CleanupService
CommandScopes
CommandService

Data that extensions offer to each other as text: providers about a book (ManuscriptPluginData) or a story part (ChatMessagePluginData) are registered under a bundle identifier and a key (registerManuscriptProvider / registerChatMessageProvider), listed in registration order (getManuscriptProviders / getChatMessageProviders: bundle → key → name) and asked with getManuscriptData / getChatMessageData (null when the provider is gone). OsgiServiceImpl removes the providers of a bundle's symbolic name when the extension is unloaded. See Sharing data between extensions.
Database backups with VACUUM INTO, upload, staged restore, the cron schedule (CronSchedule, Spring ThreadPoolTaskScheduler) and its rotation. See Database backups and restores.
DatabaseBackupService
IPCService

Loading extensions and the @Extendable decorators (which read arguments and locals and can replace the return value of the decorated method), see Plugin development. OsgiService lists the installed extensions that are invalid (getInvalidExtensions, shown as a red bar in the workspace), also stops and starts extensions without uninstalling them (stopExtension / startExtension / isStopped, the jar name.STOPPED flag next to the JAR), gives the SHA-256 of an extension's JAR (getSha256, cached until the file changes) and gives each extension its own logger: createLogger(bundle) returns an SLF4J logger (implemented by ExtensionLogger) that appends to jar name.log in the extensions folder (moved to .log.old over 2 MB) and chains each line to the application log (logger extension.name); readLog / clearLog serve the Admin page. See Logging.
Makes the CommandScope a command runs in: session() the open book of the user, forRun(run) the working copy of an agent run (the cage, see The scope).
OsgiService, ExtensionService

Registry and dispatcher of commands (the Commands section describes them in full: writing a suite, the command bar). A command is a public void name(CommandContext) method annotated with @Command (commandName; optional humanName, description and llmDescription for agents, availableForAgent (false keeps the command from agents), dataSeverity (a CommandDataSeverity: DESTRUCTIVE, the default, or NON_DESTRUCTIVE, see Data severity), each an L key with a plain-text variant humanNameText... for extensions, see Texts; async, signature, returns); an object with such methods is a command suite. Overloads: methods with the same commandName are forms of one command (same humanName), told apart by signature = @CommandParameterSignature(@CommandParameter(name, type, description), ...); an empty @CommandParameterSignature is a form without arguments, and a method that declares no signature takes any arguments (@CommandParameterSignature(any = true), the default): the objects are in CommandContext.getPositional() and a list of objects can be passed as one argument of type Object ("any"). returns = @CommandReturn(name, type, description) declares the returned value (String.class...; void.class by default). registerCommands(Object) registers all the commands of the suite (or none: it refuses a class without annotated methods, a method that is not public void with a CommandContext as its only parameter, a name with characters other than letters, digits, _, -, ., two forms with the same signature, forms with different human names, a signature that is also any, a duplicate parameter name and a name another object holds) and returns the CommandDefinitions (one per form); a suite is shared by all users and runs in parallel, so it must be stateless: no fields with the state of a run or a user, the current state is read when the command runs from the services and from the session-scoped SessionPoint (getLanguage(), getWorkspace()); unregisterCommands(Object) removes the whole suite, unregisterCommand(String) one command with its forms (an extension does that in onExtensionUnload, the service does not track bundles). The application's own commands (impl.commands.HelloWorldCommands: /hello-world and /hello-world message, and /hello-world-async, the same after 10 seconds on a worker thread, the example of an async command that polls isTerminated() and the interrupt flag; impl.commands.BackupCommands: /take-backup, an async @Configurable suite that backs up the open book and reports its progress with the status lines) are registered in afterPropertiesSet. Running: execute(name, Map) (arguments by name), executePositional(name, List) and executeLine(/name a b) return a CommandRun (a CompletableFutureObject that also holds the two status lines a command sets with setStatus / setSubStatus: getStatus(), getSubStatus(), addStatusListener); the form is chosen by the number of arguments and the closest types (a value that already has the type, then Object, then text converted to a number, boolean, character or enum; ties go to the form declared first by parameter count; a form that takes any arguments is the last resort). A command line separates arguments by spaces, \ is a space inside an argument, \\ a backslash and \ a quote; an argument can be wrapped in double quotes (two words, spaces inside need no escape, is an empty argument, a quote that is never closed runs to the end) (CommandLine.parse / escape). A command with async = false runs on the caller's thread and must call setReturn before its method returns (otherwise the result is null, later calls are ignored); with async = true it runs on a worker thread with the caller's request attributes and the future completes with the first setReturn, from any thread. Cancelling the future stops the run: CommandContext.isTerminated() becomes true (it is true as soon as the future is done, never while a non-async command runs), the worker thread is interrupted and a command that has not started does not start; an async command checks isTerminated() in its loops and returns at once. A throwing command, or CommandContext.fail, fails the future with a CommandException; no form that fits fails it with IllegalArgumentException. CommandHelp (pure; takes a function that localizes L keys) computes the matching names and the forms that fit what is typed, for the command bar. CommandUtils (package utils) gives a command the current state of the session: the workspace, the open book window (the same interface on the desktop and the phone) and the open book, all delegated to the SessionPoint (for an agent session the AgenticSessionPoint holds the book directly). The commands that read the book are one class each in impl.commands.manuscript.read (see Commands that read the book).
Responsible for
Service

The services behind the Administration screen check on the server that the caller is an administrator, so they stay safe if something other than that screen (an API, an extension) ever reaches them. They call AdminGuard.requireAdmin() (bean in services-config.xml), which loads the current user from the database - the session copy of admin is not trusted, a user demoted or deleted mid-session loses access at once - and throws SecurityException for nobody, a deleted user or a non-administrator. Guarded: every DatabaseBackupService method except createScheduledBackup and getNextScheduledBackup, CleanupService.getReferenceModel/analyze/purge, OsgiService.installPackage/uninstallPackage, and UserService.deleteUser/clearPassword/unlock. Code that runs without a request (the backup schedule, loading extensions on start, registerContributor) is not guarded, and inside these services it calls private unguarded variants (listBackups, removeBackup). A new administrator-only service method calls adminGuard.requireAdmin() first.

The trash: lists soft-deleted objects (find/count with a TrashFilter of owner and type), shows their extended content as JSON and restores them. Implemented by CleanupServiceImpl (same bean as CleanupService) because it needs the cleanup reference model. Not administrator-only: a user is limited to their own objects, an administrator (AdminGuard.isAdmin()) sees and restores everything, and objects of others raise SecurityException. deletePermanently removes deleted story parts and lorebook entries for good (children of a removed part move to its parent). restore also restores the deleted objects the selection owns (messages of a book...) and is all or nothing: an object that depends on a deleted object outside the selection (STRONG and OWNED_BY references it holds, and the OWNS reference of the object that owns it) blocks the whole restore, see RestoreResult.getBlocked(). See Trash.
TrashService

ManualService (ManualServiceImpl, a plain bean with init-method=load) holds the user manual in memory: the Markdown pages of manual/user that the build packs as classpath:/manual/ (see Packaging). It is global read-only data, so it has no user and no transaction. load() reads every manual/**/*.md and keeps the pages, a missing or unreadable page is only logged. ManualParser turns a page into a ManualPage: removes the front matter, pictures and Retype admonition markers (!!!warning Title becomes a bold **Warning: Title** line), rewrites links between pages to paths in the manual (books/story-editor.md#images, links into the developer manual become plain text) and splits the page by its second and third level headings into ManualSections with the Retype anchors. ManualIndex is an immutable BM25 index over the sections (heading and page title weigh more than the body, light English stemming, stop words dropped, no support for Japanese or Chinese text). getPage tolerates a leading slash, an #anchor and a missing .md, search(query, limit) returns ManualHits, best first.

HelpAssistantService is the model behind the help chat (ui.components.HelpAssistantWidget). getSettings / saveSettings are for administrators (AdminGuard) and keep Settings(aiUuid, ...prompts, adminData) in AppSettings (what depends on the user is in their HELPER permission: Permission.helperApplyLimits and helperInteractions; an administrator without the permission has both off); saveSettings accepts only an AI the administrator owns (IllegalArgumentException otherwise); requests are made without a protocol. isAvailable() and stream(payload, functions, callback) are for administrators and the users with the permission PermissionType.HELPER (target() checks it at every request). The AI is loaded by uuid whoever owns it (the user could not see it), and only while it is not deleted and its owner is still an administrator, which is checked at each request, so a demoted administrator's AI is never handed to everybody. A request is metered (the normal path, AILimitService.check and UsageService.record for the current user) only for a shared AI when the permission has helperApplyLimits; any other request runs in an UnmeteredScope: a thread-local, opened by the caller around the call that starts the request, that an inference service reads once when the request starts (before it moves to other threads) and then skips the limit check and does not count the usage. OpenAICompatibleInferenceService and the google-genai plugin do this; an extension AI must too, see AI providers. The tokens of an unmetered request are not counted anywhere: not for the user, not for the owner.

getInfo() tells any user which AI answers (Info(aiName, model, metered), null when unavailable). ask(history, uiState, callback) is what the chat calls: it puts the instructions in front of the conversation, binds HelpTools and calls stream. HelpTools are ManualTools (search_manual over ManualService.search, read_manual_page over getPage; read only, answers cut to a size a small model can use) and get_ui_state(path, deep), which asks the UiStateSource (the page the question comes from; null when there is none, the function then fails with a message the model can read), see Letting the help assistant see the UI. When the the permission has helperInteractions and there is a UiStateSource, ask binds InteractiveHelpTools instead (adds interact_with_ui(path, interactions), which calls UiStateSource.interact) and appends HelpPrompts.INTERACTIVE to the instructions; see Interactions. HelpTools also has read_last_errors(count) (what the user was shown that went wrong, read through UiStateSource.readProblems, see What went wrong); the rules for it are HelpPrompts.PROBLEMS, added to every prompt after the one the administrator may have edited. Manual tools print the address of what they found (URL: next to Page:): ManualPage.url() / ManualSection.url() turn the path in the manual into the address on the published site (ManualPage.WEB_BASE, https://enerccio.github.io/Marginalia/user/, the GitHub pages of the project: books/story-editor.md#images is .../user/books/story-editor/#images; ManualServiceTest checks that every page has its file under docs/), and the default prompt tells the model to cite pages as Markdown links with those addresses only; the widget opens them in a new tab.

The data of the Admin page. With Settings.adminData (AppSettings.helpAdminData, off by default, a checkbox of the Help assistant tab) and an administrator asking, ask binds a second set of functions beside the others (FunctionSet.and), AdminHelpTools: get_admin_data(topic) (extensions, users, backups, cleanup, application) and read_extension_log(extension, lines), with HelpPrompts.ADMIN_DATA added to the instructions. They read through AdminDataSource, implemented by HelpAdminData: the extensions with their state and verification (OsgiService, optional: it is not in the test context), the counts of the users (no names), the database backups and schedule, what CleanupService.analyze() would purge (nothing is changed), memory and uptime, and the last lines (40 by default, 200 at most, 6000 characters) of the log of an extension, found by its name, symbolic name or JAR (OsgiService.readLog). The functions run on threads of their own, so HelpAdminData runs each read in the request of the administrator that asked (ThreadCopyRequestAttributes taken in ask) and checks AdminGuard.requireAdmin() again. Log lines and verification reports go through UiProblem.clean (cut, keys removed), nothing more: the setting exists because they can still carry text an extension wrote, on its way to the AI of the assistant. The instructions are one of two prompts, for administrators (AdminGuard.isAdmin()) or for the other users: the text in AppSettings.helpPromptAdmin / helpPromptUser or, when that is null or blank, the default (HelpPrompts.ADMIN / USER); saveSettings stores a blank prompt or one equal to the default as null, so a default follows the new version. `` in a prompt is replaced by the list of pages (path, title, 110 characters of the description), a prompt without it gets no index. The settings are installation wide, so a test that saves them must reset them first. It does not store anything. The conversation of the user is the list SessionPoint.getHelpChat() (a synchronized ListLLMChatMessage, user and assistant messages only), which lives and dies with the HTTP session (logout invalidates it). A model without function calling fails the request; there is no fallback to a prompt with searched sections.
Long operations - generating a part, a summary, streaming from a model - return immediately and report through a callback:
Operation
Returns
Callback
StoryGenerationService.generateNextTurn
CancellationToken
GenerationListener
SummaryService.createSummary, createMetaSummary
SummaryService.AsyncCallback
InferenceService.stream
InferenceAsyncCallback
InferenceService.infer
InferenceResultCallback / TypedInferenceCallback

CancellationToken.cancel() stops the operation (the inference callback's isDead() reports it to the stream). Callbacks run on worker threads: UI code in them must use ui.access(...) (see Threads and push), and service calls need the request scope shown above.
Interface in domain/service/; for an entity extend ExtendableServiceEntity, EntityRepository.
Implementation in domain/service/impl/ extending ExtendableServiceImpl...; repository extending JpaExtendableRepositoryEntity with getEntityClass().
Beans in services-config.xml:
Annotate every public method: @CommonTx, @CommonTxReadOnly or @NoTx.

Use currentUser for ownership, findForUser(uuid) for anything coming from outside, and call AdminGuard.requireAdmin() for administrator operations - hiding a button in the UI is not a permission check.
Keep the class non-final with public methods (CGLIB proxies subclass it).
Test it on top of MarginaliaTestBase (see Testing).

Extensions can't add beans to the application context. They keep their logic in their own classes annotated @Configurable (plugins are compiled with the AspectJ compiler too), which get the application's services @Autowired - for example the Reviewer's ReviewerService. Transactions then come from the application services they call. See Plugin development.
c: <bean id="bookmarkRepository" class="com.github.enerccio.marginalia.domain.repository.impl.JpaBookmarkRepository"> <property name="entityManager" ref="em"/> </bean> <bean class="com.github.enerccio.marginalia.domain.service.impl.BookmarkServiceImpl"> <property name="repository" ref="bookmarkRepository" /> </bean>

p: A command is a named action with typed arguments and a return value, run by name: from the command bar the user types, from code in the application or in an extension, and later by agents (each command carries a description written for a model). This page explains the model; Writing commands shows how to write and register a suite, and The command bar how the UI side works. The user's view is in the user guide.
@CommandParameterSignature(@CommandParameter(name, type, description), ...): the arguments of one form. An empty signature is a form without arguments; any = true is "any arguments".

A name (commandName: letters, digits, _, -, .) with a humanName for the user, a description, an llmDescription for agents (each as an L key or, for extensions, a plain ...Text, see Texts), a signature, a return declaration, async, the dataSeverity and availableForAgent (false keeps the command from agents, see Available for agents).
Any object whose class has methods annotated with @Command. Registering the object registers all of them.
Command
Command method
CommandContext: the arguments (get, getPositional), the answer (setReturn, fail), the two lines of status (setStatus, setSubStatus) and isTerminated(). It belongs to one run.
Concept
Context
Form (overload)
Methods of a suite that share a commandName are forms of one command. They must have the same humanName and dataSeverity and each its own signature. One CommandDefinition exists per form.
One call, which returns a CommandRun (a CompletableFutureObject) that completes with the value given to setReturn and holds the status the command reports.
public void name(CommandContext context): the only parameter is the context, nothing is returned from the method itself.
Run
Signature
Suite
What it is
A command never receives its arguments as Java parameters; it reads them from the context by the names of its signature:
As type; IllegalArgumentException when it is not an instance (numbers are converted when they fit).
Declares the run can't be stopped now (see Uninterruptable runs). Any thread; ignored once the run is over.
Ends the run with a CommandException (for async commands that report from another thread; a synchronous command can throw).
fail(error)
get(name, type)
get(name)
getPositional()
has(name), getArguments()
isTerminated()
Method
setReturn(value)
setStatus(text), setSubStatus(text)
setUninterruptable(flag), isUninterruptable()
The answer. A form with async = false must call it before its method returns, otherwise the result is null. Later calls are ignored.
The arguments in order. For a form that takes any arguments, the objects the caller passed.
The value as passed (converted to the parameter's type), null if not passed.
True when the run is over for the caller: the command answered or failed, or the caller cancelled the future. Never true while a synchronous command runs.
Two lines of progress for the user: what the command is doing now, and the detail of that step. They are independent, null or blank clears one. Any thread; ignored once the run is over.
Use
Whether an argument was passed, and all of them (read only).
A call names the command and passes the arguments in one of three ways:
Call
Arguments
execute(name, Map)
By name. The form whose parameter names are exactly the keys is called; a form that takes any arguments gets the map.
executePositional(name, List)
By position. The form with as many parameters as there are arguments, all convertible, is called.
executeLine(/name a b)
A command typed as text; the arguments are strings, split by CommandLine.parse (see below).
Each of them also has a form with a last argument boolean uninterruptable, see Uninterruptable runs.

When several forms fit, the closest types win. Each argument costs 0 when it already has the parameter's type, 1 for a parameter of type Object ("any"), 2 when text or a number has to be converted (to a number, boolean, character or enum); a form that takes any arguments costs 1000, so it is the last resort. The form with the lowest total is called, ties go to the form that is listed first (declared forms by the number of parameters, then by method name). The Object.class parameter is "any": it takes the argument as it is, including a List of objects, so a command can be given a list as one argument.
Conversions (CommandValues): an instance of the type is passed as it is; a number to another number type when the value fits; text to a number, boolean, character or enum constant.
CommandLine.parse(text) splits a command typed as text. The text is a command when it starts with /.
Arguments are separated by spaces; repeated spaces count as one.
\ is a space inside an argument, \\ a backslash and \ a quote.

A double quote starts or ends a quoted part in which spaces need no escape. Quotes may start anywhere in an argument (ab cd is ab cd), is an empty argument, a quote that is never closed runs to the end of the text.
Any other backslash stays as it is (C:\dir is unchanged).

trailingSeparator tells whether the text ends with a space that starts a new, still empty argument; with typingName() and currentArgument() the help knows what the user is typing. CommandLine.escape(argument) writes an argument so that parse reads it back as one argument.

@Command(returns = @CommandReturn(name, type, description)) declares what the command returns; the type is a direct class reference (String.class, Object.class for "any", void.class by default). It is documentation for the user and for agents (the help shows it); the service does not check the value against it.
async
The method runs
Answer
false
On the thread of the caller; the future is complete when execute* returns.
setReturn before the method returns, or null. A thrown exception fails the future.
true
On a worker thread (a daemon cached pool) with the request attributes of the caller, so session-scoped beans resolve.
The future completes with the first setReturn or fail, from any thread, whenever the command likes.

A caller can cancel the future (the Stop button of the progress window does). Then isTerminated() becomes true, the worker thread is interrupted, and a command that has not started yet does not start. A long-running async command must cooperate: look at isTerminated() (and the interrupt flag) between the steps of its work and return at once. What it sets afterwards is ignored. /hello-world-async (HelloWorldCommands) is the model of such a loop.

Some work can't be abandoned half way, a change that is being written to the database. A command declares that with context.setUninterruptable(true) just before it, and false after it: meanwhile CommandRun.cancel does nothing (it returns false) and the progress window of the command bar disables its Stop button (CommandRun.isUninterruptable(), addUninterruptableListener(...), called on the thread of the command like the status listener). The search and replace commands do so for the replace, after the user confirmed it.

A caller can start a run that way too: every execute* has a form with a trailing boolean uninterruptable (execute(name, Map, true), executePositional(name, List, true), executeLine(line, true)). Such a run is uninterruptable from the start and the command can't lift it with setUninterruptable(false). A command that is uninterruptable and starts another asynchronous command passes context.isUninterruptable(), so the nested one is not abandoned either.

A command that takes time tells the user what it is doing with setStatus (the main line, "Taking a backup of Dune") and setSubStatus (the detail, "Chapter 3 of 12"). The lines are kept in the CommandRun that execute* returns (getStatus(), getSubStatus()); addStatusListener((status, subStatus) - ...) is called on the thread of the command on each change, so a view must hop to its own thread (the progress window of the command bar does with ui.access). A listener does not get what was set before it was added: read the getters after adding it. A listener that throws is ignored. /take-backup (BackupCommands) is an example.
@Command(dataSeverity = ...) says what the command does to the data that exists, as a CommandDataSeverity:
Value
Means
DESTRUCTIVE
The command changes or removes data that exists (replaces text, deletes, overwrites). The default.
NON_DESTRUCTIVE
The command only reads data or adds new data; whatever exists stays as it is (/take-backup, /hello-world).

The default is the safe assumption: a command that does not say is treated as destructive, so a command that only reads or adds declares NON_DESTRUCTIVE. All forms of a command have the same severity (registerCommands throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise), and CommandDefinition.dataSeverity() returns it. The severity is for two readers: the command bar shows it as a label next to the command for the user, and an agent that runs commands on its own is meant to ask the user before it runs a DESTRUCTIVE one. Nothing in the service enforces that today: the severity does not stop a run, and a command that must ask the user still does it itself, see Asking the user.
A future fails with:
CommandException when the command throws or calls fail (the cause is the original error),
IllegalArgumentException when there is no command of that name, no form fits the arguments, or the text for executeLine does not start with /.

registerCommands(Object suite) validates the whole suite and registers all of it or nothing, and throws IllegalArgumentException for: a class without a @Command method; a command method that is not public void with a CommandContext as the only parameter; a name with characters other than letters, digits, _, -, .; two forms with the same signature; forms with different humanName; a signature that is also any; a duplicate parameter name; a name another object already holds. It returns the CommandDefinitions. Registering the same object again does nothing.

unregisterCommands(Object suite) removes the suite, unregisterCommand(String) one command with all its forms. The service does not know which bundle a suite came from: an extension unregisters its suites in onExtensionUnload. Runs in progress are not interrupted by unregistering.
The application registers its own suites in CommandServiceImpl.afterPropertiesSet (HelloWorldCommands, BackupCommands, the two search and replace commands and the commands that read the book).

A suite is one object shared by all users and runs in parallel, so it must be stateless: no fields that hold what a run or a user did. What a command needs to know about the current state it reads when it runs:
from the services, which resolve the current user and check ownership (ManuscriptService, and so on),
from the scope of the call, context.getScope() (below): the book the command works on, its lorebooks and the way to ask a question,
from the session-scoped SessionPoint (getLanguage(), getWorkspace()), through CommandUtils.
A command that changes the UI does it on the UI thread: from a synchronous command that is the calling thread, from an async one use ui.access(...) (see UI extensions → Threads).

CommandContext.getScope() is a CommandScope: what the command works on and who answers its questions. A command takes the book from it (getManuscript(), read again from the database every time, getLorebook() the root lorebook of the book) and asks with context.confirm(question); it never reaches for the open window. The user at the command bar gets the scope of their session (CommandScopes.session(): the open book, a dialog for the questions), an agent the scope of its working copy (CommandScopes.forRun(run): the copy of the run, whichever it is now, and a yes without asking, since what an agent may do without asking was decided when it called the command). CommandService.execute, executePositional and executeLine have a form with a last argument scope; without one the scope of the session of the calling thread is made on that thread.

CommandUtils (package utils) reads the session of the caller – also on the worker thread of an async command, which gets the request attributes – and returns null when there is nothing to return (no session, no workspace yet, no book open), so a command checks its results. The book-related methods only delegate to the SessionPoint, which knows where the book comes from: for a user the SessionPoint reads it from the open window of the workspace, for an agent the AgenticSessionPoint (a SessionPoint without workspace and window) holds the book directly, so the same command runs for both:
confirm and reloadManuscriptWindow talk to the window, so in a session without one they answer no and do nothing (CommandContext.confirm is what a command calls, it is routed by the scope).
getCurrentAI()
getCurrentManuscript()
getManuscriptSection()
getManuscriptWindow()

getModel() answers which AI and protocol work that a command starts should use when the user did not choose (a ModelChoice; null is "no opinion"). For an agent it is the model of the agent, or the one of its book when the agent was told not to use its own (Agent.useAgentModel); the user at the command bar has none, so a command falls back to its own choice (the Lore Generator to the default model of the user, the Arc Outline to the model of the book first). A command of an extension that calls a model must ask it first, or it ignores what the author of the agent decided. A command that writes through the story services asks nothing: the working copy already holds the model (see Agents). Tools with their own request to a model inside a long-lived agent should also take a place at the AI with AIGate (ManuscriptWriteSupport.placeAt).
getSessionPoint()
getWorkspace()
Method
Returns
The AI of that book.
The open book (SessionPoint.getCurrentManuscript()) or the book of the agent session; a command takes the book from context.getScope() instead.
The open book window (ManuscriptWindow, the same interface on the desktop and the phone); null for an agent.
The part of the workspace that holds book windows (ManuscriptSection); null for an agent.

The scope is also the cage. resolveMessage(uuid), resolveLorebook(uuid) and resolveEntry(uuid) find an item by the uuid, and only the ones of the book of the scope: the parts of the book, the lorebook of the book and its subbooks however deep, and their entries. A uuid of anything else (the original book of a copy, another book, a lorebook the book does not use, a deleted item) is refused with an IllegalArgumentException as if it did not exist, so a command that takes an item as an argument can't be aimed outside of the book by what it is given. A command that takes an item does it through the scope and not through findForUser or find(id).

The SessionPoint of the session: the bean of the servlet session, or for other request attributes (an agent run) the AgenticSessionPoint kept under AgenticSessionPoint.SCOPED_TARGET_NAME in their session scope.
The user's Workspace (desktop or phone); null for an agent.

The package domain.service.impl.commands.manuscript.read holds one class per command (GetBookInfoCommand, ListPartsCommand, GetPartCommand, ListSwipesCommand, ListBranchesCommand, GetPartMetricsCommand, ShowPromptCommand, SearchPartsCommand, FindOccurrencesCommand, ComparePartsCommand, CountTokensCommand, ListSummariesCommand, GetSummaryCommand, CheckSummariesCommand, GetTemplateVariablesCommand), each a @Configurable suite registered by CommandServiceImpl. They share ManuscriptReadSupport (the services, the Book loaded again from the current manuscript, the JSON helpers) and StoryTree (the parts as a tree, with the numbers of the branches). All are NON_DESTRUCTIVE, synchronous and answer JSON text.

Handles, positions and numbers. Every row of an answer has a handle, the uuid of the part (an agent sees it as h:m17: the border of the agent turns the uuids of its copy into handles and back, see CommandCage; a command knows nothing of it). A part parameter is a String that Book.locate(part, branch) reads as a handle (CommandScope.resolveMessage, so only a part of the scope's book is found) or as a position (depth on a branch, the first part is 1); a branch is the handle of one of its parts (the branch through it to its end, StoryTree.leafOf) or its number: the ends of the branches (parts without children) ordered by creation, the oldest is 1. Positions and numbers move when parts are added or deleted, so the commands that write accept handles only. list-branches gives the numbers and list-swipes, search-parts and find-occurrences say the branch that shows a part that is not on the active branch. Without a branch the active branch (getBranchFromLeaf, the root first) is used; the other branches need the whole tree (ChatMessageService.getAllMessages, one query), so a command loads it only when asked for one. A form with a single String that could be a text or a part (count-tokens, preview-lore-activation) takes the handle in the text: the dispatcher can't tell two one-String forms apart.

Time limited patterns. The regular expressions of find-occurrences (and search-lore) run over utils.TimeSafeText: the text is wrapped in a CharSequence whose charAt checks the clock and throws RegexTimeoutException after 30 seconds for the whole command (the system property marginalia.regexTimeoutMillis changes it), which the command turns into an error with ERROR_REGEX_TIMEOUT. A pattern the JDK can't optimise, such as one with a back reference ((a+)+\1b), can run for hours otherwise; TextSearch uses the same wrapper for each text.
Bounded answers. Lists take offset and limit (50, at most 200); texts come in slices (offset, length, 6000 characters, at most 20000) with totalLength and truncated.
Forms. The options are the usual ladder of overloads (every prefix of the parameter list is a form), so a command can be called by name only with a prefix of its parameters.

Summaries. The state of a summary (valid, outdated) comes from SummaryService.collectBlocks; the "covers" range of a block runs from the part after the previous block to the part that holds the summary.
compare-parts uses utils.TextDiff, a longest common subsequence of the sentences (a line break ends a sentence too), refused above 4 million cells.
Tests: ManuscriptReadCommandsTest runs them in an agent session (AgenticRequestAttributes in the test sources puts an AgenticSessionPoint into the session scope of the logged in test user).

The package domain.service.impl.commands.lorebook.read has ListLorebooksCommand, ListLoreEntriesCommand, GetLoreEntryCommand, SearchLoreCommand and PreviewLoreActivationCommand on LorebookReadSupport, which extends ManuscriptReadSupport (so the Book, the paging and the slices are the same). Its Lore is the lorebook tree of the open book: the root lorebook of the manuscript, then the subbooks level by level, each once (LorebookService.getSubbooks skips the deleted ones). A lorebook is its number in that order (the root is 1), an entry its number in the lorebook (LorebookEntryService.getEntriesForLorebook: by ordinal, then by id, deleted ones left out). Nothing outside the tree is reachable, so an agent never sees the other lorebooks of the user, and no uuid is given out or accepted. list-lore-entries filters by name and tag in Java and keeps the numbers of the whole lorebook; search-lore scans name, text and comment case-insensitively (plain text or a regular expression) and reports one hit per entry with the fields that match.

preview-lore-activation asks LorebookActivationService (domain.service), the rules the generation step ProcessLorebookStep uses too: collectLorebooks (the enabled tree with the entries filled in), orderedEntries (by order, the older first), evaluate(entry, bookTags, text) (a Verdict with a Reason: CONSTANT, FILTER_MATCHED, DISABLED, NEGATIVE_TAG, MISSING_TAG, FILTER_NOT_MATCHED) and renderPayload. The step only adds its events around them, so what the command shows is what a generation does. With a part the filters are looked for in the user prompt of the book rendered from the turn input stored with the part, in a fresh TemplateContext (the book, the narration settings, the variables of the book and of the part; not the story), so a payload that reads the story renders without it. The form with text and the form with part both have one argument, a number on the command line is taken for the text: give a part as a number to executePositional, or by name as an agent does.
Tests: LorebookReadCommandsTest, the same way, with a lorebook tree, a lorebook the book does not use and a deleted entry.

The packages domain.service.impl.commands.manuscript.write and lorebook.write hold the commands that change the book, on ManuscriptWriteSupport (which extends ManuscriptReadSupport) and LorebookWriteSupport (which extends LorebookReadSupport): PartEditCommands (edit-part, replace-part-text, append-to-part, set-part-fields), PartStructureCommands (create-part, insert-part, branch-part, delete-part, switch-branch), SummaryWriteCommands (set-summary, remove-summary, revalidate-summaries), BookSettingsCommands (set-book-info, set-book-prompts, set-book-tags), StoryGenerationCommands (next, swipe, regenerate), SummaryGenerationCommands (regenerate-summary, create-meta-summary), LoreEntryWriteCommands and LorebookWriteCommands. They call the services the screens use (ChatMessageService.updateResponse / createPart / insertPart / branchAndSwitch / swipeAndSwitch / deleteNodeAndMigrateChildren, SummaryService.updateSummaryText / removeSummary / revalidate, ManuscriptService.updateSettings, LorebookEntryService.create / update / move / deleteEntry, LorebookService for the subbooks) and add no rule of their own, so what the user does in a window and what a command does is one path.

Handles only. A part, lorebook or entry parameter must be a handle (ManuscriptWriteSupport.part, LorebookWriteSupport.book / entry); a position or number is refused with ERROR_COMMAND_HANDLE_REQUIRED.

Severity. Adding and changing is NON_DESTRUCTIVE; what removes text or data (replace-part-text, delete-*, remove-summary, regenerate, set-book-prompts) is DESTRUCTIVE and calls context.confirm(question): the user at the command bar gets a dialog, an agent is not asked again (its destructive mode decided before the call). A refusal answers Nothing was changed.

Outdated summaries. An edit can invalidate the hash of a summary block. reportOutdated puts the summaries an edit made outdated (the ones outdated now and not before) and a hint into the answer; revalidate-summaries is the author's way to say they are still right.
The window. After a change changed() reloads the book window of the user (CommandUtils.reloadManuscriptWindow, nothing for an agent, which has none).

Generation. next, swipe and regenerate are async and call StoryGenerationService.generateNextTurn with a listener that completes a future; each moves activeLeaf, so one generation of a book runs at a time (a lock per manuscript, the others wait). Swipe and regenerate need the part to be the end of its branch (they make it the active leaf first, as the pipeline expects), and take the turn input from the part unless given. profile names a model profile of the agent of the run (AgentService.resolveProfile, GenerationOptions.withModel); for the user it is refused. The generation question about outdated summaries is passed on with context.confirm and the answer yes is reported as a warning. Stopping the command cancels the generation (CancellationToken).
search-replace-parts and search-replace-lore-entries have maxHits (refuse above it) and dryRun (count and show five matches, change nothing).

This page shows how to add commands, in the application and in a plugin. Read Commands first for the model.
A suite is a plain class (no interface, no base class) with public methods annotated with @Command:

/roll and /roll 20 now work. The two methods are two forms of the command roll: the same name and human name, a different signature. Typing /roll 20 is text; because the parameter is Integer.class the text is converted, and /roll many fails with a notification instead of calling the method.
Rules to remember:
The method is public void and takes only the CommandContext. Anything else makes registerCommands throw.
Fill in description (for the user, shown in the list and the help) and llmDescription (for an agent: what it does, when to use it, whether it has side effects). See Texts for how they are given.
Declare returns. The help shows it. void.class is the default.
Declare dataSeverity, see Data severity. The default is DESTRUCTIVE; a command that does not change or remove anything that exists says NON_DESTRUCTIVE.

No signature means any arguments: the objects are in context.getPositional(). Use it for commands like echo, or when the arguments are truly free-form. A declared signature that fits always wins over the any-form.
An argument of type Object.class is "any" and also accepts a list of objects, passed as one argument.

A parameter can say more for an agent (it is the schema of the function, see Commands as functions): optional = true (it may be left out), defaultValue = 0 (text, converted to the type) and allowed = {short, long} (an enum type needs none, its constants are the values). Without optional a parameter is required when every form of the command has it, so with a ladder of forms that each add a parameter only the first ones are required. The command line ignores all three.

A parameter of the type LLMAttachment[] takes images for the model the command talks to (the Lore Generator's generate-lore-entry has one, images). An agent passes paths of image files of its workspace and the command gets the attachments (see Images); the command line can't convert text to attachments, so keep such a parameter in a form of its own at the end of the ladder, optional = true.
The suite is stateless. Do not keep the book, the user or the result in a field. See Statelessness.

The attributes are arrays only so that "not given" can be told from "given" (the default is the empty array); write the value alone: humanName = L.LABEL_X, humanNameText = X. The human name needs one of the two; the other texts are optional. A pair may hold only one value: both attributes of a pair, more than one element, or none for the human name make registerCommands throw IllegalArgumentException that names the method and the attribute. The registry keeps each as a CommandText (key() or text(), isEmpty(), get(...)); an annotation attribute needs an enum constant, so use L.X directly there, not a constant that holds it.

The localized one takes an L key and is resolved in the language of the user every time it is shown (CommandText.get(loc)), so the application's own commands use it (humanName = L.LABEL_COMMAND_TAKE_BACKUP; the key goes to L and to the English, Japanese and Chinese bundles as usual). The plain one is for an extension that brings no translations and is shown as it is. The identifiers (commandName, a parameter's name, the return name) are not texts and stay strings.

dataSeverity tells the user, and later an agent, whether the command changes or removes data that exists: CommandDataSeverity.DESTRUCTIVE (the default, also for a command that says nothing) or NON_DESTRUCTIVE.
Use NON_DESTRUCTIVE for commands that read, compute or only add (a backup, a new entry). Nothing that was there before changes.

Leave DESTRUCTIVE for everything that replaces, deletes, overwrites or moves existing data (search and replace, delete, restore, import over a book). When in doubt it is destructive: the safe assumption costs only a red label.
All forms of one command share the value; registerCommands throws when they differ.
It is information. The service does not ask or refuse because of it, so a destructive command that has no preview still asks itself, see Asking the user.

@Command(readOnly = true) declares that the command changes nothing (no book, lorebook, or data of an extension); the default is false, so a command that does not say is taken to change data. The runner of an agent takes an automatic checkpoint before a round in which a call may change something, and a round of read only commands needs none. All forms of one command share the value (registerCommands throws when they differ), CommandDefinition.readOnly() returns it. All the read commands of the app and the get- / list- commands of the Arc Outline and the Character Tracker declare it.

@Command(availableForAgent = false) keeps a command from agents (the default is true). Use it for a command that only makes sense for the user at the book window, such as /take-backup, which backs up the book the user has open: an agent works on a copy, and its backups are the checkpoints. A command that is not available is not in the allowlist editor of the agent dialog, is never turned into a function for the model (CommandFunctions, even when the allowlist of an older agent names it) and is not offered in the command box of the console; the user still runs it from the command bar. All forms of one command share the value (registerCommands throws when they differ), CommandDefinition.availableForAgent() returns it. It is independent of the severity, and such a command needs no llmDescription.

The label is shown by the command bar in the list and in the help, with an explanation as its tooltip; the texts are the keys LABEL_COMMAND_DESTRUCTIVE, LABEL_COMMAND_NON_DESTRUCTIVE, HELP_COMMAND_DESTRUCTIVE and HELP_COMMAND_NON_DESTRUCTIVE, carried by CommandDataSeverity.getLabel()/getDescription().

getScope().getManuscript() returns null when nothing is open (no workspace yet, no book). The same code works in the desktop and in the phone layout and for an agent, whose scope is its working copy (see The scope); a command that must work for agents takes the book from the scope and does not go through the workspace or the open window itself. An item that is given to the command (a part, a lorebook, an entry) is found with getScope().resolveMessage(uuid) and its siblings, which keep the command inside the book. Use the services for data; they check ownership of the current user.

A synchronous command can throw; the caller gets a CommandException with the exception as its cause. fail does the same and is the way for code on another thread. A message intended for the user goes into the exception message – the command bar shows it in a notification.
Set async = true when the command takes time or waits for something. Such a command:
runs on a worker thread, never blocks the UI,
may answer later, from any thread, with setReturn (or fail),
must check context.isTerminated() in its loops and return at once when it is true, because the user can press Stop in the progress window.

A part of the work that can't be abandoned (a transaction that is being written) is marked with context.setUninterruptable(true); the Stop button is disabled and cancelling does nothing until you set it back to false. See Uninterruptable runs.

Tell the user what is going on with context.setStatus(Taking a backup of Dune) (the main line) and context.setSubStatus(Chapter 3 of 12) (the detail under it); they appear in the progress window. Set them as the work advances, null clears a line.

Blocking calls (Thread.sleep, a network call) are interrupted when the run is cancelled; let the InterruptedException end the command or set the interrupt flag again and return. A command that is stopped should not call setReturn; if it does, the call is ignored.
Add the suite in CommandServiceImpl.afterPropertiesSet:

The application's suites are plain objects, not Spring beans, and are created with new; one that needs services is @Configurable and gets them @Autowired, like the UI classes (BackupCommands). Keep the logic in services and make the command a thin adapter that reads the current state through CommandUtils.

c: registerCommands(new HelloWorldCommands());

p: The plugin gets the CommandService injected into its (@Configurable) extension and registers the suite in onExtensionLoad:

Keep the suite instance in a field: unregisterCommands takes the registered object. Unregistering in onExtensionUnload is required – the service does not track bundles, and a command left behind would keep the class loader of the unloaded bundle alive. registerCommands throws when a name is taken, so give plugin commands a prefix (dice-roll) unless the name is meant to be shared.
Add true as the last argument (executeLine(/x, true)) to start the run uninterruptable; a command that is uninterruptable and calls another asynchronous one passes context.isUninterruptable().
Do not block the UI thread on an async command: use whenComplete and ui.access(...). To stop it, cancel the future.

c:
CommandRun result = commandService.executeLine("/roll 20");   // a CompletableFuture<Object>; also getStatus()
Object value = result.get();                         // blocks; fine for a synchronous command
commandService.execute("roll", Map.of("sides", 20)); // by name
commandService.executePositional("roll", List.of(20));

p: Commands are plain classes, so they are tested without the application: create a CommandServiceImpl, register the suite and run it (see CommandServiceTest and CommandDispatchTest in src/test/.../command).

Test the dispatch (every form), the failure of a bad argument, and for an async command that cancelling the future ends the work: assert isTerminated() becomes true and the worker returns. CommandUtils returns null outside a session, so a test of a command that reads the workspace needs the request attributes (see CommandUtilsTest).

A command that changes data without a preview asks first. context.confirm(question) asks whoever called the command: the user gets a yes/no dialog in the UI of the book window, on top of the progress window (so over its Stop button), the command waits on the worker thread and gets false for no, when the run is stopped meanwhile or when there is no window; an agent is not asked again and gets yes (the destructive mode of the agent decided when it called the command). Declare the command uninterruptable only after the answer. /search-replace-parts and /search-replace-lore-entries (SearchReplaceChatMessageCommand, SearchReplaceLoreEntryCommand) are the examples; their confirm method is a hook that tests override.
The question of /search-replace-parts
Each form has description, llmDescription (as L keys when the texts are translated), signature, returns.
Each command declares dataSeverity (NON_DESTRUCTIVE only when nothing that exists is changed or removed).
The suite has no state of a run or a user in fields.
async commands look at isTerminated().
A plugin unregisters its suites in onExtensionUnload.
The user guide or the plugin's documentation lists the command and its arguments.
CHANGELOG.MD mentions new commands.

CommandBar (package ui.components) is the input line for commands, a CompositeHorizontalLayout with a ComboBox and a run button. It is a separate component: it can be placed anywhere (a dialog, a sidebar, a toolbar). The story tab of the book window places it next to the menu bar; the bar knows nothing about the book.
The list the bar shows when / is typed, and the help popover of a command while its arguments are typed:
The list of commands
The help of a command
CommandBar is @Configurable: create it with new in a session; the services are injected. It implements HasEnabled (the story part disables it while the story is frozen by a running generation).
The bar does not show what a command returned. It hands a CommandResult(commandName, humanName, value) to its CommandResultTarget, an interface with:
onCommandResult(CommandResult) – called on the UI thread, inside the session, once for every command that finished (result.text() is the value as text, empty for null),
clearCommandResult() – the user started something new (typed, or ran another command), so a result that is still shown is out of date. Default: does nothing.

Each place implements the target as it needs: the story tab shows the result in a popover (CommandResultView), another component could insert the text into a field, use the object as a value, or ignore it. Failures and stopped commands are reported by the bar itself with notifications.

CommandResultView is a plain @Configurable class implementing the target; create(Component target) builds a Popover above target (TOP_START) with a title, a close button and the body. It closes with the cross, with Esc and with a click outside.

The help and the result are popovers over the target, so the bar is one row high and never changes the layout (an earlier version put the help under the field and misaligned its neighbours). Popovers are opened and closed from the server (setOpenOnClick/Focus/Hover(false), setModal(false)). The CSS classes are in shared-styles.css and CssStyles (command-box, command-bar, command-help*, command-item-*, command-severity*, command-result*).
A Popover that opens while the field has focus (focus/blur listeners) and the text is not a plain name; rebuilt by showHelp() as the text changes.
A small primary play icon; runs the typed text.

The callback always applies query.getOffset()/getLimit(), also when the list is empty. Each row shows the name, the human name, the data severity label and the description.

CommandHelp.of(allCommands, text, localizer) is pure (no UI; the localizer turns an L key into the text of the user, the bar passes loc::getValue) and returns the typed name, the command, its forms that fit what is typed, the index of the argument being typed and whether there are too many arguments. The bar renders: the description, the description with the data severity label, the forms with the current parameter highlighted and its description, the return value, and an error line for too many arguments, an unknown command or text without a slash. The texts are localization keys (LABEL_COMMAND_*, HELP_COMMAND_*, ERROR_COMMAND_*); the Japanese and Chinese bundles carry them too.

The label of the data severity is a Span made by severityBadge, in the list and in the help: red (command-severity-destructive) for DESTRUCTIVE, green (command-severity-non-destructive) for NON_DESTRUCTIVE, the explanation in its title. The texts come from CommandDataSeverity.getLabel() and getDescription().

run(line) closes the help, clears the result (clearCommandResult()), empties the field (clearInput(); text that is not a known command returns earlier and stays) and calls commandService.executeLine. For a command that completed (synchronous) the result is delivered at once. For an async command the bar opens a CommandProgressDialog – modal, an indeterminate ProgressBar, the two status lines of the command (setStatus, setSubStatus; a line that is empty is hidden) and a Stop button whose handler cancels the future. The bar feeds the lines from CommandRun.addStatusListener through ui.access(...), after reading the status already set, and the state of the button from addUninterruptableListener (disabled while the command is uninterruptable, setStopEnabled). When the future completes, ui.access(...) (with the request scope and UIPushGuard.push) closes the dialog and delivers the result, or shows a notification for a stop, a CommandException or an IllegalArgumentException. This is why an async command must react to isTerminated(): Stop only cancels the future.
The CommandProgressDialog of an asynchronous command
Create the CommandBar where the component is built (a @Configurable class or a plugin decorator) and set its result target.
Give it a CSS class for sizing. Do not use inline styles; command-box (flex 1 1 40%, minimum width 12 em) is the one the story tab uses.
Disable it with setEnabled(false) while something locks the UI.
Decide what a result means there. Reuse CommandResultView if a popover fits.

In the story tab, ManuscriptStoryPart.createCommandBox() builds the bar and the result view and returns the bar; setFrozen enables and disables it. The method is @Extendable/@PublicAPI (from 1.4.0), so a plugin can replace or wrap the bar through a decorator on its return value (see Extendable classes).

An agent is an LLM that works on one book on its own, for a long time, and calls commands as its tools; one execution of it is a run. This page is how it all works inside: the pieces, the life of a run, what the model sees and can call, how the user is brought in, and how to add to it. What the user sees is in the user guide; the entities (Agent, AgentRun, AgentMessage) are in the domain model.

The central idea: an agent is not a new kind of program but a loop around the things that already exist. The model is asked through the same InferenceService as everything else, the tools are the same commands the command bar runs, and a run works on an ordinary (hidden) copy of a book in the same services. What an agent adds is a way to run all that without a browser: a request context made from the database, a state machine that can be paused and resumed, a workspace of files, and a transcript that is saved after every round.
