p: An agent can look at images when the author says its model can (AgentModelProfile.isImages(), a checkbox of the AgentDialog for the main profile; the API of an OpenAI compatible endpoint does not report it). Everything image related is built from three existing facts: LLMAttachment (an image on a user message becomes an image_url content part in OpenAICompatibleInferenceService.toUserMessage), the cage (an image is a file of the workspace) and the transcript (rows must stay small).

Files. An image is a workspace file whose bytes start like a PNG, a JPEG, a GIF or a WebP (ImageFiles.mimeType, never the name; SVG is text and is not one). VirtualFileSystem.writeImage checks that (ImageFiles.check: the type, and for the types ImageIO reads the pixels from the header, at most MAX_PIXELS, so a decompression bomb is not stored) and writes through VirtualMount.writeImage (a default method that refuses; WorkspaceMount shares write with it). An image may be WorkspaceLimits.maxImageBytes (5 MB by default; the three argument constructor makes it the larger of that and maxFileBytes), a text file keeps maxFileBytes; both count against the total and the number of files. WorkspaceMount.read reads up to the larger limit and VirtualFileSystem.read refuses what is over maxFileBytes and not an image, so the text rules did not change. readText of an image says "is an image ... view_image shows it to you". The agent can't write bytes (its tools write text), so images come from the user: the Upload button of the AgentWorkspaceBrowser and the attach button of the console, or a command result in a later version.

What the model is sent. ImageFiles.prepare returns an image as it is when its longest side is within MAX_SIDE (1568) and the file within 1.5 MB, otherwise it is scaled with ImageIO in its own format (a PNG stays PNG, a JPEG stays JPEG, a GIF is its first frame as PNG, an image with alpha is PNG); a WebP is not decoded here and goes as it is. VirtualFileSystem.readImage is prepare(read(...)).

view_image(path) (ImageTools, ImageToolsImpl) checks the image and notes the path in the ShownImages of the worker. A tool result is text only in Chat Completions, so after the results of the round the worker appends one more message of the user: the text "The image you asked to look at: /refs/map.png" and an attachment per image. The tool is bound only when the main profile has images (Worker.seesImages).

The transcript keeps paths. The attachment of a stored message is ImageFiles.reference(path) (kind IMAGE, the path as its name, no bytes, no URL; isReference tells it). A message of the transcript with such an attachment is turned into the real image when a request is made: Worker.withImages works on a copy of the transcript, reads and scales the newest MAX_SHOWN_IMAGES (4) images, and writes a note into the text of the older ones (... is not shown any more, view_image shows it again), of the ones that are gone (can't be shown: reason) and of all of them for a model that does not see images. The images are re-read for each request, which costs a decode and keeps the stored run small and valid after a resume.

Images with a message of the author. AgentRunner.send(run, text, images) takes paths of image files of the workspace (at most MAX_ATTACHED_IMAGES = 8; the text may be empty): it refuses a model that does not see images, checks each path with readImage, appends "Attached image: /uploads/a.png" to the text and adds the references. The console (AgentConsoleDialog) keeps the picked images (attachImage, an Upload that takes image/* and a paste handler, JavascriptLibrary.forwardPastedImages) until Send, then writes them with writeImage into /uploads (uploadPath: a taken name gets -2, -3) and passes their paths.

Commands that take images. A command parameter of the type LLMAttachment[] is a list of paths for the model (an array of strings with Defaults.AGENT_IMAGES_ARGUMENT_HINT): CommandFunctions.forAgent(..., FunctionString, LLMAttachment images) reads the paths with readImages (at most MAX_IMAGES = 8; a path that is not an image is an error naming the argument) and the command gets LLMAttachment[]. Without a reader the parameter is not in the schema. The worker gives the reader whatever the profile says: the images go to the model of the command, which is not the model of the agent (generate-lore-entry of the Lore Generator is the first). In the command bar the argument is text, which can't be converted, so a form with such a parameter is not reachable there.

CommandFunctions (package domain.service.agent) turns the commands an agent may call into a FunctionSet: forAgent(commandService, agent, lookup, approval) offers the commands on the allowlist of the agent, create(commandService, names, mode, lookup, approval) the ones named. lookup gives the texts (localization::getValue; the descriptions are for the model, so build the set inside the context of the run). It is built for a run and combined with the tools of the runner by FunctionSet.and; the arguments may hold references.

One function per command. The forms (overloads) of a command share one schema: the union of their parameters in the order of the ladder, a type that differs between the forms is "any". A call goes to the form with the fewest parameters that has every argument the model passed, the parameters of it the model left out are null or their defaultValue; a middle option left out therefore works. Arguments no form takes, a missing required one or a value outside allowed are an INVALID_ARGUMENTS error that says which. A command without a declared signature takes any properties.

Required is not declared: a parameter is required when every form with a signature has it and none marks it optional (see writing commands). The schema carries description, enum (enum types and allowed) and default.

Names. A command name that is a valid function name ([a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}) is the function name. Any other is written with _ for every character that is not allowed, cut so that it fits, and _ plus six hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 of the command name (functionName). The rule looks at the name only, never at what else is registered, so the name in a stored transcript means the same command after a restart (and foo.bar is never taken for a command foo_bar). Names are resolved by the name at every call, so a command that is gone answers "not available now".

Result and errors. The result is bounded (MAX_RESULT_LENGTH, 20 000 characters, cut at a line with a note how much there was): a string as it is, anything else JSON, nothing "OK". A failure is the message of the cause (no class names), which the inference service writes as Error: message.

Policy. Only the allowed commands exist for the model. A DESTRUCTIVE command follows Agent.getDestructiveMode(): DENY leaves it out, AUTO runs it, ASK asks the Approval (a future of the decision of the user; the call waits for it and no thread is held) and refuses when there is none.

Context. The commands run as whoever the thread is: the inference service calls the functions in the request context of the caller, which for a run is the AgentRequestAttributes of openSession, and the command service hands it on to the commands that run on a worker. Nothing is aimed at the working copy by the adapter itself; that is what the context (the AgenticSessionPoint of the run) does.

A long text should not pass through the model twice: the model pays for every token it writes (time, and the limit of one answer), and a text it has already read is in its context. Two references let a call name the text instead of writing it. Both are a whole value of an argument (@file:/notes/a.md, @result, @result:3; text inside a longer value is just text) and both are replaced before the call, so the command (and the approval dialog) gets the real text, while the transcript keeps the short call.
Reference
Is
Works in
@file:/path
The text of that file of the workspace.
The text parameters of the commands, the content of write_file and append_file.
@result
The whole result of the newest call of a command in the run.
The same places.
@result:3 (also @result:#3)
The whole result with that number.

CommandFunctions.readReferences does the replacing, once the arguments are known and before the form of the command is picked, and only for a parameter that is a text in every form that has it: a number or a boolean is left as the model wrote it. A reference that cannot be resolved is an error naming the argument (The argument text: There is no result #7, list_command_results shows the ones that are kept), so the model corrects it. The functions are told about the references in the schema (the description of every text parameter gets the hint) and in the runner note; @file: is a reference only when the agent has files (a files reader was given) and @result only when results are kept (a CommandResults was given), otherwise the text is passed as it is.

CommandResults is the holder of the results: one per tools(), shared by the commands (which add to it) and the file tools (which read it). CommandFunctions.run adds the result of every call that returned (a failure keeps nothing) with the function name, the arguments as one short line (describeArguments; an argument that was a reference shows the reference) and the text before the model's 20 000 characters cut, so what a reference inserts and save_command_result writes is all of it even when the model saw a cut one. The last KEEP = 10 are kept, numbers count from 1 in the run, the holder lives as long as one worker (a resumed run starts empty). list_command_results shows them newest first, save_command_result(path, id?, append?) writes one to a file by the same atomic write as write_file. A result is added after the command returned and before the next call is read, so the newest is always the one of the previous call.

AgentVirtualFileSystemService hands out the files of agents. Two folders in the application folder (not in data/, which is named by logins): agent-workspaces/agent uuid is the workspace, which belongs to the agent and stays between its runs (the notes it keeps), and agent-runs/run uuid is the folder of a run (base/ with the snapshot of the original, written when the copy is made, and checkpoints/, see Checkpoints; RunFolder is the layout). The uuids are checked, so no value of the database makes a path leave these folders. open(run) is the file system of a run (the workspace, /checkpoints and /AGENTS.md), openWorkspace(agent) the workspace alone for the user to look at; both refuse (IllegalArgumentException) what is not the user's own. Both use the WorkspaceLimits of getLimits(agent): the defaults of the service (getLimits()) with the quotas of the permission of the agent's owner over them. getFileTools(fileSystem) binds AgentFileTools to it (a FunctionSet, to be put with the other tools of the run). clearWorkspace refuses while the agent works, copyWorkspace is what AgentService.cloneAgent calls, and a workspace is deleted with an agent that is deleted for good (not with a soft deleted one: it can be restored) and by the cleanup (the service is a CleanupContributor), a run folder with its run; the files go after the transaction committed, a rollback does not bring them back.
The model never gets a path of the disk. A string it wrote goes through three steps, all in domain.service.agent:

VirtualPath is the immutable value. Parsing normalizes (NFC), requires / at the start, lets .. go up and stop at the root (a chroot), and refuses empty and . parts, \, control, format and unassigned characters, : | ? *, a name that starts or ends with a space or ends with a dot, Windows device names and too long names, paths and depth. That takes drive letters and UNC paths with it. Percent encoded or full width dots are letters: names like any other, leading nowhere. Every method that builds a path from a name checks the name again.

VirtualFileSystem routes a path to a VirtualMount (stat, list, read, write, writeImage, createFolder, delete, move, toVirtual): the workspace is the root, /checkpoints (CheckpointsMount) lists the checkpoints and is read only, /AGENTS.md (InstructionsMount, only in the file system of a run) is one read only file with the instructions of the agent as open(run) read them. A mount is a folder or a file (mountEntries() gives how each shows at the root); a file of the workspace with the name of a mount is hidden by it. Other mounts, backed by services, can be added the same way. toVirtual(Path) is the reverse mapping for everything that goes to the model and throws for a path outside every mount.

WorkspaceMount is where the cage is made of real checks: it walks the path name by name from the real root and refuses a symbolic link, anything but a file or a folder, and a name present in another spelling (also on a case sensitive file system, so Notes.md and notes.md are never both there); a workspace folder that is itself a link is refused when it is opened. Files are written whole to a temporary file (.marginalia-tmp- prefix, not listed, not creatable) and moved over the target, so a reader sees the old or the new content. Writes and deletes of one workspace take one lock (kept by the service per agent), which makes the limits of WorkspaceLimits (file size, total size, number of files) true under parallel threads. The name checkpoints and AGENTS.md are reserved at the root.
Errors are VirtualFileExceptions whose message names virtual paths only; the cause (with real paths) goes to the log. The tools pass nothing else to the model.

AgentFileToolsImpl implements the functions: list_files, read_file (line ranges, cut at 20 000 characters at a line with the line to go on from; a result that is the whole file and has at least Defaults.AGENT_FILE_HINT_FROM (500) characters ends with Defaults.AGENT_FILE_HINT, a line that tells the model to pass the file as @file:/path instead of writing its text out in a call: the model has just got the text, which is when it copies it, and its output is what costs the time), write_file, append_file, replace_in_file (the old text must be in the file exactly once; a file with Windows line breaks is matched too), regex_replace_in_file, grep_files (at most 100 lines, 1 000 files), move_file (a free target name, the folders above it are created; not between mounts), copy_file (a file or a folder to a free name; all or nothing, checked against the file, size, depth and path-length limits before a byte is copied, through a temporary file or folder moved into place; the same mount only), merge_files (up to 100 files, read and joined in Java, one write; a * / ? in the last name of a path stands for the files of that folder by name, the target left out), unzip_file (see Zip files) and delete_file. list_command_results and save_command_result work on the results of the commands, see References. list_files and grep_files take a glob (VirtualGlob: *, **, ?, [a-c], {md,txt}, case-insensitive, matched on virtual paths only; without a / against the name at any depth, with one against the path below the folder). The regular expressions use TextSearch and read the text through a DeadlineCharSequence, which throws after three seconds, because a thread cannot be stopped from outside and a pattern with a back reference backtracks for hours.

c: text -> VirtualPath.parse -> VirtualFileSystem (mounts) -> WorkspaceMount: checked real path (never returned)

p: The workspace holds three kinds of file: text (UTF-8, no NUL), images (ImageFiles) and zip files (ArchiveFiles.isZip: the PK signature). A zip file is written by VirtualFileSystem.writeArchive (the upload of the workspace browser does it; the model has no tool that writes one) up to WorkspaceLimits.maxArchiveBytes (10 MB by default, or the file limit when that is more), counts like any file, and cannot be read as text (readText says to use unzip_file). maxAnyFileBytes() is the most any file may be, which is what WorkspaceMount.read allows.

unzip_file(path, target) is VirtualFileSystem.unzip -> WorkspaceMount.unzip, under the lock of the workspace, all or nothing: the archive is opened with java.util.zip.ZipFile (so its central directory is the source of the sizes), ZipExtractor unpacks into a temporary folder next to the archive (.marginalia-tmp- prefix, so no folder is made before the archive is known to be good), and the folder is moved to the target, which must not exist. ZipExtractor trusts nothing of the archive:

Names: an entry with .. or a leading / refuses the whole archive (zip slip). Other names lose their . and empty parts, are normalized (NFC) and must pass VirtualPath (an entry that does not is left out and reported; a \ is a forbidden character, never a separator); the real path is built from the checked names below the temporary folder. A name starting with .marginalia-tmp- is left out. Two names equal in lower case, and a name that is both a file and a folder, refuse the archive.
Only regular files and folders are made; a link in the archive is an ordinary entry with the target as its bytes, judged as any file.

Content: text, images (ImageFiles.check) and zip files are kept within their limits; the rest is left out and named in the answer (the first 20). A zip file inside is stored, never unpacked, so there is no recursion.

Bombs: at most 5 000 entries; the bytes inflated by all the entries (the ones left out too) must not pass maxTotalBytes; an entry is read to the size it declares and refused when it inflates to more; the ratio of inflated to packed bytes is limited to 100 for an entry and for the archive (not looked at below 256 KiB); the files and bytes must fit what the workspace has room for.
Encrypted and damaged archives give an error without details of the disk.
ZipUnpackTest covers it, with the archives made in the test.
Agents work while the user is away, so nothing here depends on an open browser.

Attention. Every status change writes agent_runs.attention in the same SQL update as the status (AgentRunStatus.needsAttention: IDLE, WAITING_APPROVAL, DONE, FAILED, a PAUSED with a reason of its own), so it is stored while the user is away; acknowledge(run) clears it. After the transaction commits, AgentAttentionService.publish calls the listeners of the owner, an observer in memory with no UI in it. The Agents tab of every open UI subscribes in create() and runs the notice through ui.access + InRequestScope: the number on the tab, a notice with Open. Opening the console acknowledges the run.

Webhook. AgentAttentionServiceImpl.publish also hands the notice to AgentWebhookService.notify(notice, screenOpen) (screenOpen: some UI of the user is subscribed). On its own thread (agent-webhook, the publishing thread is inside the commit of the change) it checks that the administrator allows it (AppSettings.agentWebhooksDisabled, null is allowed; setAllowed is admin only), that the change needs the user (Notice.attention), that the user has UserSetting.agentWebhookUrl (check: http / https with a host, at most 2000 characters) and, with a screen open, agentWebhookAlways; the text is the MSG_AGENT_NOTICE_* of the user's language (Localization.getValue(Language, L), the default language where a bundle lacks it) and goes out as WebhookFormat.PLAIN (the body, the agent name as the Title header when it is printable ASCII), DISCORD ({content}) or GOTIFY ({title,message,priority}) with java.net.http (no redirects, 5 s to connect, 10 s for the answer, the answer is not read). Nothing that holds the URL is logged or returned: the URL may hold a secret, and the call is a request of the server to an address a user typed. sendTest is the button of the settings. A failure is a line in the log.

Approvals. For an agent in the ASK mode a destructive command waits. CommandFunctions calls the Approval the runner gave it (Worker.approve), which registers the request with AgentApprovalService, moves the run to WAITING_APPROVAL, and returns the future of the decision. The console shows the oldest pending command in AgentApprovalDialog; Approve / Deny complete the future, and the continuation runs on a thread of the run in its own context, never in the session of the user's browser. backToWork moves the run to RUNNING when nothing else waits. Pausing, stopping, finishing or failing the run refuses every pending command (rejectAll).

Questions. ask_user, or a reply with no call, ends the round with IDLE; the question is the status reason. The console does not show the status reason (it holds only the last one): the calls of finish and ask_user are rendered as bubbles of their own (specialCall) at their place in the transcript, their acknowledgement (RunToolsImpl.isAcknowledgement) hidden, so they stay when the run goes on. AgentRunner.send(run, text) appends the answer, moves IDLE to RUNNING and starts a worker.

All under ui.dialogs.agent except the tab. They are ordinary @Configurable classes created with new, so they use the services and never touch the runner's internals.
Called by the screens that open a book: tells which agent holds a locked book.
Class
Copies the definition and the workspace (not the runs) to a new agent of another book.

Create / edit an agent. The editor lists every registered command with its severity; the presets tick them at once: all, none, non-destructive and the roles AUDITOR, LORE_KEEPER, EDITOR, DRAFTER (AgentCommandPreset.includes(row): every readOnly command, also of extensions, plus the named write commands of the role; none has a destructive one; the selection shows the first preset whose set equals it). An allowed command that is not registered now (its extension is not loaded) stays allowed when saved. Each row carries tokens, what its definition adds to a request (CommandFunctions.create for that one command, the name, description and schema counted with TokenizerService.countTokensApprox as the runner's toolTokens does, destructive mode AUTO so none is left out); the dialog adds the ticked ones, the prompt and the instructions (a blank field counts its default) into the line under the instructions (AgentDialog.showSize).
Does
Keep or discard the result.
One pending command, Approve / Deny.

Puts messages into a box as the blocks of the console (bubbles with markdown, folded reasoning and calls with their results, the report and the question of the agent, the author's commands, the compaction summary, the time of each); the console uses it for the transcript of the run and AgentSubAgentsView for each sub-agent (setLabels names who speaks; setOnSubAgent gives the spawn_agent calls a button).

The Agents tab (a WorkspaceComponent): the table of agents with the state of their run, the buttons that call AgentRunService / AgentRunner (Pause now is AgentRunner.pauseNow), and the attention badge. new AgentPart(workspace, true) is the phone variant, used by PhoneWorkspace.addAgentsTab: one column with a card for each agent (createCard: name, state, the same buttons wrapping). The dialogs call UIUtils.fitPhone(dialog, fullHeight) (the width of the phone workspace, UIUtils.isPhone()): full screen with the phone-dialog rules, footers wrap, the review splits vertically.

The Book copy tab (AgentConsoleDialog.COPY_TAB): a branch of the copy's story part by part (a combo of the branches) and its lorebooks in a grid with the detail of the row; read-only, made when the tab is picked and by Refresh; also opened by the review at an item, see Reading the copy.

The Checkpoints tab of the console (AgentConsoleDialog.CHECKPOINTS_TAB, read again only while shown): the list with who made each, the usage of the quota, save / restore / rewind / download / delete. Saving, restoring and rewinding wait until the agent does not work; a rewind needs a paused or stopped run and a checkpoint that is rewindable.
The console shows the model's results cut at RESULT_LIMIT (20 000), the same as the model got. Texts for the screens are L keys like any other (English, Japanese and the Chinese plugin bundle).

The Context tab of the console (AgentConsoleDialog.CONTEXT_TAB, made when the tab is picked and by Refresh, never by the poll: it counts tokens): three ChartJs charts (the kinds against the cap as a doughnut, every part in order as bars, and the context per answer as a stacked bar of the estimated kinds with the reported size and the cap as lines; the lines get stacks of their own, or a stacked scale would add them up), a grid of the parts and a read only viewer of the picked one, Download and Copy of AgentContext.toMarkdown().

The Diagnostics tab (AgentConsoleDialog.DIAGNOSTICS_TAB, made when the tab is picked and by Refresh, never by the poll): the report of AgentRunner.diagnostics as a Markdown, with Download (Markdown), Download JSON and Copy.
The review of the result of a finished or kept run: the changes in a grid to tick, the detail with the text to apply, apply and discard, see Merge and apply.
The Runs tab: every run, open one in the Run tab, download it (AgentTranscriptExport, the transcript as Markdown, nothing cut), delete it.

The Sub-agents tab (AgentConsoleDialog.SUBAGENTS_TAB): a combo of AgentMessageService.threads(run) (the rewound ones marked) and the conversation of the picked one, rows added as they come (shownRows), read when the tab is picked and on every poll while it is shown; showCall(callId) picks the thread whose callId is the call, for the button of a spawn_agent call in the Run tab.

The window of a run: eight tabs (Run, Runs, Workspace, Checkpoints, Context, Book copy, Sub-agents, Diagnostics), the state above, the box and the buttons below. It polls (ui.setPollInterval(2000) while it is attached, restored on detach) and reads only the rows of the transcript it has not rendered (shown), so a long run costs no more than a short one; the model's reasoning is a folded block, a command is a folded line that opens to its arguments and result. The command line is the CommandBar of the story tab (list, help popover, severity badges), set to the commands of AgentConsoleCommands.of(commandService, AgentRunner.consoleCommands(agent)) (setCommands: the registered ones the agent is allowed and the definition of /compact, which no suite registers) and to hand its line to AgentRunner.command (setLineRunner) instead of running it as the user in their browser session; it sits, with a one line hint, between the transcript and the message box, enabled for a run that waits, is paused or is a conversation that works. Messages and commands the author queued while the agent works (AgentRunner.queued) are dashed bubbles after the last row, each with a small Send now / Run now button (AgentRunner.force); they come off while the transcript grows and go back after it. In the Workspace tab the list and the viewer split the height (flex 3 : 2), so only they scroll.

The Workspace tab: the folders and files of the agent over AgentVirtualFileSystemService.openWorkspace. A text file is shown cut at VIEW_LIMIT (2 000 characters) in a text area of a fixed height (otherwise Lumo grows it with the content), the whole file is the download; nothing can be changed while the agent works. New folder (VirtualFileSystem.createFolder, WorkspaceMount.createFolder) and Upload file (an InMemoryUploadHandler; a file that starts like an image goes to writeImage, anything else through VirtualFileSystem.decodeText, the same UTF-8 without NUL as readText, then writeText) keep the cage, the names and the limits of the agent's own writes; an existing file is not replaced, and both are refused while the agent works.
An agent calls the commands that the user ticked in the editor, so every command is also an agent tool. The rules for writing commands apply; for an agent these matter most:

Get the book from context.getScope(), never from the UI; return the data (text, JSON) instead of showing it. An item that is passed in is found through the scope (resolveMessage, resolveLorebook, resolveEntry), which keeps the command inside the working copy.

Mark the severity honestly. NON_DESTRUCTIVE commands are what the default selection offers; DESTRUCTIVE follows the agent's mode (DENY hides them). A command that only returns text and leaves the storing to the caller (the lore generator commands do this: they return the text, the agent writes the entry with the commands that exist for that) is the safest tool to hand out.

Describe it for a model. llmDescriptionText is read by the model, descriptionText by the human; say when to use it, what the arguments mean, what the result looks like and what it costs. A required prompt argument that is vague gives vague results: say what a good one contains (the lore generator throws "Give the prompt: what the entry is about, ..." for an empty one). Parameters can carry allowed, defaultValue and optional; they become the enum, default and required of the schema.

Order the forms as a ladder. The overloads are positional, the adapter picks the form with the fewest parameters that has every argument the model passed, so put the rarely used options last and make them optional.
Keep results short or paged. Over 20 000 characters the model gets a cut with a note; give the command a limit or a page argument. The whole result is still kept for @result and save_command_result.

Long work goes async = true. The command then runs on the command service's worker pool with the request context of the run (ThreadCopyRequestAttributes). A command that calls a model (lore generator) uses the blocking InferenceService.infer; with one slot on the model server that is sequential and re-reads the prompt, which is why such a command is worth its cost only for a task the agent cannot do itself. The runner cancels the CommandRun of a call when the run is paused at once, stopped, thrown away or sent a forced message (see Cancelling a call below): the command sees CommandContext.isTerminated() and its thread is interrupted, so check the one between the steps of the work and honour the other (CancellationException, InterruptedException), and leave the book in a state the agent can read; a synchronous command is not stopped.
Fail with a message for the model. The text of the exception is what the model reads as Error: message; no class names, say what to change.

Extensions bring commands the same way for the command bar and for agents: register a suite in onExtensionLoad, unregister it in onExtensionUnload. lore-generator (list-lore-templates, generate-lore-entry, compact-lore-entry), name-generator (list-name-categories, generate-names) name-provider (list-real-name-lists, pick-real-names), arc-outline (the outline and its generators) and character-tracker (characters and relationships) are examples; the example plugin shows the registration.

The engine never blocks a thread while it waits - for event listeners, for a question to the user or for the model. Every step is written as a chain of callbacks: it emits an event and passes the rest of its work as the continuation, which the engine runs on a pool thread once all listeners are done:

Decides which part of the story goes into the prompt and renders the system prompt.

Summaries. The branch from the root to the active leaf is read, and the summaries on it are collected (oldest first) into SUMMARIES with SummaryService.collectBlocks: a meta summary replaces the summaries it merged, which are skipped, see the summary chain. Each summary stores a hash of the story it covers; when that was changed since, the summary is removed (a meta summary is unwound to the summary it replaced, which is checked in turn) and the user is asked whether to continue without it (listener.askQuestion). The newest part with a summary is the stop part: it and everything before it is represented by the summaries.
Token budget. With TokenLimits:

If baseTokens + reserved ≥ limit, the generation stops with Contextual limit not sufficient. Otherwise parts are taken from the newest backwards - skipping the part being regenerated, stopping at the stop part - starting from baseTokens + reserved and counting each part as its tokenCount + 100. A part is added only if the running total with it stays within limit − 256; the first part that doesn't fit ends the loop. The chosen texts, oldest first, become MANUSCRIPT_CHRONICLE.

Token breakdown. When the budget is computed, the step creates a PromptTokenBreakdown (domain.components) and puts it into the TOKEN_BREAKDOWN property. It holds the raw counts of each section - context, response and prompt limit, jailbreak, system template (the system prompt without lore and summaries), lore, summaries, story, lore in the user prompt, the user prompt and reserved - and what was cut: the parts that didn't fit (cutMessages, cutTokens), without the parts a summary replaces. The counts are measured separately, so they need not add up exactly to the payload.

System prompt. The master template is rendered with MasterTemplateData (backgroundLore, summaries, narrativePov, narrativeTense, style + the template context) into systemPrompt. The estimate above renders it with a fork of the template context, so macros that change variables don't run twice.
Events: BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT, BEFORE_SUMMARIES (SUMMARIES can be changed), AFTER_MANUSCRIPT_CONCATENATION (MANUSCRIPT_CHRONICLE can be changed), AFTER_PREPARE_CONTENT.

limit      = context tokens − response tokens        (smaller of protocol and provider limits)
baseTokens = system template rendered with lore and summaries (no story)
           + jailbreak + rendered user prompt + 100
reserved   = PrePromptData.reservedTokens            (set by extensions, 0 by default)

p: Builds the chat completion messages:

Earlier parts are sent as the model's own previous answers, each preceded by a short placeholder user turn. The final user message carries the instructions. Only the text of the parts is sent: the images attached to a part are not part of it and the model never sees them.

An LLMChatMessage can carry LLMAttachments (images, audio, files) for models that accept them, and the OpenAI compatible provider sends those of a user message as content parts. This step adds none; a listener of AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD can put them on a user message. A message can also carry function calls (toolCalls, an assistant message) or be the result of one (LLMRole.TOOL with toolCallId); the pipeline builds none of them, they are added by OpenAICompatibleInferenceService when the model calls a function, see Function calls.

The part gets the TurnInput, the model and protocol names, the payload as JSON (builtPrompt, shown by Show Prompt), the activated lore and the request time. The token breakdown gets the tokens of every message of the final payload (as listeners left it, counted with the provider's tokenizer) and is stored as the part's tokenBreakdown (shown by Token Usage, see UI). Parts generated before it existed have none, getTokenBreakdown() is null for them. The template variables of the generation are stored: local ones in the part's attributes, global ones in the book's. The part becomes the book's active leaf, both are saved and listener.onNodeCreated(part) lets the UI show it. Counts the prompt tokens (when the prompt plus the response limit still exceeds the context, the UI gets GenerationListener.onWarning; the request is sent anyway), then calls InferenceService.stream(payload, protocol, callback). For each chunk:
reasoning chunks are appended to responseReasoning (REASONING_CHUNK_RECEIVED, the text in REASONING_CHUNK),
response chunks are appended to response and to originalResponse (the text as generated, which later edits leave alone), with approximate token and word counts (CHUNK_RECEIVED, the text in CHUNK),
the first chunk sets the time to first token, the first response chunk the end of reasoning,
the part and the book are saved and the UI gets onReasoningChunk / onResponseChunk and onMetricsUpdated,
once the response has some non-blank text, the state becomes PARTIAL_SUCCESS (reasoning alone doesn't count).

Listeners of the chunk events can change the chunk text before it is appended. The stream is pulled: the inference service delivers the next chunk only after the step calls continueInference(), so a slow listener slows the stream down instead of piling up chunks.

On completion the exact token counts are computed, the state becomes SUCCESSFUL (AFTER_INFERENCE) and the engine moves to CLEANUP. An error goes to CLEANUP too: a failure of the provider (InferenceException, see Services) is reported with onInferenceError (a default method of GenerationListener that calls onSimpleError; the story editor's listener also writes it to the session's problem log for the help assistant) and a localized text of what to fix, anything else with onError.

OpenAICompatibleInferenceService counts every request in the Usage of the user who started it, so the generation, summaries and extensions that call stream are all counted without doing anything. The request carries stream_options.include_usage (unless the AI's additional parameters set stream_options), and the provider's last chunk then reports the prompt and completion tokens. Without a report (the provider doesn't send it, or the request was stopped) the service counts the payload and the text that arrived with countTokensApprox. It is recorded once, when the stream completes, is stopped (terminateInference, cancellation) or fails after some text arrived; a request that fails before any text is not counted. The stream threads have no request, so the service takes the ThreadCopyRequestAttributes of the thread that called stream and records inside it (currentUser resolves).

Before a request is built, stream asks AILimitService.check(ai, promptTokens, reservedTokens) (with our estimate of the payload and the response size the request reserves): a user with the AI not available or over their token limit gets an InferenceException (NOT_AVAILABLE, LIMIT_REACHED) in the caller's thread and nothing is sent, so the steps, summaries and extensions handle it like any provider failure. The limits are described in the domain model.

All templates of one generation - user prompt, lorebook entries, master template - share one TemplateContext (GenerationProperties.TEMPLATE_CONTEXT), created by GenerationStepBase.getTemplateContext on first use. It holds what the macros read: the TurnInput fields, POV / tense / style, the book's name and description, the model name and token limits, the generation type (normal, regenerate, swipe), the story so far (``...), the last instructions and time, the latest summary, and the variables - local ones loaded from the last part of the branch, global ones from the book. Because it is shared, a variable set in the user prompt is visible in lore entries and the master template. See Templating & macros.
Extensions hook into generation by registering listeners:
Rules:

Call chain.next() exactly once in every listener, also when it fails. chain.terminate() skips the remaining listeners of this event and continues the generation; event.terminateEvents() marks the event so the remaining listeners are skipped when next() is called. A listener that calls neither leaves the generation hanging.
A listener may call next() later, from another thread - for example after an asynchronous request of its own.
An exception thrown by a listener is logged and the chain continues with the next listener.

Listeners are global: they receive the events of every generation of every user. Use event.getManuscript() and the current user to decide whether to act, and keep per-generation data in event.getProperties() under a key prefixed with the extension's package.
Listeners run on generation threads inside the user's request scope, so services work; UI changes need ui.access(...).
Unregister on unload - registrations are not removed automatically.

The bundled Author's Note plugin is a complete example: it reserves tokens in BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT (PrePromptData.reservedTokens) and inserts a message into the payload in AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD, see Generation events.

Stop in the UI calls CancellationToken.cancel(). Every step, continuation and chunk checks the token and jumps to CLEANUP, which keeps what was generated so far (PARTIAL_SUCCESS) - or, when nothing arrived yet, removes the new part or restores the regenerated one, like after an error. Only CLEANUP reports the end to the listener.

Errors - an exception in a step or continuation, a failed request - are reported with GenerationListener.onError and also end in CLEANUP. Validation problems (no provider, context too small) use onSimpleError with a localized message; failures answered by the provider (wrong key, context too long...) use onInferenceError, which does the same unless the listener overrides it.
Questions - listener.askQuestion(text, yes, no) lets a step ask the user and continue in one of two continuations (controller.wrapCallback(...)); used for invalidated summaries.
Small changes (prompt wording, lore filtering, post-processing the answer) - an event listener in an extension is usually enough; see above.

Replacing a step - installedSteps in services-config.xml lists one implementation per GenerationStepType. A replacement must emit the same events and properties, call next() / jumpTo() exactly once per path and set the controller state the later steps expect.

A new step needs a new GenerationStepType value at the right position (the order of the enum is the order of execution) and an entry in installedSteps. Steps without an implementation make the generation report NOT IMPLEMENTED.

Every prompt Marginalia sends is rendered from a template: the master template, the user prompt, lorebook entries and the summary prompt. Templates are Handlebars with SillyTavern-compatible macros on top. This page explains how that is implemented and how to add variables and macros. What users can write is documented in the user guide: Prompt templates and the Macro reference.
The code is in domain/templates/ (data objects, context, variables), domain/templates/macros/ (translator, helpers, macro registry) and domain/service/impl/TemplateServiceImpl.java.
TemplateService.processTemplate(template, name, data):
Translate the SillyTavern syntax into plain Handlebars (MacroTranslator.translate).
Compile the result with Handlebars. Compiled templates are cached by template text (Caffeine, 500 entries, 24 h after last access), so a lorebook entry is parsed once, not on every generation.
Render it against a Handlebars Context built from the TemplateData (MacroHelpers.createContext).
Post-process the output: {{trim}} markers are removed together with the newlines around them.
Handlebars runs with EscapingStrategy.NOOP - the output is a prompt, not HTML, so quotes, and stay as they are.

isValidTemplate(template, name) only does steps 1-2, so it catches syntax errors. isValidTemplate(template, name, dataClass) also walks the compiled template (Template.collect of variables and sections, in all branches) and reports names that would end in helperMissing (see Template data) in ValidationResult.unknownNames(). They are warnings, isValid() stays true; the UI shows them as the field's helper text (TemplateHints.showWarnings). Names relative to the current context (this, ., ../x, @index) and parameters ({{#if name}}) are not checked.

The order of the generation pipeline matters: the user prompt is rendered first, then the lorebook entries, then the master template - a variable set in the user prompt is visible in lore, and lore can set variables the master template reads.
User prompt
UserPromptData

Each template gets an instance of a TemplateData subclass. Its bean properties (getters declared in the subclass - TemplateData's own methods are excluded) are the template's variables. A field annotated @LocalizedTemplateDescription(loc = L.DESC_TEMPLATE_...) is listed, with that description, in the hints popover of the prompt fields (TemplateHints), followed by the shared context properties the class doesn't declare.
Names are resolved by MacroHelpers.TemplateDataValueResolver, in this order:
a property of the data object - null renders as an empty string,

a property of the shared TemplateContext (povCharacter, presentCharacters, sceneSetting, instructions, narrativePov, narrativeTense, style, manuscriptName, manuscriptDescription) - that is why these work in every template,
an argument-less macro used as a value, so {{#if user}} works like {{if user}},
otherwise the name is missing and Handlebars' helperMissing hook renders the word Error, so typos are visible in the prompt (MacroHelpers.resolves is the same check, used by validation).

Reflection into anything else is blocked: the resolver returns nothing for other names instead of letting the default resolvers call methods of TemplateData (there is deliberately no getTemplateContext() getter).

TemplateContext is the environment macros read: the turn fields, POV / tense / style, book name and description, model name and token limits, the generation type, the story so far (storyMessages), the last instructions and time, the latest summary, the variables, a clock, a random generator and the seed for {{pick}}.

One context is created per generation (GenerationStepBase.getTemplateContext, stored as GenerationProperties.TEMPLATE_CONTEXT) and set into every data object of that generation, so all templates see the same variables. fork() makes a copy with copied variables for renders whose side effects must not count - the token estimate of the master template uses one.

{{pick}} is stable: the choice is derived from SHA-256 of the book id (pickSeed), the template key (a hash of the template text), the call site and the options. The same template in the same book picks the same option every time; editing the template or moving the macro can change the pick.

Time macros ({{time}}, {{date}}, {{weekday}}, {{datetimeformat}}...) use the context's clock, which is the server's default time zone - UTC in the Docker image - unless an offset is given ({{time::UTC+2}}). MomentFormat converts moment.js patterns (SillyTavern's) for {{datetimeformat}}.
{{trim}} outputs a marker - the word trim wrapped in the private-use character U+E000, so normal text can't contain it - which postProcess removes together with the surrounding newlines.

Marginalia's UI is written in Java with Vaadin Flow 25: the component tree lives on the server, the browser renders it with Vaadin's web components (Lumo theme, dark color scheme) and sends events back over HTTP and a push WebSocket. There is no hand-written frontend code apart from one CSS file and a small connector for the story tree. This page explains how the UI code is organized and the conventions to follow when you change it. The code is in ui/.

Most UI classes are not Vaadin components themselves. They are plain classes with a create() method that builds and returns the component tree, and keep references to the fields they need later:
This shape is deliberate:
@Configurable - the class is created with new, and the AspectJ-woven configurer injects its @Autowired fields (services, Localization, the session User). See AspectJ weaving.

@Extendable - the class is instrumented at startup so extensions can run code before and after any of its methods and read its local variables (see Extensions). Small methods with descriptive local variable names (menu, toolbar, detailLayout) are what make a class easy to extend.
Dialogs (AIDialog, ProtocolDialog, UserDialog, LorebookDialog, ManuscriptDialog...) extend Vaadin's Dialog but follow the same pattern: construct with the entity, call create(), then open().

The session's SessionPoint holds the workspace, and CommandUtils (package utils) reads it for commands: getWorkspace(), getManuscriptSection(), getManuscriptWindow(), getCurrentManuscript() and getCurrentAI() return null when there is no session, workspace or open book. The book-related methods delegate to SessionPoint (getManuscriptWindow(), getCurrentManuscript(), getCurrentAI()), which AgenticSessionPoint overrides for a session without a browser: the book is held directly and there is no window.

Command bar (see The command bar). CommandBar (package ui.components, a Composite) is the input line for the commands of CommandService, to be placed anywhere: a ComboBox with custom values, where the user types /name arg arg, plus a run button. The list is filled lazily from the registry (CommandHelp.matchingNames), the help is a Popover above the bar (it covers what is above and moves nothing in the layout), rebuilt as the text changes (description, the forms that fit, the next parameter highlighted, the return value, "too many arguments"); it opens for the arguments, for text that is not a command and for a name nothing matches, and while the name is typed the list (with the descriptions) is the help; picking a command writes /name into the field, or runs it when it takes no arguments. The bar shows no results: it hands them to its CommandResultTarget (setResultTarget), an interface (onCommandResult, and clearCommandResult when the user types or runs something else) that each place implements as it needs; the story tab (ManuscriptStoryPart.createCommandBox(), next to the menu bar) uses CommandResultView, a popover above the bar with a close button, and other places can consume the value differently. An async command opens CommandProgressDialog (modal, the two status lines of the command, Stop cancels the future); failures and stops are shown by the bar. Not on the phone story tab yet.

Main.proceedWithLogin picks PhoneWorkspace instead when the body of the page is narrower than 768 px (ExtendedClientDetails.getBodyClientWidth()). The choice is made once per login: resizing or rotating the device does not switch the workspace until the page is reloaded, and a tablet or a phone in landscape gets the desktop one. PhoneWorkspace replaces the left-hand tab sheet with an AppLayout: the parts are listed in a drawer (opened with the toggle in the top bar) whose footer holds the language selector, Change Password and Logout, and the active part fills the screen. There is no Admin button and no AdminPart on a phone: the administration (users, database backups, cleanup, extension install) is only reachable in the desktop layout. The services still check AdminGuard.requireAdmin() themselves. The user manual describes this for users in Using Marginalia on a phone. Only the book list, the lorebooks, the settings, the protocols, the models and the trash differ. PhoneManuscriptPart renders the book list like the Viewer (stacked filters, sort buttons, one column) with the controls of ManuscriptPart; both share the Add Book flow in NewBookAction. The workspace is autosaved so the next login opens it where it was left. Everything that has state worth coming back to implements Restorable (ui): JsonObject storeState() serializes the state the class needs into a new object and asks the children it has for theirs (nested under their own key), restoreState(JsonObject self) reads it back and passes the nested objects on. RestorableState has the defensive readers (string, bool, strings, object) and put, which leaves out an empty state. Workspace, WorkspaceComponent (default: no state), ManuscriptDialogPart and PhoneManuscriptDialogPart (default: no state), both book dialogs, LorebookView/PhoneLorebookView and NewTurnForm are Restorable. What is stored:

WorkspaceAutosave (ui.workspace, one per workspace) keeps the state in UserSetting.workspaceState, an @ExtendedAttribute(inject = true) JsonObject (so no migration). Workspace.autosave() stores the state of the whole workspace; the parts call it after the user did something worth coming back to - selected a tab, changed a filter, opened or closed a book, selected a tab of the book window (ManuscriptDialog.stateChanged()), opened an entry or chose a lorebook (setOnStateChange of the views), typed into the new turn form (NewTurnForm.setOnChange). It writes nothing when the state did not change, and failures are only logged. Main.proceedWithLogin calls Workspace.restoreAutosaved() after create() and refresh(): the autosave is off until then, because building the workspace fires the same change events and would overwrite the stored state, and it stays off while restoring (the restoring fires them too). The book window is restored after open(): ManuscriptPart.openManuscript is the one place that creates and opens it, for the Edit button and for restoring. Code that saves a UserSetting must load it right before, not hold on to one (UserPart.save does), or it writes back an older workspaceState.

The left bar (leftBar) is a TabDock (ui.widgets), a reusable widget: a row of columns, each a stack of tab sheets, whose tabs the user can drag out into sheets of their own (a strip between the sheets of a column) or into a column of their own (a strip between the columns and at the sides) and back (the drag and drop is Flow's DragSource/DropTarget, no JavaScript; the strips show while a tab is dragged). The columns and the sheets of a column are separated by SplitLayouts the user can resize; a split layout has two sides, so the cells of a row or column are a chain of nested split layouts, the position of each being the share of its cell in what is left (chain, shares). When a splitter is dragged the shares of all cells are read again and stored as size (percent of the dock / of the column) in the layout, onLayoutChange saves them; a cell without a size gets the average. Tabs have a stable id (add(id, caption, content), the outline is ManuscriptStoryPart.CHAPTERS_TAB); the layout, {columns:[{size:50,groups:[{size:50,tabs:[id, ...]}, ...]}, ...]} (size optional) (getLayout/setLayout; a layout with groups at the top level, as the dock stored before it had columns, is one column), names tabs only by id and keeps the place of tabs that are not there now, because extensions add their tabs late (a tab the layout does not know goes to the first sheet). ManuscriptStoryPart stores the layout in the attributes of the manuscript under $desktopManuscriptStoryPartTabsConfig (TABS_CONFIG_ATTRIBUTE): saveTabsConfig() runs after a drag, applyTabsConfig() in load() before the story is drawn. The position of the splitter between the dock and the story is saved the same way, as a number in the attribute $desktopManuscriptStoryPartSplitPosition (SPLIT_POSITION_ATTRIBUTE): saveSplitPosition() runs after the drag, applySplitPosition() in load(). The selected tab of each sheet is not part of the layout but the Restorable state of the dock. PhoneManuscriptStoryPart uses new TabDock(false), one plain sheet.

The tab with the id ManuscriptStoryPart.LOREBOOK_TAB (lorebook) of the left bar is the LorebookPreview (ui.components), a read only preview of the lore of the book, desktop only (the phone has the PhoneLorebookView). It is a TreeGrid of Rows (a lorebook or one of its entries) over a TreeData it rebuilds in refresh(lorebook): with the Include sub lorebooks checkbox the lorebook and every lorebook below it (found breadth first like ProcessLorebookStep does, each once, so a cycle ends) are the top level rows and their entries the children, otherwise the entries of the lorebook are the top level rows. The item details of an entry row show the content, rendered with a Markdown component, and the filtering (text or pattern). It saves nothing; the opened entries and the lorebooks the user closed are kept (as uuids) over a refresh. ManuscriptStoryPart.load() refreshes it, and onTabEnter() calls load(), so the lore is read again every time the user returns to the Story tab. Like the other views of this kind the components are built in create(), the injected services are not there in the constructor.

The checkable Highlight Generated Text item is the diff view: setShowGeneratedDiff(show) stores the flag (a field of the tab, not saved) and calls ChatMessageCard.renderResponse() of every card, which sets the content of the response Markdown - with the flag on, the text from GeneratedTextHighlighter.highlight(response, originalResponse, CssStyles.GENERATED_TEXT), which diffs both texts word by word and wraps the shared words in mark. The card calls renderResponse() whenever its response changes (construction, streaming, end of an edit), and StoryGenerationListener.onResponseChunk copies originalResponse into the card's own ChatMessage while streaming. The phone tab has no diff view.

SummariesDialog shows the summaries of the active branch (SummaryService.collectTree) in a TreeGridSummaryNode: the summaries generation uses are the top level, the summaries a meta summary stands in for are its children (including the summary it replaced, read from replacedSummary, which has no id). Columns: database id (the hierarchy column), message id, order in the branch, content, tokens, a checkbox and a delete button. Checkboxes, delete buttons and the edit pencil exist only on the top level - the text of the merged summaries is part of the hash of their meta summary, so editing them would invalidate it.

Content (SummaryContent): reasoning (a Details with Markdown, reasoning is mostly markdown), badges (Meta summary, Replaced) and the text as plain text (white-space: pre-wrap, summaries are not markdown and the model's single line breaks must show), in a scrolling Div of a fixed height, so all rows have the same height. The pencil is in a gutter next to the scroll area (not over the text); it swaps the text for a TextArea of the same size and the buttons for a green check (SummaryService.updateSummaryText) and a red trash icon (back to the Markdown).

Delete goes through SummaryRemoval.confirmAndRemove, shared with the part menu of the story editor: a normal summary is confirmed with yes/no, a meta summary asks Unwind / Delete / Cancel (ConfirmDialog with custom button labels).
Create meta summary takes the ticked summaries, uses the newest as from and the oldest as to and opens SummaryDialog with a meta request (createMetaSummary); it needs at least two.
The grid is reloaded after every change (refresh()): editing, deleting, and closing the dialog of a meta summary.

Both dialogs are @Configurable(preConstruction = true) (they use injected services in their constructors) and @Extendable; the overview's menu bar above the grid is empty, populateMenuBar(bar) is where extensions add tools.

TrashGrid is a self-contained widget (@Configurable, create it with new TrashGrid(allUsers).create()) over TrashService: a lazy multi-select GridTrashItem (items identified by their EntityKey, so the selection survives paging), a filter by type (names from Localization.localizeDomainObject(Class)) and, with allUsers, a filter by owner and an owner column. allUsers only decides what the widget shows; the service decides what the current user may see and restore. Restore Selected confirms and calls TrashService.restore; when it returns blockers the widget shows them in a dialog (nothing was restored), otherwise it refreshes and runs the listeners from addRestoreListener (TrashPart uses it to refresh the whole workspace). Delete Permanently (createDeleteButton, the field deleteButton) is enabled while the selection has only types of TrashService.getPermanentlyDeletableTypes() (story parts, lorebook entries), confirms and calls TrashService.deletePermanently, shows the reasons in a dialog when it is blocked and refreshes the table otherwise (nothing to refresh elsewhere, nothing came back). The Extended Content link opens the JSON from TrashService.getExtendedContent in a read-only text area. TrashPart (the Trash tab, allUsers for administrators) and CleanupPanel (a Details section, created when first opened) both use it.

PhoneTrashGrid (used by PhoneTrashPart) subclasses it through the createToolbar() (it adds the same createDeleteButton()) and addColumns() hooks: the filters are stacked over the whole width, the description is behind an info button (a Popover) instead of above the table (createDescription()), and the table has only the check box column and one content column that shows name, type, owner (allUsers), delete time and the Extended Content link below each other.

Generic dialogs: ConfirmDialog.show(message, onYes), TextInputDialog.Builder, ListSelectDialog, ErrorDialog (message and expandable stack trace), ProgressBarDialog, SearchReplaceDialog. DialogFocus.onOpen(dialog, field) (ui.widgets) puts the cursor into the field a dialog is about every time it opens, so the user can type at once; the form dialogs (AIDialog, ProtocolDialog, UserDialog, ExportDialog, TextInputDialog, ListSelectDialog, AILimitEditDialog, SearchReplaceDialog) call it. ExtensionLogDialog.show(bundle, name) is the read-only, monospace view of an extension's log. UsageDialog.show() is the read-only table of every user's Usage (administrators). AILimitsDialog.show(ai) is the table of the limits of a shared AI with add / edit (AILimitEditDialog) / delete, AILimitInfoDialog.show(ai) the current user's limit and usage of it.

SearchReplaceDialog (ui.dialogs.search) is the search and replace window without any knowledge of what it searches. A subclass supplies the title, its own options (createOptions(), shown next to the regex option and locked with it) and createSearcher(SearchRequest), which runs on the UI thread (the place to read the options) and returns a Searcher for the worker thread; that gives a SearchResult (the rows as SearchReplaceItems with their TextHits, an optional warning to confirm before the replace, and the Replacer that does the work). The dialog goes through the states INPUT → SEARCHING (inputs frozen, only Stop works) → PREPARED (inputs locked, Search is Search again, which drops the result, and Replace works; a warning goes through confirm) → REPLACING (everything frozen) → INPUT; the work runs on a ThreadAccessDialog thread and reports to the progress bar through TaskProgress. The constructor flag phone selects the layout (the fields and buttons below each other, one column in the table), so one class serves both layouts. ManuscriptSearchReplaceDialog adds the summaries and all branches options and calls ManuscriptReplaceService; the story parts of both layouts open it from the settings menu and show the story again when onReplaced fires. LorebookSearchReplaceDialog is the second subclass, for the entries of a lorebook (no extra options, getIdColumnHeader() makes the table show entry names); LorebookView has a button for it after Add Entry and PhoneLorebookView an icon button.

Never hard-code user-visible text. Add a key to loc/L.java and the text to LocalizationBundleEN (and LocalizationBundleJP), and use loc.getValue(L.KEY) (Localization is injected into every UI class). Date formats come from the same bean (loc.getDateFormat()...). The name of a kind of entity (book, lorebook...) is loc.localizeDomainObject(entityClass); it falls back to the closest known superclass, then to the simple class name, so a new entity type needs a mapping in LocalizationImpl.loadMaps(). The texts are in the language of the user's session, so never keep a text in a field that outlives the page or the request - look it up when you show it (Localization).

Wrap event handlers in try/catch and report unexpected exceptions with UIUtils.internalServerError(loc, e) - it logs the exception and opens an ErrorDialog with the stack trace. Expected problems (validation, missing configuration) are shown with Notification.error(...) or a message next to the field; UIUtils.showValidationErrors(loc, e) formats a binder's ValidationException. Failures of a request to the model API (InferenceException: wrong key, wrong URL, timeout...) go through UIUtils.inferenceError(loc, e), which shows the localized cause (InferenceErrors) as a notification and falls back to internalServerError for anything else. AIDialog has, for the type Extension (offered while an extension provides AIs), a Provider selector and the settings form of the chosen ExtensionAIFactory (see Inference providers from a plugin); the type of an existing AI is read-only. It has the Test Connection button (InferenceService.testConnection() with the values of the form) and, for administrators only, the Shared with all users checkbox. The API key stays editable when its tab is not the one shown (the tab sheet disables the hidden tabs, so the dialog keeps its own apiKeyEditable flag), and Refresh of the model list keeps the model that was selected. AIPart / PhoneAIPart (the type column shows the name of the extension's provider, AITypes.label) list the user's AIs and the shared ones with the user's own Usage (tokens sent / generated); the edit and delete buttons are only shown for AIs the user owns (AIService.isOwnedByCurrentUser) and the add button only when AIService.canCreate(). The service refuses the same things itself. Rows of shared AIs have an info button (AILimitInfoDialog), and the owning administrator a Limits button (AILimitsDialog, AILimitService). AIPart also has a Usage per user button, visible to administrators only, that opens UsageDialog (UsageService.findAllUsages(): user, model, tokens sent / generated, requests, last used); the service checks the administrator itself.

Most forms save automatically: value change listeners call an autosave() method of the part (guarded so that loading values into the fields doesn't trigger a save). The story editor saves an edited part when the edit is closed (autosaveAndSwapToMarkdown) and before a generation starts (autosaveAndSwapAllToMarkdown). Entities held by the UI are detached copies - reload them through the service before changing them, and keep the object returned by save.
Vaadin component state may only be touched on a thread holding the session lock. The rules:
Long work (generation, summaries, backups, imports) runs on another thread; the UI thread returns immediately.
Updates from that thread go through ui.access(() - ...), with the UI captured on the UI thread (UI.getCurrent() is null elsewhere). UIPushGuard.push(ui) sends them right away.
Service calls on that thread need the user's request scope - capture ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.create() on the UI thread and wrap the work in InRequestScope (see The current user).

ThreadAccessDialog packages all of this for dialogs: run() starts runInThread() on a new thread in the request scope, and vaadinLocked(...) / vaadinLockedSync(...) run UI updates with ui.access / ui.accessSynchronously and push. ProgressBarDialog builds on it.

The story editor is the main example: startGeneration freezes the book window, calls StoryGenerationService.generateNextTurn with a GenerationListener, and every callback (onNodeCreated, onResponseChunk, onComplete...) updates the cards inside ui.access(...) and pushes.

Prefer Java components. When the browser has to do something (scroll positions, element sizes), the script is a static method of ui.JavascriptLibrary - UI classes don't call executeJs themselves. The element is passed explicitly ($0, not this), and a script that returns a value returns the PendingJavaScriptResult, read with .then(...); see UIUtils.getPositionAndSizeOfElement, the scroll handling in ManuscriptStoryPart and JavascriptLibrary.scrollTextAreaToBottom (the extension log is shown scrolled to its newest line). Extensions keep their own scripts.

There are three JavaScript modules, all documented in Custom components. src/main/frontend/chart-connector.js is loaded by ChartJs (@JsModule, with the npm package chart.js); it registers Chart.js and draws the configuration it gets from JavascriptLibrary.renderChart, taking the text and grid colors from the Lumo variables of the page.

src/main/frontend/treant-connector.js is loaded by TreantTree (@JsModule) together with the npm packages treant-js and raphael (@NpmPackage) and treant's CSS (@CssImport). It draws the story tree; TreantTree sends the tree as JSON and receives clicks back: node-click (a card was clicked, with the data-node-id of the card) and node-goto (an element with data-goto-id inside a card was clicked; the card itself is not clicked then). src/main/frontend/graph-connector.js is loaded by GraphView (npm package cytoscape).

ManuscriptTreePart has a search bar above the tree: an editable ComboBox (the last 15 searches; typed text is a custom value that the part sets as the value) and a button. A search calls ChatMessageService.searchFulltext and keeps the result as lastQuery and hitSnippets (part id → text around the match); renderTree then adds the CSS class search-hit (shared-styles.css) to the cards of the found parts and, in them, the snippet and a "Show in story" link (data-goto-id). Stretches of more than 20 parts that would be collapsed stay open when they contain a hit. The search is kept while the tab is open and repeated on every onTabEnter; load (opening the book) clears it.

The link fires NodeGotoEvent. onNodeGoto resolves the id among the messages of the book only, asks ChatMessageService.findLeafFor for the end of the branch to show, makes it the book's active leaf when it is not (ManuscriptDialog.save) and calls ManuscriptDialog.showMessage(id). That tells ManuscriptStoryPart which part to scroll to (scrollToMessageOnNextRender) and selects the story tab; entering the tab renders the story, which scrolls to the part (and flashes it) instead of restoring the saved scroll position.

Global styles are in src/main/frontend/styles/shared-styles.css (imported by AppShellConfig): spacing helpers, the loading indicator, the story text (.chat-message), the story tree (.Treant) and the utility classes (.text-secondary, .hint-text, .min-width-0...). The book style of the reader and editor (.manuscript-styles .chat-message-markdown) is in reading-mode-styles.css, imported separately by AppShellConfig. Components are styled by adding these classes (addClassName(CssStyles.TEXT_SECONDARY)), not with getStyle().set(...); keep that only for values computed at runtime (the combo box overlay width). A new class goes into the stylesheet and into CssStyles together. All vaadin-markdown elements wrap long lines (and break long words of paragraphs, code, headings, lists, quotes, tables and links) through the rules there, so a Markdown needs no extra call. Class names used from Java are constants in CssStyles; column widths and offsets in UIConstants. Use Lumo's CSS custom properties (--lumo-space-m, --lumo-contrast-10pct...) instead of fixed colors, so the dark theme stays consistent.

Styles of plugins are not in the stylesheet. Main and Viewer (the ApplicationEntryPoints) own a CssRegistry that injects the CSS returned by loaded extensions (ExtensionHasCss.getCss) as style elements and removes it when the extension is unloaded (Styles of a plugin).
