Arc Outline offers its outline as two sources about a book, so the user chooses how much the caller gets: arc-outline / outline (the arcs with their states, descriptions and chapters) and arc-outline / outline-with-notes (the same with the note of every arc and chapter).

Side Query lists all providers: the button with the plug icon above a tab opens a popover with a checkbox for each. Checked book sources are added to the system message after the lorebook; checked story part sources are asked for each story part in the Chat Logs range and put after the text of the part. The checked sources are stored in the options of the tab, a source that is gone is skipped until it comes back.

A plugin can bring a model API of its own. The user then creates an AI of the type Extension, chooses the provider of the plugin in the AI dialog, and the AI works like an OpenAI-compatible one: books use it, it is shared and limited, its usage is counted. The bundled Google Gemini plugin is the worked example.
Piece
What it is
AIType.EXTENSION
The type of such an AI. Stored as an ordinal like the others (1), so it must stay the last value.
ExtensionAI (ais_extension)

An AI subclass with one column, extensionId. Everything else the provider needs lives in getSettings(): the object under the key extensionId of the dynamic attributes, so there is no migration for it and it travels with the AI.
ExtensionAIFactory
What the plugin registers: its getExtensionId(), a getName() for the user, createInferenceService(ExtensionAI) and createForm(ExtensionAI).
ExtensionAIForm
The settings of the provider in the Per Type Settings tab of the dialog: getComponent(), validate() and apply(ExtensionAI).
InferenceServices
registerExtensionFactory / unregisterExtensionFactory, getExtensionFactory(id) and getExtensionFactories(), and forAI(ai), which asks the factory of an ExtensionAI.
The extension id is stored in every AI of the provider and never changes: use the symbolic name of the bundle (the Google plugin uses google-genai).
Register the factory in onExtensionLoad and take it back in onExtensionUnload, like the other registrations (see Plugin basics):

createForm is called by the AI dialog each time the user picks the provider (and when an existing AI is edited), with the ExtensionAI being edited, or a new one that only has the extension id. The form reads the AI's getSettings() and builds its fields (a FormLayout is the usual root; use @Configurable(preConstruction = true) to get Localization into the constructor). The dialog:
calls validate() before it saves or tests, and does not go on when it returns false - the form tells the user why (a notification);

calls apply(ai) on the AI it saves, and on a throw-away copy (a deep copy of the attributes with the values of the dialog, no id) when the user clicks Test Connection, which runs testConnection() of the service the factory creates for the copy. A form that lists models (a Refresh button) can create a service for such a copy itself and close it afterwards.

The general settings of the AI (name, context and response size, jailbreak, reasoning) stay with the dialog; the service reads them from the AI (getMaxContext(), getEnabledReasoning(), getReasoningEffort()...) and the protocol (TokenLimits).

The attributes are not encrypted. Keep an API key with inferenceServices.protectSecret(key) (AES with the installation key, the same as the API key column of an OpenAI-compatible AI) and read it with revealSecret, which returns null for a key from another installation. Never show a stored key: disable the field and offer a Reset button, as the bundled forms do.

Call AILimitService.check(ai, promptTokens, responseTokens) at the start of stream and infer, in the caller's thread: it throws InferenceException (NOT_AVAILABLE, LIMIT_REACHED) when an administrator's limit for the user forbids the request.

Call UsageService.record(ai, prefill, generated) once per request, whichever way it ends, with the numbers the API reported (otherwise your own estimate - TokenizerService.countTokensApprox). It needs the user: capture ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.create() in the thread that calls stream/infer and run the recording in InRequestScope.
Callbacks
countTokens is called very often (every part of the prompt): do not make a request for it. TokenizerService.countTokensApprox is local.

createInferenceService(ai) returns an InferenceService. InferenceServices.forAI calls it once and keeps the service in the AI (ExtensionAI.getInferenceServiceFactory() remembers which factory made it), exactly as for an OpenAI-compatible AI. Saving the AI in the dialog clears the cache (setAiType), so new settings reach the next service. Read the settings in the constructor: the service is not rebuilt per request.
Errors

Fail with InferenceException and the right Type (authentication, rate limit, context overflow...): the application has a localized text for each and InferenceErrors.describe adds the provider's message. Anything else is shown as an internal error.
Functions
Limits

Read UnmeteredScope.isActive() once, in the caller's thread, when the request starts. When it is true the application asks on its own account (the help assistant with an AI that is not shared or has no Apply limits): skip AILimitService.check and do not call UsageService.record for that request, however many rounds and threads it takes.

stream hands chunks one at a time: call onChunk(controller, type, text) and wait for controller.continueInference() before the next, then onCompletion(). ChunkType.REASONING is the thinking, shown apart from the answer. Check callback.isDead() and the CancellationToken between chunks and end with onCancel(). Cut a blocked read short by cancelling the HTTP call when the token is cancelled (the Google plugin does it with an OkHttp interceptor).

The core calls a service for many things (the generation, summaries, other plugins), so implement all of InferenceService that your API can do and throw UnsupportedOperationException for the rest, as the defaults do. What a service has to take care of itself, because nothing above it does:
Tokens
Unmetered requests
Usage

When a FunctionSet is passed, offer its definitions, run the calls the model makes with FunctionSet.call(...) (asynchronously, in the request scope), report each with onFunctionCall, ask again with the results, up to MAX_FUNCTION_ROUNDS. See callFunctions in the Google plugin.

l: When the plugin is not loaded
p: AIs are rows in the database: the AI of an unloaded plugin stays in the list (AITypes.label shows its provider name, or Extension: id) and works again when the plugin is loaded. In between:

InferenceServices.forAI(ai) returns null and drops a service cached from the unloaded plugin; so it does when the plugin was loaded again meanwhile, because the cached service was made by the old factory: the next call asks the new one.

forAIOrThrow(ai) throws InferenceException of the type EXTENSION_UNAVAILABLE ("The extension that provides this AI is not loaded...") and is what the generation steps and the summaries call. Code that has a sensible fallback (the token count in StorySupport) keeps using forAI and its null.
The AI dialog opens such an AI with a notice instead of the form, saves the general settings and leaves the settings of the plugin untouched.

Unregistering does not stop the services that exist. Close what they hold in onExtensionUnload (the Google factory keeps its services in a weak set and closes their clients) and let a closed service fail with EXTENSION_UNAVAILABLE.

AIDialog offers the type Extension only while a factory is registered (or when the AI being edited is one). The type of an existing AI cannot be changed, because the type decides the entity class. For the type Extension the dialog shows a Provider selector - preselected when only one plugin provides AIs, read-only when editing - and, under it, the form of the chosen provider and the Test Connection button. The methods that do this (addExtensionSettings, currentExtensionAI, testExtensionConnection...) are @PublicAPI like the rest of the dialog.
ApiException and IO failures as InferenceException.
Bundle start; the extension registers GoogleGenAiFactory and closes it on unload.

Cancellation. The SDK hides its HTTP call. Every request carries a header with the id of the run, an OkHttp interceptor stores the Call under it (and removes the header before the request leaves), and the CancellationToken cancels that call, so a generation stops at once even if Google is slow to send the next chunk.
Class
google-genai, "Google Gemini"; creates the services and keeps them (weakly) to close their clients.
GoogleGenAiActivator, GoogleGenAiExtension
GoogleGenAiErrors
GoogleGenAiFactory
GoogleGenAiForm
GoogleGenAiInferenceService
GoogleGenAiMessages
GoogleGenAiSettings
marginalia/plugins/google-genai uses the Google Gen AI Java SDK:
Role
stream, infer, function calls, JSON schema (responseJsonSchema), usage, limits, thinking (ThinkingConfig: a level for gemini-3*, a token budget for the others), safety settings, cancellation.
The fields, Refresh for the model list, validation, apply.

The payload as Gemini Contents: leading system messages are the system instruction, system messages later in the conversation become user messages, neighbouring messages of one role are one content, the results of the calls of one message are one content.
The settings of an AI (apiKey encrypted, model, baseUrl, requestTimeoutSeconds, maxRetries, safetyFiltersOff) read from ExtensionAI.getSettings().

Thought signatures. Gemini 3 refuses the next round of a function call unless the model's previous answer comes back with its thought signatures. The service therefore keeps the model's own Content (with the signature parts, without the thinking summaries) and puts it in front of the results of the calls, instead of rebuilding the turn from the LLMToolCalls.
Two things in it are worth copying:

l: Packaging a library only the plugin needs
p: The SDK is not a dependency of the application. The plugin's pom.xml lists it as a normal dependency and embeds it:

maven-bundle-plugin puts the JARs inside the bundle and adds them to Bundle-ClassPath. The framework is started with org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=* and the application's class loader as the parent, so a class the application has wins over an embedded copy (the bundle looks in its own JARs only for what the application does not have). Hence:

libraries the application ships already (OkHttp, Jackson, Kotlin, Gson, slf4j, jspecify) are exclusions of the SDK and provided for compiling - the SDK then runs on the application's versions (OkHttp 4.12, Jackson 2.22), which must stay compatible with the ones the SDK was built for;
nothing is imported (Import-Package lists only the negated own package), so no package of an embedded library has to be exported by the application;
the JAR is large (about 14 MB: the SDK, Guava, Protobuf, google-auth).

The plugin has unit tests for the pure parts (GoogleGenAiMessagesTest, GoogleGenAiErrorsTest, GoogleGenAiSettingsTest); the core has ExtensionAIFactoryTest, ExtensionAICrudTest, ExtensionAIGenerationTest and AIDialogExtensionTest with a fake factory, which is the way to test your own provider's contract without a plugin.

c:
<Embed-Dependency>*;scope=compile|runtime;inline=false</Embed-Dependency>
<Embed-Transitive>true</Embed-Transitive>
<Import-Package>!com.github.enerccio.marginalia.extensions.googlegenai.*</Import-Package>

p: This page builds a small plugin from scratch - Bookmarks, which lets you bookmark story parts - and then walks through three bundled plugins: Chapter Marker, the smallest one that changes the UI, Author's Note, which changes the prompt sent to the model, and Chinese localization, which adds a language and no code besides the texts. Together they use everything from the previous pages: a bundle, decorators reading arguments, locals and fields, data in attributes, generation listeners, and cleanup on unload.
What it does:
every story part's menu gets a Toggle bookmark item,
bookmarked parts are marked with ★ in the story sidebar,
the bookmark is stored on the part, so it's kept in backups and copied by Branch Story.
The Bookmarks example: a bookmarked part in the sidebar and the Toggle bookmark menu item
The plugin compiles against the application's classes, installed in the local Maven repository:

c:
mvn -N install                  # in the repository root: the parent POM the application's POM refers to
cd marginalia
mvn install -DskipTests

p: Copy marginalia/plugins/chaptermarker/pom.xml and change:

groupId to com.example.marginalia, artifactId to bookmarks, and replace the parent (the plugin is outside the repository) with a version of its own, e.g. 1.0.1; the dependency on marginalia then needs the version of the installed application instead of ${project.version},
Bundle-Activator to com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.BookmarksActivator,
Import-Package to !com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.* and Export-Package to com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.*.
Keep the rest - the provided dependencies, the AspectJ plugin (for @Configurable) and the bundle plugin. See Plugin basics → pom.xml for what each part does.

c:
bookmarks/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/example/marginalia/bookmarks/
    ├── BookmarksActivator.java
    └── BookmarksExtension.java

p: It only registers the extension:
How it works:

Two decorators. menuDecorator runs after ChatMessageCard.createMenuItems() - the card's constructor calls it, so every card gets the item. sidebarDecorator runs after ManuscriptStoryPart.createSidebarButton(msg, orderId, dbId), which renderStoryContent() calls for each part of the branch.

Reaching the components. The menu is the card's field hamburgerMenu; the sidebar button is the local variable sidebarBtn of createSidebarButton, the part is its argument msg. Both names are checked before use (hasLocalVariable) or fail with a logged warning if the application changes.
Adding once. ComponentUtil.setData(menu, MENU_ITEM_KEY, item) marks the menu; a second call for the same menu does nothing.

Data. The bookmark is one boolean under the plugin's key in the part's attributes. The click listener reads the card's message field at click time and reloads the part (chatMessageService.find(id)) before changing it, because the card's copy may be stale (Extended attributes).

Redrawing. After saving it calls the story part's private renderStoryContent() through callReflectiveMethod, reaching the outer ManuscriptStoryPart through the inner class's this$0 field. The redraw runs createSidebarButton again, so the sidebar decorator adds the ★.

Unloading. Decorators are unregistered; menu items are removed from the tracked menus inside each menu's own ui.access(...), because they belong to other users' sessions (Extending the UI → Unloading). Sidebar buttons lose their ★ on the next redraw.
Errors. onExtensionLoad runs without a UI, so it throws instead of opening an error dialog; Marginalia logs the error and unloads the extension again.

With Chapter Marker installed too, both plugins decorate createSidebarButton, and decorators run in the order the plugins were loaded. Bookmarks prefixes the text, so it works after Chapter Marker; Chapter Marker replaces the text of chapter parts, so the ★ of a bookmarked chapter is lost when Chapter Marker runs second (and when the part is edited).

Load target/bookmarks-1.3.0.jar in Admin → Extensions and open a book (books that were already open need to be closed and opened again). Open a part's menu, choose Toggle bookmark - the part's sidebar entry gets the ★.

If nothing appears, look in the log for Mod 'com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.BookmarksExtension$...' skipped on ... (a name that doesn't exist) or Unhandled exception in extension .... The lines of the extension itself (here log.error(Cannot toggle bookmark, e)) are in Admin → Extensions → Log of the extension, see Logging.

c:
cd bookmarks
mvn package                     # target/bookmarks-1.3.0.jar

p: Show the bookmarks in a tab of their own: decorate renderStoryContent() and add a tab to leftBar, like Side Query (A tab next to the story).
Put bookmarked parts into the prompt: register a generation listener, like Author's Note (Walkthrough: Author's Note, Generation events).

marginalia/plugins/chaptermarker turns the story sidebar into a table of contents: a part whose text contains a Markdown heading is shown as 5. Chapter 3: The Harbour, highlighted. It has two classes and no data of its own - the heading is part of the story text.
ChapterMarkingActivator is the same as the Bookmarks activator. ChapterMarkingExtension registers two decorators in onExtensionLoad.
Labelling the sidebar - after ManuscriptStoryPart.createSidebarButton(msg, orderId, dbId):
It remembers the button's original text, the order and the part's uuid on the button (ComponentUtil.setData(...)), then sets the chapter title and style if the part has a heading.
Following edits - after ManuscriptStoryPart$ChatMessageCard.autosaveAndSwapToMarkdown(), which saves an edited part:

It finds the sidebar button whose stored uuid matches the edited part and relabels it - or restores the original text when the heading was removed. The data stored on the button in the first decorator is what makes this possible without rebuilding the sidebar.
Unloading unregisters both decorators. Labels already changed stay until the story is redrawn, which is acceptable here: they're just text.
What to take from it:
arguments, locals and fields are all used, each with the right accessor;
primitive arguments are read with the primitive type;
a fallback for the local variable keeps the plugin working if the variable is renamed;
component data (ComponentUtil) carries state from one hook to another.

The other bundled plugins build on the same pieces: Reviewer and Side Query add menu items, tabs, settings panels and call the model (Extending the UI); Lorebook VCS stores larger data in a lorebook's attributes (Extended attributes); Lore Generator adds a button to every row of the lorebook grid and streams a generation from the model into a dialog; Author's Note, below, changes the prompt of every generation.
Adds the tab on leave of ManuscriptStoryPart.renderStoryContent() (like Side Query) and registers the listener.
AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD comes when the list of chat messages for the model is complete; what the listener sets is what is sent:
AuthorsNoteData
AuthorsNoteExtension
AuthorsNoteService
AuthorsNoteView

BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT comes before the generation decides how much of the story fits into the context. The listener loads the note, keeps it in the generation's properties and reserves its tokens, so the story gets less room:
build a new payload and setPayload(...) it instead of changing the list you got.
chain.next() in finally - the generation waits for every listener;
Class
Does
Generation events explains the payload, the choice of the events and reserving tokens in detail.
Hooking into generation - onExtensionLoad registers two listeners next to the decorator and keeps the registrations:
listeners are global, so act only on the data of the book being generated;
Loads and saves the data, counts the note's tokens, inserts the note into a payload.

marginalia/plugins/authorsnote sends a per-book note to the model with every generation: an Author's Note tab next to the story outline edits it, a generation listener inserts it into the prompt. It shows the one thing decorators can't do - change what the model gets.
pass state from one event to the next in event.getProperties(), under your package name;
reserve the tokens of what you add (PrePromptData.reservedTokens) before the budget is computed, and add to the reservation instead of overwriting it;
The note: on/off, the text, a private scratchpad, the insertion depth and the role. Stored in the book's attributes under the package name.
The sidebar tab with a token estimate of the note; every change is saved right away.
Unloading unregisters both listeners besides removing the decorator and the tabs - a listener left registered would keep changing the prompts of every user.
What to take from it:

marginalia/plugins/chineselocalization adds Simplified Chinese to the language selector of the workspace. It is the smallest possible plugin - no decorators, no UI, no data - and shows the third optional interface of an extension besides ExtensionHasCss: ExtensionHasLocalization.

The pom.xml is the one of the other plugins without what the plugin doesn't use: it needs only the application (classes classifier) and the Felix framework, both provided, and the bundle plugin - no AspectJ, since there is no @Configurable class, and no Vaadin.
The extension implements MarginaliaExtension as always - both methods stay empty, there is nothing to set up - and ExtensionHasLocalization:

Marginalia calls getLocalizationBundles() right after onExtensionLoad and registers the bundles in Localization; when the extension is unloaded they are removed again. Nothing else is needed: the language shows up in the LanguageSelector of every workspace the next time it is attached, and a user who picks it is shown the whole UI in it after the page reloads.
The bundle extends LocalizationBundleBase: loadMessages() fills the texts with setValue, the other methods describe the language.
What to take from it:

a language code is the identity of a bundle: only one bundle per code exists. A second one is refused (and logged) - an extension can add languages but not replace the English texts or the Japanese ones of the application;

a bundle doesn't have to be complete: a key it lacks is shown in the default language, and the application logs a warning listing the missing keys when the bundle is registered. A plugin built for an older version keeps working when the application adds keys;

the placeholders (%s, %d) of a text must match the English text in number and order of their types, the application formats the text with them. Copy LocalizationBundleEN as the start and translate in place;
the bundle is created in getLocalizationBundles(), and the texts are looked up when needed, so a plugin's own user interface that uses Localization gets the right language without more work;
unloading the plugin makes sessions that used its language fall back to the default one - nothing is lost, the user's setting stays and works again when the plugin is loaded.
To try it, build and load it like any plugin (Build and load): in Admin → Extensions load chineselocalization-1.3.0.jar, then pick 中文（简体） in the language selector.

c:
chineselocalization/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/github/enerccio/marginalia/extensions/chineselocalization/
    ├── ChineseLocalizationActivator.java   registers the extension service
    ├── ChineseLocalizationExtension.java   returns the bundle
    └── LocalizationBundleZH.java           the texts

p: Marginalia's tests are integration tests first: most of them start the real Spring XML configuration against a throwaway SQLite database and talk to a fake OpenAI-compatible server. They need no network, no model and no API key, and they run in CI on every push and pull request. This page explains the test infrastructure and how to add tests.
All test code is in marginalia/src/test/java/com/github/enerccio/marginalia/; paths below are relative to it.
From marginalia/:

Setting
Why
-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading -Djdk.attach.allowAttachSelf=true
RuntimeInstrumentationTest installs the ByteBuddy agent into the test JVM.
marginalia.test.home=target/test-home
Folder for the test databases (see The application folder).
Reports are written to target/surefire-reports/; the CI job uploads them as an artifact when a test fails.

mvn test -Dtest=LorebookActivationTest       # one class
mvn test -Dtest='Backup*Test'                # a pattern
mvn test -Dtest='MacroRenderingTest#name'    # one method

p: Tests run from IntelliJ IDEA like any JUnit test, with two conditions:
the classes must be compiled with AspectJ (see Building from source), otherwise UI classes and @Configurable beans miss their dependencies;
add -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading -Djdk.attach.allowAttachSelf=true to the VM options of the JUnit run configuration template if you run RuntimeInstrumentationTest.
Without marginalia.test.home the tests fall back to target/test-home relative to the working directory, so run them with marginalia/ as the working directory (IntelliJ's default for the module).

Spring caches the application context, and with it the database, for the whole test run. All test classes that use MarginaliaTestBase share one SQLite database. Write tests so that they don't depend on what else is in it:

When a test really needs an empty database or changes global state, mark it with @DirtiesContext. The next test then gets a new context with a new folder and database:
A new context costs a few seconds (Spring, Hibernate, Flyway), so use it sparingly.

Each context gets its own folder under target/test-home/ with the database, data, backup and extension folders. They are not deleted after the run, so you can open a test database with any SQLite tool after a failure. mvn clean or deleting target/test-home removes them.

test/llm/MockLLMServer is a small OpenAI-compatible server on 127.0.0.1 with a random port, built on the JDK's HttpServer. One shared server lives for the whole test JVM (MockLLMServer.shared()); each test gets its own scenario with its own base URL, http://127.0.0.1:port/scenario-id/v1. A provider created with createAI() points to the test's scenario, so tests never see each other's requests or answers.
It answers:
Endpoint
GET /models
The scenario's model list (default mock-model; change with llm.models(...)).
POST /chat/completions
Streaming (server-sent events) and non-streaming chat completions.
Chat completions are answered in this order:
queued responses - llm.enqueue(...) or llm.reply(text), one per request;
the responder function - llm.respondWith(request - ...), if set and it returns a response;
the fallback - llm.fallback(...);
otherwise HTTP 500 no response programmed.
MockLLMResponse builds one answer:

waitFor(latch) is the tool for "while generating" states: the request is received, the pipeline waits for the stream, and the test can stop the generation or inspect the state before releasing the latch.

The openai-java client retries 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses. A queued error response is consumed once per attempt, so enqueue it several times (or use fallback) when a test expects the error to reach Marginalia. The server closes the connection after every response, so a retry never reuses a stale pooled connection.

c:
MockLLMResponse.text("Hello world")                        // one content chunk
MockLLMResponse.chunks("Hel", "lo").chunkDelay(ofMillis(50))
MockLLMResponse.split(longText, 20)                        // chunks of 20 characters
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("thinking")   // reasoning chunks first
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("...").reasoningField("reasoning")  // instead of reasoning_content
MockLLMResponse.text("cut").finishReason("length")
MockLLMResponse.error(429, "slow down")                    // OpenAI-style error body
MockLLMResponse.chunks("a", "b", "c").disconnectAfter(2)   // stream ends abruptly
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").usage(120, 8)               // token counts in the last chunk (only if asked for)
MockLLMResponse.text("late").waitFor(latch)                // held until the latch is released
MockLLMResponse.toolCall("add", "{\"a\":1}")               // the model calls a function; .andToolCall(...) adds one

The instruct tests check the bytecode that makes @Extendable methods extensible (see Plugin development):

ExtendableMethodVisitorTest transforms fixture classes from instruct/fixture/ with instruct/Instrumenter - the same transformation the agent applies, without an agent - and checks that the result verifies, keeps the class schema, behaves like the original and exposes arguments and locals to decorators.
RuntimeInstrumentationTest installs the real agent into the test JVM and checks classes loaded both before and after the installation (fixture/agent/).

ExtensionVerifierTest runs the extension verification on the extensions of fixture/verify/VerifyFixtures (decorators that are valid, ask for things that don't exist, or can't be followed) against the decorated VerifyTarget. Their class files are packed into a JAR on the fly and served by a stand-in Bundle. Decorators must be anonymous classes with the context calls inside them, as in a real extension - a decorator that delegates to a helper class would not be checked.

PublicAPISignatureTest checks the @PublicAPI of every instrumented method of every @Extendable class of the application against the compiled classes (target/classes). It reads them with ByteBuddy's type pool and the local variable table (PublicAPISignatures), so the application classes are not loaded or initialized, and it needs the classes compiled by ajc like the application. A failure names the method and prints the annotation the method needs.

The fixtures are compiled with the same -parameters and preserveAllLocals options as the application; if you change the compiler settings in pom.xml, these tests tell you whether extensions still see names of arguments and locals.

Marginalia is built once as a WAR and then shipped in two forms: a Docker image for servers and a desktop app with its own Java runtime and Jetty. This page describes how each is built, what CI does, and how a release is made. For everyday builds see Building from source.

mvn package in marginalia/ produces target/marginalia-1.3.0.war (see Building the application). The WAR always runs in Vaadin production mode: build-frontend writes the production flow-build-info.json into it, and a development one left in src/main/resources is never packaged (see Development and production mode).
One resource differs between a development build and a release build:
File
Development
Release
log4j.properties
src/main/resources/ - com.github.enerccio at DEBUG
src/main/resources-release/ - everything at INFO, no story content in the log

The build decides, not the packaging: IDE runs and mvn jetty:run use target/classes, which has the development file. The WAR plugin adds src/main/resources-release/ to WEB-INF/classes and leaves the development file out, so every WAR from mvn package - the Docker image, the desktop profile, a WAR deployed by hand - logs at INFO.

The user manual is packed too: resources in marginalia/pom.xml copies the Markdown pages of manual/user (no pictures, never filtered) to classpath:/manual/, where ManualService reads them (see Services). The source folder is outside marginalia/, so a build that copies only marginalia/src must copy manual/user as well, as both Dockerfiles do (/build/manual/user); without it the WAR builds, with an empty manual.

The build also needs the Git history: git-commit-id-plugin writes the commit id and the closest tag into git.properties, and the WAR filters them into its build info. Build from a clone, not from a source archive.

The app image: Marginalia.app (macOS), Marginalia/Marginalia.exe (Windows), Marginalia/bin/Marginalia (Linux).
The portable folder: bin/marginalia, bin/marginalia.bat, app/, server/, runtime/.

DesktopLauncher is the main class of the app image and of the portable scripts. It depends on the JDK only and starts Jetty in its own JVM by loading start.jar through a class loader, so it never needs Jetty on the classpath and never ends up in the WAR. On start it:
resolves the data folder home/.marginalia (--home sets user.home) and redirects its output to .marginalia/desktop/logs/;
finds server/ next to or above the launcher JAR (jpackage places app content differently per OS);
checks the port (default 8765): if Marginalia already runs there, it just opens the browser; if another program uses it, it picks a free port (unless --port was given);

writes a Jetty base into .marginalia/desktop/jetty-base/ (modules ee11-*, webapps/ROOT.xml pointing to the WAR, a persistent work folder) - so the installation itself can stay read-only, e.g. inside a signed app bundle;
starts Jetty on 127.0.0.1, waits up to three minutes for the start page, then shows the tray icon (or a small window where there is no system tray) and opens the browser.

The JVM options needed by the extension agent (-Djdk.attach.allowAttachSelf=true -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading, plus --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED for SQLite) are passed by jpackage --java-options and by the scripts in bin/. The scripts add MARGINALIA_JAVA_OPTS. Keep the three places in sync - the desktop.javaOptions property and both scripts. On macOS, -Dapple.awt.UIElement=true keeps the app out of the Dock; it lives only in the tray.
Command-line options are described in Desktop app.

jlink and jpackage only build for the platform they run on, so each operating system and CPU is built on its own machine. CI does this with a build matrix (below). Locally you get only your own platform.

If you add a dependency that needs a JDK module not in desktop.modules (a ClassNotFoundException or NoClassDefFoundError for a java.* / javax.* / jdk.* class in the desktop log only), add the module to the list. jdeps --print-module-deps on the WAR's libraries helps to find it.

The app images are not signed or notarized. macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen warn on the first start; the Desktop app page tells users how to get past it. Signing would be added to the jpackage call (--mac-sign, --mac-signing-key-user-name...) and, for Windows, as a separate signtool step in CI.

Each plugin in marginalia/plugins/ is a Maven project with bundle packaging (Apache Felix maven-bundle-plugin) that depends on the application's classes JAR with provided scope. They are built against one exact version of the application:

server.yml builds all the plugins against the freshly installed application and attaches the JARs to the release of a v* tag; the Docker image doesn't contain them (server users put them into data folder/extensions or install them in Admin → Extensions). When you change application classes that a plugin uses (decorated @Extendable methods, UI classes, services), rebuild the plugin and test it against the new application. See Plugin development.

p: marginalia/plugins/Dockerfile is a separate build environment for the plugins, used by servers that build from source (and by anyone without a local JDK/Maven). Its builder stage (Maven + JDK 25, like the main Dockerfile) installs the application into the image's local Maven repository (with -Dvaadin.skip=true: the plugins need only the classes JAR, so the frontend is not built, see Building) and builds every plugin against it; the final stage is a small Alpine image that holds the JARs in /jars. Its command copies them to /output, replacing the *.jar files there, so the compose file (marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml, build context ../..) mounts marginalia/plugins/build as /output. The plugins are built one after the other and none of them needs another one installed first (the Lore Generator finds the Name generator at run time, not at build time). The Name generator's build clones the sources of its names from GitHub (the Maven image has git); without network it keeps the tables committed in the repository, see its README:
The JARs are not copied while the image is built, because a bind mount exists only when a container runs.

rebuild.sh (Linux, macOS) and rebuild.bat (Windows) in the repository root update a Docker server: when the upstream branch has new commits they stop the container, git pull, build the plugins as above, copy the JARs into data/extensions (overwriting the installed ones; extensions load on start) and run docker compose up -d --build. --force skips the check for new commits. The two scripts must be kept in step; .gitattributes keeps the shell script on LF and the batch file on CRLF.

Version. Set the new version in the parent pom.xml in the repository root and in the parent of the application and the plugin POMs - mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=version -DgenerateBackupPoms=false in the root does all of it (the plugins' marginalia dependency follows ${project.version}). The archive names and the app version shown by the OS come from the POM, not from the tag, so the two must match: for a v* tag the test job first checks that the tag is v + the POM version and fails otherwise, so no archives are built or attached. jpackage on macOS requires a version of the form x.y.z with x ≥ 1.

Database. If the release changes the schema, check that the migrations upgrade a database of the previous release (keep a copy of one around) - FlywayMigrationTest covers only the migrations themselves.
Manual. Update the manual for user-visible changes, run tools/retype_build.sh, commit docs/.

Create the GitHub release for the tag (by hand or gh release create v1.3.0) with the release notes. desktop.yml attaches the ten desktop archives when its matrix finishes, server.yml the WAR and the plugin JARs and pushes the Docker image - whichever finishes first creates the release if it doesn't exist yet (softprops/action-gh-release).
Plugins. The plugin versions must match the application version (point 1); the JARs are attached automatically.

p: The manual is part of the repository: Retype reads manual/ and writes the static site to docs/ (configured in retype.yml). GitHub Pages serves docs/ from the master branch, so the published manual changes when a commit with a new docs/ reaches master. Rebuild and commit docs/ in the same change as the sources - see Building the manual.

Contributions are welcome: bug reports, fixes, new features, extensions, and corrections to this manual. This page describes how to report a problem, how changes are made and what a pull request should contain.
Marginalia is released under the MIT License. By contributing you agree that your contribution is released under the same license.
Open an issue on GitHub. For a bug, include:
what you did, what happened and what you expected;
the version (desktop app archive name, or the commit for a Docker server) and how you run it;
the inference provider type and model, if the problem is about generation (never your API key);
the relevant part of the log - see Where are the logs?. Logs may contain story text; remove what you don't want to share.
Security problems (access to other users' data, login, cookies) should not be reported in a public issue - contact the maintainer privately through GitHub first.
TODO.md is the list of planned work for the first release, ordered by priority. Items marked 🧩 are good candidates for an extension instead of a change to the core.

For anything larger than a small fix, open an issue (or comment on an existing one) first and describe what you plan. Some features belong in an extension rather than in the core - see Plugin development.
Read Architecture and the page about the area you are changing.
Set up the build and make sure mvn test passes on a clean checkout - see Building from source.
Fork the repository and create a branch from master with a short descriptive name (fix-summary-prompt, lorebook-tag-filter).
Make the change, with tests where the area is testable (see Testing).
Run mvn test in marginalia/. If you touched a plugin or classes plugins use, build the plugins too.
Start Marginalia and try the change in the browser - most of the application is UI, which the tests don't cover.
Update the manual if users or developers will notice the change (see Documentation).
Push and open a pull request against master.

CI runs the tests and builds the desktop app on all platforms for every pull request that changes marginalia/ (see Continuous integration). A pull request is merged when CI is green and the change has been reviewed.
Commit messages follow the style already in the history: one line, lowercase, starting with a verb in the imperative, class and method names in backticks, related changes separated by a semicolon:
Common verbs: add, fix, update, remove, refactor, rename, migrate, handle. Mention the issue number when the commit fixes one (... (#17)).

Keep commits focused - one fix or one step of a feature per commit, not a mix of a feature, a reformat and an unrelated fix. Don't commit generated or local files: target/, src/main/frontend/generated/, src/main/bundles/, flow-build-info.json in src/main/resources and .idea/ are ignored by Git for this reason.

p: A good pull request:
does one thing, and says in the description what changed and why, with the issue it fixes;
for a UI change, includes a screenshot or a short description of what to click to see it;
adds or updates tests where it can, and passes mvn test;
adds a Flyway migration for every entity change (see Database & migrations) - never edit a migration that is already in master;
updates the manual;
doesn't change formatting of code it doesn't otherwise touch.
There is no formatter configuration in the repository; match the code around your change. In short:
Java 25. Modern language features (records, switch expressions, pattern matching, text blocks, var where the type is obvious) are welcome.
4 spaces, no tabs; opening braces on the same line; lines up to about 120 characters.
Javadoc on classes and on public methods whose purpose isn't obvious from the name. Write why and the contract (what null means, which thread, which transaction), not a restatement of the signature.

Logging through SLF4J (private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class)), with {} placeholders. Story content, prompts and lore are logged at DEBUG only; API keys and passwords never. Plugins don't use LoggerFactory: they take the logger from OsgiService.createLogger(bundle) so their lines reach the extension log (Logging).
Return null for "not found" where the existing service API does (find, findForUser), and keep that consistent within a class.

Entities keep their historical names: a book is Manuscript, a part is ChatMessage, an inference provider is AI. Use the user-facing words (book, part, inference provider) in UI text, the manual and log messages.
Services are an interface in domain/service and an implementation NameImpl in domain/service/impl, registered in the Spring XML (see Services).
UI classes: a tab of the book window is ManuscriptNamePart, a dialog NameDialog, a reusable component in ui/components or ui/widgets.
Transactions live on services (@CommonTx, @CommonTxReadOnly), never on UI classes. Entities held by the UI are detached; reload them through the service before changing them.
The current user comes from the session-scoped User bean; services check ownership (findForUser) - the UI must not be the only thing protecting other users' data.

UI text is never hard-coded: add a key to loc/L.java and the text to loc/LocalizationBundleEN.java (and to LocalizationBundleJP.java and to the Chinese plugin's LocalizationBundleZH.java; a language without the key shows the English text), and use loc.getValue(L.KEY) (see User interface).
Threads: long work runs off the UI thread, and UI updates go through ui.access(...) (see Background work and push).

Extension points: methods that extensions decorate are @Extendable, and each of them declares its signature with @PublicAPI (PublicAPISignatureTest fails when a method has none or the annotation is out of date). Renaming or removing such a method, its parameters or its local variables breaks plugins - update the annotation, check the bundled plugins and mention the change in the pull request (see The public API and Keeping hooks working).
Schema: every entity change comes with a migration; Hibernate only validates the schema.
Use JUnit Jupiter and AssertJ, the test bases and the fake LLM server; no real network calls. See the checklist for a new test.
The manual you are reading is in manual/ (Markdown for Retype); docs/ is the generated site.

Change the Markdown in manual/, then run tools/retype_build.sh (retype build with the project version and commit in the site) and commit docs/ in the same pull request. Never edit files in docs/ by hand.
Preview with retype start.

Write for the reader of that part: the User guide talks about what users see and click (UI names in italics, no class names), the developer guide about code (paths relative to the main package, class names in backticks).

Screenshots go to manual/images/. When a page needs a screenshot you can't make, link the path anyway and add a line to TODO.IMAGES.md describing what it should show. Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks, not images.

The screenshots are retaken with the scripted environment in the screenshots/ folder (its own data folder, a fake model server and headless Chrome, so no API key and no personal data), described in screenshots/SCREENSHOTS.md: all pictures show the same dataset, and a single picture can be retaken from the step backup it belongs to.
A screenshot that shows a third-party picture needs a credit on the Credits page (author, source, license, changes), and must be shared under the license of the picture.

The class labels on dev-ui-map-book.png and dev-ui-map-workspace.png are drawn by tools/annotate_ui_maps.py (needs Pillow) onto a plain screenshot saved as dev-ui-map-name-not-annotated.png next to it. After the screen changes, take a new plain screenshot, adjust the coordinates at the top of the script if something moved, and run it.

Every developer page has verified (the commit it was last checked against the code) and covers (the code it describes) in its front matter. python3 tools/check_dev_docs.py lists the pages whose covered code changed since then (-v names modified files, --check fails when any page is behind). After you review a page, mark it with --stamp page.md in a commit of its own. When a page starts describing other code, extend its covers.
Bugs you find while writing documentation are reported as an issue (see Reporting bugs and ideas).

New features that not every user needs - and anything experimental - are often better as an extension than as a change to the core. An extension can be developed and released on its own, and doesn't need a pull request at all. If you want it bundled with Marginalia in marginalia/plugins/, open an issue first. See Plugin development and the example plugin.
